Recent advancements in machine learning, particularly with graph neural networks, have led to significant growth in subspace learning.  A particular type of neural network called the linear scan graph neural network has been proposed to learn a subspace by processing data.  We develop a comprehensive framework for analyzing the linear scan graph neural network and demonstrate that under specific conditions, it converges to a solution that minimizes a particular objective function in an extended objective space.  We also establish that this convergence occurs at a linear rate within a naturally defined objective space for these networks.  A particular application of this framework yields a subspace method that outperforms established subspace methods, including those based on ridge regression and semi-supervised learning.  We also identify conditions under which this linear scan graph neural network is robust to graph perturbations.  We complement our theoretical findings by conducting experiments on various datasets, which showcase its computational efficiency and ability to generalize effectively.

This paper completes our approach to examining the completeness of Sidon sets in the finite affine plane. We demonstrate that the completeness problem for convex Sidon sets can be resolved using hyperbolas and ellipses, while we infer that parabolic arcs might not be feasible. We also establish a criterion for a convex curve to host comprehensive convex Sidon sets, and use this criterion to analyze certain curves under various metric definitions. Furthermore, we find new instances of complete convex Sidon sets using this criterion, including a large collection where points maintain a convex position, x-coordinates form a complete Sidon set in integers, and y-coordinates consist of constant multiples of integers.

A method to dynamically adjust the sampling likelihood of entries in a sparse binary matrix is proposed, with the sampling probability distribution being non-uniform. This approach, which leverages a geometric probability model, is compared to uniform sampling through simulations. The comparison focuses on estimating the sparsity of a binary matrix and reveals that geometric non-uniform sampling significantly improves estimation accuracy and reduces bias compared to uniform sampling. Furthermore, the researcher outlines a basic framework for non-uniform estimation bias correction and demonstrates its applicability in various contexts, such as estimating the total number of entities from partially observed relationships.

A comprehensive method is presented for adjusting PDFs to a specified perturbative scale and determining their evolution across different scales using DGLAP evolution. This process involves incorporating numerical artifacts from discrete proton grid spacing into the PDF formula. Effectively eliminating these artifacts requires including logarithmic terms that result from UV/IR mixing between the proton's UV and IR domains. These additional logarithmic terms are not merely technical corrections but also influence the PDF's UV evolution, thereby impacting the fit of other PDFs. This formalism was tested by deriving a NLO log-UV-squared-resummed log-UV-singlet-proton PDF, incorporating QED effects, and demonstrating its convergence with a standard DGLAP-evolved PDF. This new PDF can be utilized in high-energy photon-photon collision calculations involving virtual photons, as well as in calculations of rapidity divergence in gluon-gluon and photon-photon collisions.

Our open-source data mining and analysis suite, ELKI, enables efficient exploration of various distance functions through numerous parallel algorithms, which speed up computation by using multiple cores on a single node system. By integrating diverse algorithms and facilitating rapid testing of numerous methods on different datasets, our system supports both educational purposes and research needs, as evidenced by its widespread adoption of over 800,000 downloads. This paper outlines the design and implementation of our suite, highlighting its ability to scale across multiple nodes using a distributed framework, while providing a substantial library of distance aggregation functions and analysis tools to facilitate the comparison of various spatial data structures and distance metrics on multiple CPUs or nodes simultaneously.

We've developed an approach to produce the spectral patterns of microcombs on a numerical platform. By utilizing a transfer matrix, we can calculate the spectrum of a microcomb when given the spacing of the pump-sidebands. Next, we determine the amplitude and phase relationships among the modes through a coupled-mode equation. Ultimately, our results align with theoretical predictions in the appropriate limit and our method can be applied to compute the spectrum of a microcomb when provided with the amplitudes and phases of the pump-sidebands. Furthermore, our approach allows for the calculation of various microcomb characteristics such as optical transmission, power distribution, and noise.

For any infinite discrete abelian group G, its power group G^X has a randomly selected subgroup that is both characteristically mixed and faithful, where X has to be of sufficient cardinality for the effect to be observable. This result extends previous findings that established similar results for infinite finite groups and proved that these selected subgroups are actually normal.

Analyzing neural networks in a fixed input support is challenging due to their eigenvalues lacking a clear spectral gap, complicating convergence and limit characterizations. We introduce a spectral filtering technique for the neural tangent kernel that targets the quasi neural network's behavior, where certain parameters scale proportionally with the number of weights. By applying an eigenvalue-based filter to the neural tangent kernel, we isolate only those eigenvalues capable of creating a spectral gap. Through an variational principle, we establish that the filtered kernel's largest eigenvalue decays at a rate of O(1/sqrt(N)), enabling a characterization of the filtered kernel's limiting behavior. This new method can be generalized to other types of neural networks and provides a straightforward way to construct a spectral gap for the neural tangent kernel.

A key aspect of bulk entropies, the requirement of mutual information non-negativity, necessitates a similar property of boundary entropies. This requirement necessitates a similar non-negative quantity in the form of $S_{AA'} + S_{BB'} + S_{AA'BB'}$, leading to a general method for calculating Renyi generalizations of this quantity. With this tool, we establish a negative lower bound for entanglement of mutual information for multiple regions in the case of complex shapes. A related quantity, entanglement of mutual information normalized by dimension, has a similar requirement to be non-negative in bulk, which results in a specific requirement for the same quantity on the boundary to have a non-negative minimum in a particular order. This leads to a specific result that a $2^k$-th root of the aforementioned quantity is maximum in the boundary.

Probabilities of local states in a one-dimensional quantum state of the Heisenberg spin chain are calculated using the Heisenberg equation of motion. A probabilistic interpretation of the branching rule for the SOS model of ADO is developed. Local state probabilities are expressed in terms of symmetric functions. A connection between the Heisenberg equation of motion and the master equation of the SOS model is established. This enables using known properties of symmetric functions to compute time-evolved local probabilities.

We investigated how to improve four distinct signal recovery algorithms, which employ the $\ell_1$-norm to reconstruct a sparsity signal from underdetermined measurements. These algorithms, including Iterative Reweighted Least Squares (IRLS), were initially stabilized using a specific procedure to ensure their convergence. We combined this stabilization with four more recent methods, resulting in a novel IRLS approach. The result was a significant increase in the algorithm's performance, specifically its convergence rate, as demonstrated numerically.

We have tested the effectiveness of various final image creation algorithms on a set of 1000 simulated star observations, and compared them to those of galaxy simulations, which were also run for 1000 final images. The most common post-processing techniques, such as median and clipped-mean, were found to produce poor results for star profiles, as they don't maintain a consistent point spread function. These algorithms however produced reasonable galaxy images. In contrast, our developed sigma-clipping method, which involves multiple passes and final image creation from individual fits, performed well for both star and galaxy simulations, yielding more accurate and consistent images. Accurate star profile restoration is essential for a proper image calibration and is critical for a precise measurement of galaxy images.

We introduce chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution with reflection and link it to the surface of an imaginary Shimer model of sand. This connects to a theory by Barysakov, Baryakovskaia and Shephard. These findings allow us to examine imaginary Schramm-Löwner evolution when the temperature parameter is a rational number of the form 4k/n. Furthermore, this extends Barysakov, Baryakovskaia and Shephard's work to arbitrary points of insertion and exponents. Our research also shows that a deep connection exists between chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution with reflection and chordal Schramm-Löwner evolution with imaginary insertion and exponent, thereby indicating that with reflection and without it are conceptually related through the imaginary surface idea.

The Navier-Stokes equations' global-in-time existence and uniqueness of very energetic solutions in two dimensions are confirmed. Given a smooth initial velocity field with its maximum norm as a measure of intensity, there exists a global-in-time unique solution, also with its maximum norm (in the $H^1$ norm) characterized. This norm is directly proportional to the initial data, with the proportionality constant being an arbitrary positive value, and this result generalizes the known results for less intense solutions.

A novel Cavity-QED Vision Quantum Computation protocol has been designed and proposed, allowing for direct, all-optical projection of wavefunction evolution. This was done using a warm Rubidium atom and a continuous-wave laser in a Fabry-Perot cavity setup. By exploiting the proximity of the upper laser level to the upper branch of the Raman doublet, this proposal achieves Cavity-QED Vision Quantum Computation via the projection of the atom's ground state. It offers the advantage of being compatible with state-of-the-art cavity-QED technology and does not require the cavity to be extremely small or have high optical finesse. Cavity-QED Vision Quantum Computation outperforms the Raman-VQC protocol in speed by approximately 10^5 times, as it avoids the need for two-photon interactions.

Deep learning models that can create realistic cell shapes are being developed to enhance and boost the quality of cell tracking and segmentation.  These models are expected to contribute significantly in the areas of biomaterial science, image reconstruction, noise reduction, and data augmentation for tracking and segmentation algorithms.  This study presents a novel method for generating cell shapes by adapting the space and time normalizing flow approach to create a mapping between complex cell shapes and a basic geometric representation.  This mapping enables the production of diverse and realistic cell shapes by leveraging the properties of a probabilistic model that maps the complex outer cell boundary to a basic geometric representation.  This method outperforms existing state-of-the-art space and time normalizing flow approaches in terms of likelihood scores, as evidenced by a higher likelihood of boundary images being sampled from a probabilistic model.

In a series of experiments using reinforcement learning, researchers discovered a novel mechanism where an agent's ability to identify and retain key characteristics from previous tasks enhances performance on subsequent tasks. To determine the extent to which this mechanism contributes to the superior performance of hierarchical methods over flat networks in learning castles from a flat matrix of numbers, they introduced a range of modified castle designs and varied architectural layouts. The results revealed a direct correlation between a feature's persistence and task performance, and showed that the mechanism's effectiveness peaks at an intermediate point, beyond which its benefits plateau or diminish. Furthermore, studies examining its application to visual recognition tasks confirmed that a moderate level of feature persistence significantly improves performance in sequential tasks involving real images.

A revised version of the Newtonian ECMC algorithm is presented, which overcomes the issue of dynamical freeze in a three-dimensional dipolar model with a long-range force through a dynamic adjustment of the dipolar interaction's decay length during simulation cycles.

To enhance the accuracy of sound event detection in automated systems, various techniques have been developed to expand the training dataset and boost their effectiveness in specific contexts. This study evaluates the effectiveness of different data augmentation methods in their general applicability by testing seven techniques on a sound event detection task using the DCASE 2020 dataset. We compare the proposed methods against a baseline and find that their performance gains are modest in isolation, yet significant when combined. Notably, our results demonstrate that two augmentation methods excel across various scenarios and organize in an ordered hierarchy of performance. These findings diverge from the trends typically associated with image data, highlighting distinct approaches for audio data processing.

To enhance understanding of the superposition property in the context of multiple
antenna systems, we introduce a new model called the superposition multiple
antenna type-I ISAC system, which uniquely synchronizes communication and sensing
functions. We mathematically demonstrate that superposition across multiple
antennas increases both distance and beamwidth estimation accuracy, which has
implications for various applications such as federated learning and non-orthogonal
multiple access (NOMA). Furthermore, we show that superposition property also
improves target localization in passive sensing. We demonstrate this through a
mathematical model and numerical simulations, which show that the efficiency of
learning and sensing functions can be positively influenced by superposition
property in multiple antenna systems.

A novel approach to signal detection, estimation, and classification in the spectrogram is developed, utilizing level sets to characterize and represent sound signals. This method inherently encapsulates signal characteristics such as energy, continuity, shape, and timing, which are crucial in addressing classification and detection problems. Furthermore, this level set-based framework is effectively applied to the classification of complex vocal signals, including human voice types and specific speech emotions.

We introduce a novel concept of synchronized clusters in dynamic systems, 
along with a method to calculate their quantity. Our approach encompasses 
determining the number of four primary cluster types: anti-phase, and two 
 kinds of phase-dependent interactions resulting in either $x$ or $y$ 
 dominance. We also outline a strategy to simplify the analysis of numerous 
 system configurations through a plot of synchronized clusters across various 
 coupling strengths for an imposed time delay. This method is effectively 
 applied to a population of coupled oscillators with random natural frequencies, 
 where we document the number of each cluster type and provide an explanation 
 for any observed irregularities. A notable discovery is that all identified 
 synchronization patterns persist in a network of oscillators with uniformly 
 distributed frequencies, where we calculate the quantity of all previously 
 identified synchronized clusters and validate an analogy between systemic 
 synchronization and a zero-variance phenomenon.

We introduce an advanced, versatile module that accurately simulates the complex interactions between particles and moving fields in a fully coupled system. This module enhances several existing open-source software packages from the Particle-in-Cell community, including SPECTRE, PICARD, and COMET. In particular, we integrate a highly efficient trajectory integration method that ensures a precise calculation of particles' movement over extended periods of time. Furthermore, we develop a novel module that seamlessly connects particles with moving fields, enabling a precise calculation of particles' interaction with electromagnetic fields. Our approach is then compared with other state-of-the-art methods in the field, including PICGAUSS and PIC-ORBIT, and demonstrates a significant increase in computational efficiency of up to 300 times for a specific test case.

A pioneering concept, previously proposed by Landauer and later expanded upon, proposes creating an information engine through the continuous measurement of a small system's state and the application of controlled feedback. This distinct approach differs from typical information engines that operate in a cycle. In this study, we demonstrate the conversion of measurement information into work in a perpetual loop and analyze the total work output over an extended measurement period. To achieve this, we examine both simple models where the small system is coupled to an oscillator acting as a force probe, and more intricate models where information is used to modify the oscillator's stiffness. Our analysis focuses on two information extraction methods: one based on unitary dynamics and the other on quantum Jumplets, both of which are applied during intermittent measurement processes. Our findings indicate that units of work are stored in the oscillator's motion, allowing for its release in a subsequent feedback operation, and that this process is governed by the size of the small system and the strength of the coupling with the oscillator.

To investigate how the disk weight affects its role in jamming, we carried out numerical simulations with various parameters. Our results show that heavier disks tend to become the primary cause of jamming, while lighter disks are often displaced by stronger forces and are compressed into a compact state. When we assigned disk weights based on their sizes to a range of initial packings with different characteristics, we found that all of them converged to a self-similar, size-based weight distribution, resulting in a universal jamming threshold. This universal jamming threshold varies with the strength of inter-particle friction, but remains independent of initial packing details. Furthermore, we observed a transition from random to continuous jamming as friction increases and discovered that this critical friction point separates random from continuous universality classes.

Research on the impacts of El Niño and La Niña has often been based on comparing specific phases of the ENSO cycle, leading to conclusions that they are essentially opposite phenomena. A newer approach, which views them as different types of precipitation-impacting weather events, reveals that they have unique flavors with distinct effects on regional precipitation patterns. This study employs advanced machine learning techniques to analyze how various flavors of El Niño and La Niña evolve and how they influence different parts of the world. Findings indicate that certain flavors of both phases tend to cluster together and share similarities, yet others exhibit contrasting behaviors. Moreover, a specific flavor of La Niña has been identified that, similar to El Niño, is associated with enhanced rainfall in East Asia and reduced rainfall in East Africa. These results highlight the need for more nuanced forecasts of precipitation that go beyond simply predicting a single type of El Niño or La Niña, emphasizing the importance of understanding a range of possible outcomes.

The mass distribution of supermassive black holes observed today is influenced by 
their initial formation triggers and how they form in a star-forming galaxy. A 
computer simulation of a galaxy cluster's evolution is used to model two 
scenarios for the formation of black holes, one in which they form from stars and 
another from collisions of gas clouds. The first scenario produces a higher 
number of black holes with a mass of at least $10^5 M_\odot$, but their masses do 
not match the range seen in the James Webb Space Telescope. The second scenario 
produces fewer massive black holes but a larger population at a mass of about 
$10^4-10^5 M_\odot$, a range more in line with the James Webb Space Telescope's 
findings. Both scenarios generate a similar number and mass range of black holes at 
the lower end. These results suggest that even small-mass black holes can eventually 
become the supermassive black holes we see today.

In this paper, we investigate the influence of thermal fluctuations on topological properties within the square lattice Hubbard model that exhibits flat bands. Our findings show that thermal fluctuations in the square lattice have a flat band-induced significant correlation effect that gives rise to a robust Mott insulating state with a square texture. To better understand this phenomenon, we analyze the temperature dependence of the exact diagonalization spectral functions and wave functions, as well as the mean-field approximations of spectral functions and mean-field Green's functions. Additionally, we examine the temperature multi-orbital phase diagram by computing the Berry curvature and Hall conductance, revealing a robust topological insulating phase with a square texture in the square lattice. Our study highlights the importance of considering temperature fluctuations in the presence of flat bands and their role in inducing robust topological insulating phases with a square texture in multi-orbital systems within the square lattice.

Understanding which genetic variations have a significant impact on specific proteins and traits is crucial for identifying the underlying causes of complex traits.
In this study, a novel computational framework called PhenoSeq was created to pinpoint sections of proteins that are influenced by variations linked to specific non-protein traits. PhenoSeq operates under the assumption that variations affecting a specific protein are more likely to affect parts of the protein with significant functional roles. This framework operates in two stages: a functional module that identifies variations linked to a specific phenotype and a second module that correlates these variations with changes in protein function. PhenoSeq was tested on the human hemoglobin subunit beta protein and the results showed that variations affecting specific protein functions are more likely to be associated with specific phenotypic traits rather than variations affecting general protein function. PhenoSeq was further applied to the human hemoglobin subunit gamma and the results indicated an inverse relationship between the level of natural selection acting on a protein and the degree to which variations affect specific protein functions.

We have found all 2-designs where the number of points is a prime power and the automorphism group has a prime order subcollection that's not in the group's smallest normal subcollection. Our findings reveal the specific order of this prime order subcollection, as well as key characteristics of the design's block and point in terms of block and point residues. Additionally, we identified a family of 2-designs with specific characteristics, including a prime order, a prime power number of points, a specified block residue, and a specified point residue. Furthermore, we established that the prime order prime order subcollection cannot be a 2, 3, or 5.

We introduce a generalized entropy as an average of local information densities, applicable to both single particle wave functions and $N$-electron configurations. This approach can be used to quantify the Coulomb correlation influence in confined electronic systems of finite size, $R$, including atoms, doped $R^6$ fullerene molecules and quantum dots. The generalized entropies for single particle wave functions exhibit the same scaling behavior with respect to system radius $R$ as their Coulomb correlation energy counterparts. This relationship holds true for non-deformed and spherically symmetric ground state configurations and reveals significant variations in entropies for different shell fillings. Additionally, our findings for doted $R^6$ fullerene molecules indicate that Coulomb correlation effects in confined many-body electronic systems can be accurately represented by generalized entropies.

This research focuses on velocity dispersion in wide binary star systems, which is crucial for understanding the velocity offsets within these systems and assessing whether they are truly bound. By utilizing line velocities from spectroscopic data, rather than radial velocities, our method enhances the accuracy of velocity dispersion measurements. We applied this novel line-velocity dispersion approach to a sample of 290 wide binary star systems, consisting of 10 to 100 solar masses, consisting of 960 spectral lines from the VLT/SIMPLE instrument. Our study finds that line-velocity dispersion is 10-15% lower than radial-velocity dispersion, indicating that it yields narrower distributions. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that radial-velocity dispersion overestimates line-velocity dispersion by 10-15%, an effect that may lead to an incorrect conclusion that some wide binary star systems are not bound to each other. Our study emphasizes the importance of line-velocity dispersion as a more accurate tool for characterizing wide binary star systems and recommends its use for further studies.

We introduce a formal set of rules for determining whether one proof structure in multiplicative linear logic implies another, and relates these rules to the logical meaning of the proofs and the concept of representation introduced by Abadi and Ungar in 1990. Our analysis focuses on representations that utilize directed graphs to model logical content, which may be considered imperfect since they also account for structural transformations, but we believe this approach offers valuable insights, particularly in light of recent findings on representation theory and higher-order logic. Our findings reveal that representation corresponds to proof contraction, and significantly, that representation is transitive, but higher-order implication is not. To resolve this discrepancy, we propose a higher-order logic relation known as 'strong representation', drawn from our understanding of how representations interact, and demonstrate its connection to proof structures in multiplicative linear logic.

A novel approach to predicting synchronization between pairs of time-series is presented, employing a deep learning framework. The proposed method assesses whether two series, such as those representing asset prices, are synchronized, drawn from the same underlying distribution. We evaluate a range of synchronization indicators, including cross-correlation and a cross entropy metric, on an asset return time-series. The method learns to classify synchronized vs. non-synchronized pairs and is tested on a large, real-world dataset of individual stocks, revealing that a cross entropy measure yields the best outcomes. The cross entropy approach achieves an area under the curve score of 0.613, surpassing a baseline of 0.50 and cross-correlation of 0.54. Notably, our model can accurately predict synchronization 20 trading days in advance with a cross entropy metric that attains an area under the curve score of 0.60.

The concept of nanosonoporation, where sound waves increase the permeability of cell membranes, has been observed to have an even more profound impact in more recent studies. Nanosonoporation is now understood to have even more extensive implications in the realm of chemistry, where the vibration of atoms can lead to significant changes in quantum states and ultimately lower the barriers for chemical reactions to occur. This has been observed to occur within a specific frequency range that corresponds to the vibration of bonds within reactant molecules. By manipulating these vibrations, it may be possible to exert more precise control over the outcomes of reactions, which has the potential to revolutionize the field of chemistry.

This paper examines the effectiveness of visual IDs in enhancing Online Click-Through Rate (oCTR) prediction models for the purpose of optimizing online advertising performance. Studies have shown that employing a combination of text-based and image-based features tends to surpass using either feature alone. In particular, recent advances in online advertising have focused on incorporating visual IDs, which are a type of additional signal derived from the ad creative. In contrast, the text and creative signals are typically either directly combined into an embedding or one signal is used in lieu of the other. In order to better understand the ad creative's representational ability in embedding the text signal, we have developed a new method that learns a separate embedding for the ad's visual IDs. This unique approach utilizes a multi-view contrastive learning technique to develop an encoding for the ad's visual features, then integrates this with the text-based signal to produce an enhanced representation. Experimental results on the dCTR dataset confirm that this novel method surpasses existing approaches and significantly contributes to a comprehensive understanding of the visual IDs' impact on ad creative representation learning.

Business process management systems face challenges in enforcing constraints during parallel activities due to the variability in resource availability and potential conflicts in requirement interpretations. To address these issues, a new resource allocation model was developed that allows for flexible satisfaction of constraints in the presence of uncertain and conflicting requirements. The model can handle cardinality constraints, which specify the maximum number of simultaneous resource allocations, and is efficient even for constraints exceeding canonical limits. An algorithm was designed to find a valid solution by mapping processes to a temporal graph and utilizing a high-time-complexity search procedure to determine a suitable path that satisfies all constraints. The approach's efficiency was demonstrated through a number of case studies involving real business processes.

A novel statistical method is developed to model and propagate the Air Optics Device (AOD) readings generated by wild fires. This approach is rooted in a physics-driven statistical framework that leverages observable characteristics of AOD data, such as its spectral composition and propagation patterns, to predict AOD readings at unmeasured locations. By integrating this method with machine learning techniques that analyze spectral data, we construct a predictor capable of estimating AOD values at missing spatial points. This stateless nature of our method allows it to be efficiently deployed in real-time systems for tracking and predicting the air quality impacts of wild fires. To validate our method, we employ the analysis of AOD data collected during the 2016 Las Conchas fire, comparing our predictions against empirical observations and referencing expert system projections.

A novel approach is introduced that balances utility and privacy when handling conditionally dependent data within complex systems like location-based services and advanced computing models. Developed within the LBS4u context, this framework employs a sophisticated hiding technique to safeguard sensitive data, specifically addressing the risk of data inference in various data release scenarios. By measuring the data hiding impact on both utility and privacy using entropy and Fisher information, our method optimizes utility retention while ensuring a minimum level of data privacy. We enhance this approach by integrating second-order Fisher information, yielding more accurate results compared to existing methods, and validate it through theoretical and experimental analysis of multiple data release cases.

The connectivity between various brain regions remains a key area of investigation in rest-state neuroscience. However, the reliability of this connectivity measure and the effectiveness of network models that rely on it have not been fully understood. This study employed two large datasets of resting-state fMRI to assess the variability and sensitivity of inter-site effects on functional connectivity and resting-state networks. Our findings indicate that while broad inter-site similarities exist, fine-scale patterns vary significantly across sites, rendering the community structure of brain networks dataset-dependent and unreliable for the detection of individual or group characteristics. Nevertheless, the resilience of some inter-site similarities and the persistence of certain connection strengths suggest that research should shift its focus from community structure to connection strength and emphasize the importance of accounting for inter-site variability to better understand individual and group differences.

Building on C. Bandle's connection between concentration of measure inequalities and the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian, our research explores a similar relationship involving heat flow. Specifically, we explore how concentration of measure inequalities can be expressed as conditions on the heat flow, and use the heat flow's properties to derive concentration of measure inequalities for a manifold with bounded curvature. This includes examples for products of manifolds, spheres, real projective spheres and tori.

Our proposal involves incorporating a positional encoding method tailored for code-switched text, which accounts for the transition between languages. This strategy is then integrated with pre-trained models, including PosBERT and posT5, designed specifically for code-mixed environments. Experimental results demonstrate that our positional encoding method yields superior outcomes in tasks assessing language identification, generation, and text classification compared to standard embedding and free-form positional encoding methods.

To superconduct at pressures above 75 GPa, H$_{3}$S relies on two forms of lattice vibrations - high-frequency H atoms and slower, higher-energy collective motions - but these vibrations interact with each other. Our research shows that at 75 GPa, the distinct vibrations of H atoms and the slower motions contribute equally to the isotope effect, giving a combined strength of 0.50. As pressure increases, the separate nature of these vibrations decreases, giving rise to intrinsically mixed vibrations that supercharge and slowness both, resulting in a combined strength of 0.72 at 250 GPa. By comparing the predicted vibrations to experimental data, we see that the separate nature of H atom vibrations decreases, while the distinct nature of the slower motions decreases. Our findings suggest that to reach record-high superconducting temperatures, it is essential to reach conditions where intrinsically mixed vibrations occur.

Evolutionary searches in protein spaces are often guided by predictions that
relate average effects of gene substitutions to phenotypic changes. This
phenomenon can be modeled using random matrix theory that describes the
evolution of high-dimensional Gaussian distributions. A similar approach has been
developed to study the effects of multiple gene substitutions, which reveals that
variations in average fitness among gene substituions originate from non-factorizable interactions and that these non-factorizable interactions follow a universal pattern. As a result, one can predict gene substitutions' outcomes based on single gene substitutions and identify their inherent limitations. Furthermore, this framework explains why, in empirical studies, gene substitution effects follow a specific power law, where the exponent depends on the number of substituted genes. This phenomenon holds true regardless of the underlying fitness landscape or the distribution of multi-gene substitutions. Additionally, this research sheds light on the behavior of fitness distributions resulting from multiple gene substitutions, which can be applied to understand adaptations related to complex traits.

A typical model of a standing human robot, controlled through proportional feedback
using hip position and velocity, is examined in this paper in relation to its dynamic behavior.
By applying small perturbations, we analyze the influence of time-delayed control feedback
on these dynamics. Our investigation reveals that time-delayed control significantly affects
the system's spectral delay and the location of perturbation waves within each phase of the
robot's movement. Nevertheless, due to continuous exchange of energy between active control
and the robot's chaotic motion, small changes in phase and velocity remain compensated for,
maintaining stable walking patterns similar to open-loop control characteristics. This energy
transfer and compensation mechanism also enables the transition from one stable walking pattern
to another through a Hopf bifurcation. Ultimately, we demonstrate that time-delayed control
can be represented using delayed differential equations, and that under typical operating
conditions, delayed and non-delayed control produce nearly identical results in maintaining
robot stability and achieving dynamic equilibrium.

We introduce a novel framework for camera pose estimation that utilizes machine-learned descriptors to enhance performance even in challenging situations. The framework is composed of two key elements: a descriptor learning module and a matching-based pose estimation technique. Descriptors are learned through a combination of local image characteristics and point features using a multi-task learning approach. These learned descriptors are then used to calculate pointwise heatmaps from matching pairs via grid matching. The framework exhibits exceptional accuracy and robustness, even with short baseline angles, due to the power of descriptors and the heatmap calculation method. A descriptor allows a single feature point to align with multiple candidate feature locations, and the application of heatmaps provides an alternative approach to traditional keypoint detection that can accommodate this flexibility. We improve the stability of the feature matching process by incorporating heatmaps into the calculation.

Most existing methods for semi-supervised and federated learning focus on enhancing robustness against non-identical and non-iiid data. These approaches either have limited applications in the described settings or do not take advantage of the personalized labels. We introduce a novel, practical method that incorporates a small amount of labeled data from each client and a substantial amount from each client to train a local model. The model uses an entropy minimization technique on the unlabelled data and our proposed method uses an information bottleneck approach to align the representations from the local model and unlabelled data. Our method is supported by theoretical guarantees and the results of theoretical as well as the experimental as well as the experimental results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results results

Following a neutron star's disruption in a massive star's accretion disk around a black hole, we observe the evolution of the system's accretion rate, magnetic field, and other characteristics. In our numerical simulations, we find that the post-merger system initially has a small magnetic field within the accretion disk, which then rapidly evolves and amplifies within 0.01-0.1 seconds, reaching a level and scale comparable to the disk's outer radius and a characteristic post-merger timescale of approximately 0.01 seconds. As the magnetic field in the disk strengthens, it extracts angular momentum from the disk and reduces the accretion rate by about 10% to 30%, depending on the variant, through the generation of a compact, magnetically dominated region with size on the order of the black hole's horizon, located a few times the horizon size away from the black hole. At the end of the simulation, the accretion rate stabilizes into a magnetically dominated steady state characterized by an accretion timescale of a few times the black hole horizon size, achieved when the magnetic field's pressure is comparable to the thermal pressure of the disk. Our results suggest that in various types of stars with different metallicities, the accretion rate, temperature, luminosity, and other characteristics of the accretion disk will be largely regulated by this magnetohydrodynamic process in a steady state.

We establish that for compact Riemann surfaces of a given genus, the first Mumford-Morita-Miller class in the tautological ring is significantly non-zero. This is achieved by demonstrating its expression as a combination of specific geometric objects, known as level structures, whose individual counts are explicitly calculated, highlighting their underlying asymptotic patterns.

This study establishes that a specific type of Markov process on a confined, curved space bounded by surfaces will have one and only one quasi-stationary distribution, along with consistent rates of convergence. Under a set of assumptions regarding the process and the domain's shape, we derived these results. For cases involving diffusion processes where the domain's size changes slowly and remains confined within a compact region, our findings confirm the existence of a regular, periodic quasi-stationary distribution in both time and space.

Researchers have investigated interactions between dielectric nanoparticles and electromagnetic fields produced by sources with arbitrary time-varying characteristics, considering the influence of electron population in a graphenophore dielectric substrate. The source reaction field was calculated in three dimensions and used to analyze interactions between emitters and dielectric particles. A special case involving two emitters was studied, incorporating radiation exchange, while the dielectric particles exhibited spatial modulation of the electromagnetic field due to electron population variation in the graphenophore. This variation allowed control over the particles' equilibrium positions through adjustment of the graphene's chemical potential.

Patients in the Emergency Department (ED) with an anticipated treatment time of 20 minutes were the focus of this 2017 randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted in a 450-bed hospital in New York City. These patients were invited to participate in a virtual waitlist program by an interviewer, with the alternative being a traditional ED wait. Real-time updates on treatment times were provided to the patients by a live agent, and their RCT assignment determined whether they received virtual waitlist program participation or not. As they underwent their ED procedures, their assigned interviewer provided RCT participants regular check-ins at least twice daily for a period of 30 days following their visit. Data was collected on over 1,000 RCT participants and 1,000 control group patients, with the data then analyzed using a combination of hospital records and external sources. The results indicated that patients who were assigned to the virtual waitlist group experienced at least one 30-day revisit or readmission 40 percentage points less often than their control counterparts. Additionally, increasing their treatment time by 30 minutes increased their 30-day revisit or readmission rates by 8 percentage points. However, participation in the virtual waitlist program did not affect their mood during their ED visit, the frequency of their complaints to hospital administration, or emergency care-related costs.

This research investigates how varying levels of cognitive ability and task complexity impact selection methods in multi-agent systems. A computer simulation model simulates multiple agents with different cognitive abilities making choices to complete tasks of varying difficulties. The study compares three selection methods - random, ability-based and performance-based - in terms of their effectiveness across different difficulty settings. Our findings suggest that these selection methods can be viewed as different strategies to navigate task difficulty, and they perform optimally under specific conditions. For instance, both the random and performance-based selection methods excel under low difficulty settings, whereas a more cautious decision-making method is more successful under high difficulty settings.

To accurately measure charge-dependent correlations originating from charge separation in heavy ion collisions, thorough understanding and removal of influences caused by local charge conservation and charge conservation across the entire reaction zone are crucial. Researchers have developed a novel statistical method to quantify these effects, which encompasses two-level correlations resulting from local conservation and multi-level correlations stemming from global charge conservation. Through simulation of non-flow backgrounds based on radial flow and particle independent pseudorapidity distributions, the method's accuracy and capacity to isolate various charge conservation influences have been thoroughly examined. An efficient technique for extracting the impact of global charge conservation and associated background from raw two-particle correlations has been successfully implemented using this method. Additionally, the method can be expanded to higher-order correlations, with applications to data from relativistic heavy ion collisions becoming readily feasible.

Understanding the key factors that influence a project's success in funding-based campaigns, like Kickstarter, is a complex problem. These campaigns are essentially collaborations between project creators and supporters, where the dynamics of the crowd play a crucial role. We approach this problem from the perspective of a partnership, where a project is viewed as a company and the crowd as its stakeholders. By applying knowledge discovery techniques to both parties, we can identify characteristics that distinguish successful from less successful projects and creators. When it comes to predicting a project's success, its attributes play a more significant role than those of the crowd, although the crowd's behavior can provide valuable insights into a project's future performance. Furthermore, analyzing attributes related to a project's potential and those of its potential stakeholders reveals distinct differences between successful and less successful creators and projects.

In a world where data protection is a top priority, organizations share a common dataset to train machine learning models that detect network intrusions. However, sharing a common dataset is not a practical option due to data privacy concerns. A federated learning approach allows organizations to maintain a single training process without centralizing their network intrusion data. This thesis investigates the effectiveness of federated learning in a network intrusion detection context, using a network of simulated IoT devices to generate network traffic and create balanced and representative data sets. The research compares the performance of different machine learning models and models with and without a global training process. The findings demonstrate that federated machine learning is a viable approach for maintaining data privacy in network intrusion detection, and shows that certain models' performance in a federated setting is comparable to their non-federated performance.

We introduce an innovative approach to expedite robot task execution by leveraging knowledge of execution duration and employing precomputed task metrics. The proposed method falls within the active inference framework, which models tasks as objectives and utilizes active learning to select the most effective execution strategy. To calculate metrics efficiently, we employ a novel representation that decomposes execution into reusable segments with predefined metrics, enabling rapid evaluation of execution methods. The results of a thorough benchmark study demonstrate that this approach can significantly lower execution times by as much as 80% in robot vacuum-cleaning applications.

The choice of semiconductor and gate materials significantly influences a device's performance, particularly in terms of mobility. Uncovered gates lead to substantial mobility loss, while a deposited gate may introduce additional scattering mechanisms that further impede mobility. A novel two-dimensional Boltzmann transport equation model has been developed to investigate the impact of an uncovered gate and gate deposition on semiconductor devices. By solving Poisson's equation and considering surface roughness scattering, this model accurately predicts mobility without relying on empirical corrections. A comparative analysis of the simulated and experimentally observed mobility in Bodruyli et al.'s (2019) study has been conducted. The results indicate a close match between the two methods, particularly in terms of the magnitude and trends of mobility loss. However, the theoretical and experimental mobility values exhibit slight discrepancies, which may be attributed to the complexity and unpredictability of surface roughness.

In certain types of interconnected systems, especially those with identical individual components and consistent connections, stable group synchronization can occur. This phenomenon also appears in systems with inconsistent parameters but no connections. We investigate whether small deviations in system parameters or connections affect the stable group synchronization. Our research shows that for generic systems, this type of group synchronization loses stability due to very minor disturbances. Nevertheless, for systems with consistent parameters, multiple types of stable group synchronization are possible. These include scenarios where oscillations remain synchronized within groups but diverge independently from each other. We also develop a method to predict which types of stable group synchronization may occur and present various examples to illustrate these results.

This research examines the search results produced by a set of Western-based search engines for 100 distinct queries, which were analyzed over the course of 180 days. Our primary goal was to assess whether there is a discernible pattern in the presence of non-Western influenced search outcomes. To achieve this, a novel search result classification system was developed, and a total of 2,500 datasets were analyzed. Our analysis revealed a striking consensus: YouTube was consistently present in the search results of every search engine for 95% of the videos classified as potentially influenced by China, Russia, or North Korea. Furthermore, our results indicated that YouTube claims a significant portion of the search traffic for these platforms.

A detailed investigation has been conducted into the behavior of the zeta function when monodromy defects are present at the origin in a flat Riemann surface. This involves deriving expressions for eigenvalues associated with the Laplace operator under various defect configurations. Building upon previous findings, expressions for $\zeta(s, a)$ and the heat kernel trace kernel trace $K(s,a)$ are presented for general monodromy defects. Key observations include the preservation of poles from defect-free systems, with new finite values arising that depend on the defect defect's invariants. By exploiting the trace formula and expressing the determinant of the Laplacian as $\exp(-2\Omega'(0))$, where prime denotes the defective system and the unsubscripted system refers to the defect-free system. This leads to a concrete evaluation of the ratio of determinants for various types of defects, including a analysis of an anyonic defect that utilizes the Gamma function, yielding expressions for energy levels in two dimensional any systems.

If K is a real quadratic field with a K-rational 13-torsion point on an elliptic curve E, and E has a cubic Galois extension K(L), with L being an E-defined point, a specific type of models can be established for E over K(L) using generalized Fermat cubic curves. Our research identifies two types of models for E over K(L) with specific properties, including one with a unique endomorphism defined over K(L). We also introduced two invariants, which help to parametrize all such models for E over K(L) up to isomorphism. Furthermore, our results show that these two invariants represent distinct classes for E over K(L) and an exceptional case where they represent the same class. Computation was facilitated by an explicitly constructed database of real quadratic fields, fields L and tables of tables for various invariants.

We have developed an examination of the performance of a modified version of the FIBOCOX protocol, commonly used in delay-sensitive networks, under conditions of the IP protocol. This analysis is carried out within a queueing network framework. Consideration of the impact of network capacity, operation regime (local delay threshold), and packet drop probability on performance has been undertaken. An accurate, closed-form expression for performance metrics is presented, which allows for the comparison of different operation regimes based on an optimal local delay threshold that minimizes performance degradation.

This paper examines the application of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) in a semi-supervised node classification setting. Our research focuses on the influence of pseudo-labels (PLs), generated by an initial model and often used in such tasks, on the final performance. We observed that existing pseudo-labeling methods, which typically involve reusing and refining the initial model's predictions for unlabeled data, can negatively affect GNNs due to the accumulation of errors. In contrast, we propose a new method that utilizes a initial model to predict pseudo-labels independently for each sample, without considering the performance of its counterparts. Our method inverts a regularizer, accounting for the label distribution of the labeled data, to enforce on GNNs and prevent overfitting to the pseudo-labeled data. Our experiments on public datasets indicate substantial improvements using our method.

This study presents a novel deep learning architecture called PatchNet, designed to enhance video object detection. PatchNet leverages a patch convolution layer to decrease the model's output dimension, thereby reducing computational complexity. By integrating patch convolution with regular convolution, we achieve a balance of high performance and efficiency. Our experiments demonstrate that PatchNet outperforms state-of-the-art lightweight models, showcasing improved accuracy and computational speed. With a Computation Performance metric 1.7 times superior to MobileNetV2, PatchNet is now ready for inclusion in cutting-edge lightweight video object detection frameworks. Our research can be found on the arXiv preprint server at https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.02444.

In a further exploration of our previous work where we determined the time-evolving n-point probability distribution for the totally asymmetric exclusion process (TASEP) with arbitrary initial conditions, we have established a theorem that reveals how the most general initial conditions can be represented as a combination of three fundamental scenarios: uniform, empty, and blocked sites. This conclusion holds regardless of the lattice spacing. Consequently, the multi-point distribution for any given initial condition can be obtained through a combination of results from these three basic cases. This finding is valid not only for integer time instances but also for any time ratio of time to lattice spacing. To validate this theory, we have verified that the non-equilibrium entropy of TASEP aligns with the expectations derived from the superposition principle.

In this research, we have developed the Generalized Antenna-Switching Technique (AST), which allows for simultaneous information transfer and energy harvesting in networks combining wireless power transfer and information transmission. By selecting the optimal antenna at the transmitter based on the channel information of both the information receivers and energy harvesting receivers, AST enables efficient energy harvesting for the latter while maintaining zero information leakage. Our study examines the impact of RFS on AST and reveals that, by increasing the number of AST antennas, we can substantially improve energy harvesting performance and significantly decrease the information leakage probability without compromising the quality of service for the receivers. Furthermore, our analysis assesses the performance of AST in comparison to other wireless power transfer and information transmission methods.

We present a novel quantum theory that accounts for SU(N) fermions and any number of colors, with a perturbation expansion that is based on the number of colors, similar to an 'expansion by large-N'. This perturbation theory yields results that are in the form of integrals and can be applied to any order of approximation, with the ability to expand on the color symmetry. We demonstrate that, in a specific limit, this perturbation theory aligns with findings reported in the literature, with a perturbation expansion that is in agreement with analytical results to second order, but diverges beyond second order, with the difference decreasing as the half-power of the number of colors.

A major connection between option-mechanics classical and quantum models remains unclear, especially when the number of occupied states is high. This work clarifies the relationship by demonstrating that the equivalence between classical and quantum treatments relies on two factors: (i) large occupation numbers and (ii) equal strength of the quantum back-action noise at signal and inverted signal frequencies. These conditions are frequently met while not always so (e.g., in systems with ground-state occupancy). We derive conditions for equivalence that go beyond simple consideration of electric circuit models. This research enables us to develop a new approach to predicting electric circuit responses to quantum fluctuations. This model can be used to develop approximate predictions for the output of quantum-metric devices with high occupation numbers, thus making it possible to use classical methods for calculating electrical noise in quantum-metric circuits.

This paper extends previous work on the orthogonality of polynomials with respect to a modified Freud weight, which incorporates a parameter for generalisation. The original Freud weight, with a parameter of $k=1$, is specifically a limiting case of the generalised Freud weight. This weight can be seen as a combination of the sextic Freud weight and a tail weight, both of which are unique. The text provides a parameterised formula for the moments of the generalised Freud weight, as well as an explicit expression for the monic orthogonal polynomials through a DO-while type integral formula. The study also utilizes the method of parameter differentiation to derive a three-term recurrence relation for these polynomials.

This research examines the influence of the field of view (FoV) of a distance sensor on the tracking trapezoidal shapes created as a robot navigates alongside a wall at a constant distance. By using a fuzzy logic approach, a robot's navigation system interprets sensor data to adjust its path accordingly. We analyze trapezoidal dimensions - specifically base and height - generated by a robot equipped with a rotating single sensor, and investigate how these shapes vary in response to the sensor's FoV. A robotics simulation tool is used to create these shapes, allowing us to study their characteristics in relation to the sensor's FoV. Results indicate that as sensor FoV narrows, trapezoidal patterns become increasingly intricate, featuring reduced sizes compared to those produced by a wider sensor FoV. These findings present an opportunity to further research by utilizing the trapezoidal patterns as a means of identifying the sensor's FoV.

In the context of perturbative algebra quantum field theory, a specific type of subalgebras is chosen, anchored on arbitrary Cauchy surfaces, contrary to the global subalgebras, defined based on spacetime open regions, as presented in R. Haag's book "Perturbative Algebraic Quantum Field Theory". This choice, although seemingly neutral, turns out to have significant implications, particularly in the case of theories involving long-range forces. A detailed examination of this phenomenon is presented within the framework of Yang-Mills and QED theories.

Smoke can obscure a surgeon's view, making it hard to see through smoke and distinguishing it from non-smoky images. We developed an automatic smoke detection system that utilizes an image processing technique to enhance smoke images and an image classification method for smoke detection. To accurately classify smoke images, we utilized a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) on a dataset of real surgical images containing various smoke concentrations. We also applied a novel growth filter to standard smoke images to make smoke more visible to the CNN. Our experimental results show that the combination of the image enhancement and classification approaches yields a higher accuracy in smoke detection when compared to using the classification method in isolation.

The engineering of frequency-resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates is a critical task, as they influence the development of noise and the process of entanglement buildup and return in connected ion systems. This work presents a computer model that facilitates the efficient design of such gates by exploiting a specific feature of the ion system's Hamiltonian. The proposed model enables the establishment of a clear standard for assessing the reliability of entangling operations on a single shot, and we demonstrate its benefits through a practical design of frequency-tolerant MS gates with minimal phase entanglement. Furthermore, we show that this approach can enhance the reliability of entangling gates significantly, while also improving their entanglement accumulation dynamics.

Using advanced ab initio calculations, researchers have investigated how equilibrium conditions affect cations in several perovskite compositions. Their findings reveal that under normal equilibrium conditions, smaller A cations naturally lead to off-centering of the B cation. However, when larger C cations are present in the structure, both A and B cations exhibit off-centering movements. Furthermore, equilibrium volumes and the size of A cations significantly influence off-centering movements. Notably, when B cations move off-center, they primarily displace the cage of A cations rather than the entire perovskite structure. These findings challenge previous assumptions about how certain materials respond to strain. Using a simplified model, researchers successfully predicted the lattice distortions and off-centering behaviors of strontium-strontium-lead titanate and barium-strontium-lead titanate, as well as their response to compression, which matched experimental data.

We introduce a new class of structured models that can be represented as undirected graphs, which can be fitted using multivariate regression and time series analysis. These models allow us to fit multiple independent processes to different nodes in a graph, while also ensuring conditional independence between them. By utilizing a hierarchical structure, we can create more complex models and achieve better accuracy in our predictions. The effectiveness of our method is demonstrated through a case study of predicting heart rate variability in a patient.

We developed and investigated a method to improve the efficiency of using the variational multiconfigurational Fermi-hypercorrelation ansatz for variationally describing the difficult-to-compute ground states of simple molecular systems. By analyzing the recurrence in the multiconfigurational Fermi-hypercorrelation ansatz, we developed a more efficient circuit design that not only reduces computational complexity but also enhances the description of the variational wavefunction. Numerical simulations confirm that this improvement in recurrence translates to enhanced computational efficiency, particularly for variationally describing the ground states of challenging molecules.

We introduce the Generalized Chebyshev method, a family of optimization algorithms designed to achieve superior performance in average-case performance metrics. This method significantly outperforms established optimization algorithms, such as gradient descent and SGD with exponential weights, in various performance metrics. The GC method also surpasses robust exponential gradient descent and a robust variant of SGD with similar performance metrics. Notably, this method has the added advantage of generating an optimal trajectory for polynomial optimization problems, as well as an efficient sampling scheme for solving such problems in average-case performance metrics, which also surpasses that of SGD with exponential weights.

Moiré heterostructures display unique optical characteristics resulting from the presence of interlayer excitons. This phenomenon is observed in systems with specific atomic alignment, which can give rise to energy gaps and influence the optical spectrum. A theoretical framework has been developed to model the properties of interlayer excitons in moiré patterns and their impact on optical responses. The structure of interlayer excitons and the energy of their constituents can significantly affect the optical spectrum, particularly when considering the excitation of multiple particles such as excitons and phonons. The proportion of interlayer and monolayer excitations also plays a crucial role in determining the optical characteristics of moiré heterostructures.

We propose an innovative filter that utilizes probabilistic data association to estimate a mobile agent's position in a changing environment with multiple targets and obstacles. Our algorithm combines an extended Kalman filter with adaptive probability calculations, which are derived from the characteristics of multiple reflectors in the sensor's field of view. This results in an optimized beamforming metric that identifies the probabilities of relevant objects in the field of view, leading to improved position calculations in the presence of significant reflections. The effectiveness of our algorithm is demonstrated through simulations in a real-world environment using a USRPIUSB2X2 software-defined receiver, which communicates with a mobile agent via phase-based positioning in a space with multiple targets, obstacles, and varying levels of difficulty.

The ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider has analyzed data collected with an integrated luminosity of 300 fb^-1, identifying approximately 1.1 million events resulting from the decay of Higgs bosons in conjunction with bosons W and Z. This analysis identified around 10,000 events originating from bosonic decays accompanied by Higgs bosons, enabling the measurement of joint helicity fractions for the W and Z bosons. The fractions helicity were found to be 0.11 ± 0.04 ± 0.03 for W+, 0.10 ± 0.04 ± 0.03 for Z, and for H^0_A, and for W+, 0.10 ± 0.04 ± 0.03, and for H^0_B, 0.09 ± 0.04 ± 0.03. The results are in line with predictions made by the Standard Model, and a statistically significant difference of 2.1 sigma was found. The mass of the Higgs boson was found to be 125.2 GeV, and its presence was confirmed.

We develop a knowledgeability approach to understanding the vacuum state in quantum field theory by leveraging geometric properties of the vacuum manifold. This approach enables us to express vacuum transitions as Cerenkov radiation resulting from a gap in the allowed momentum trajectories. By applying this methodology to a non-relativistic model of a $U(1)$ gauge theory with two scalar vacuum fields, we demonstrate that the vacuum state remains stable due to the absence of such gaps. In contrast, when the model is modified to include an anisotropic $U(1)$ gauge field, our analysis suggests the emergence of such gaps, implying a dynamic vacuum with possible transitions and one-loop renormalization group flow behavior. This revised approach holds potential for exploration in theoretical physics contexts, such as the study of topological $U(1)$ gauge theories in three spatial dimensions and alternative models featuring anisotropic gauge dynamics in three-dimensional space.

A specific type of ordered structure known as orthomodular spaces was introduced by R. Wille in 1986. By generalizing the partial order relation, we broadened the concept of orthomodular spaces to include a more flexible ordering system. Our expansion also generalizes R. Wille's original equivalence between orthomodular lattices and orthomodular spaces. Furthermore, a distinct equivalence was established, linking certain types of orthomodular spaces and relations to equivalence relations, all derived through a different approach.

The exponential growth in the volume of digital information has led to a significant challenge in extracting and retrieving knowledge, making it difficult for individuals and organizations to manage and filter the information effectively. To tackle this issue, a novel deep learning-based approach is proposed that not only accurately extracts knowledge but also generates visual representations of the information to facilitate proof verification and enhancement. To maximize the efficiency of the information flow, the model enables proof improvement through a visual user interface that enables proof representation annotation, enabling the model to generate an initial extraction and allow users to annotate and refine the results. Such interactions enable a more efficient knowledge information flow by reducing unnecessary computations and increasing the model's effectiveness.

We use a combination of Watson's formula and the methods of Soundararajan and Harper to calculate the second and fourth moments of an $L$-function within an interval, as well as the fourth moment of a Dirichlet character $L$-function within an interval. Our approach relies on an explicit definition of the weight function, allowing us to apply existing tools to evaluate the required integrals and sums. Although our proofs don't directly use subconvexity results, they're compatible with such findings and thus also validate the results of Iwaniec, Keating, and Soundararajan for $k\geq 3$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the methods of Soundararajan and Harper and Watson work together to yield the $2k$-th moment for $k\geq 5$.

Interior point methods are well-established techniques for efficiently solving large-scale optimization problems, but can be more demanding than other prominent algorithms like gradient descent. To enhance their efficiency, especially with limited-precision arithmetic, we can take advantage of early termination within the method's iterative process. By not necessarily reaching a high precision in each matrix inversion during interior point iterations, computational effort can be significantly reduced. To maintain the effectiveness of our approach, we've developed an optimized interior point algorithm incorporating a dynamic threshold for prematurely ending inner iterations. This method adapts its tolerance criteria at each phase and leverages relevant predictions to accommodate various types of loss functions that don't escalate too rapidly. Consequently, we observed substantial speed improvements when applying our algorithm to a range of optimization tasks, particularly support vector classification, solidly classified noise-free data sets.

We introduce a newly calculated transition function, A_gq^(3)(N), which is 
necessary for N >= 3 in variable flavor number scheme perturbative QCD. 
This is a flavor-matrix element connecting the operator-Oriented 
Non-Singlet to the third light flavor singlet pseudoscalar current in N=3 
and is required to O(alpha_s^3) in QCD for a consistent matching. 
Our new result A_gq^(3)(N) = O(alpha_s^3) is further detailed in the 
supplementary material of this paper. The result is further complicated by 
two additional transition functions, A_qg^(3)(N) and A_qq^(3)(N), which are 
calculated to O(alpha_s^3) and are necessary for a consistent VFN scheme at 
N >= 3.

We have compiled a comprehensive AI Incident Database in response to the AI fiasco symposium calls for action. This database, which is accessible online at https://ai-incident-db.github.io, is a dynamic resource that documents past AI system failures in a structured format. By analyzing these cases, researchers and practitioners can draw valuable lessons from history, preventing the repetition of similar mistakes in developing intelligent systems. The database is also a research tool, enabling the exploration of AI failure patterns and underlying causes. This is achieved by categorizing reported incidents and allowing researchers to conduct time-series analyses, identifying correlations between different types of AI system failures. We have utilized the structured entries to answer specific research questions, such as: (1) Can AI incidents be classified into recurring patterns? (2) Do certain AI architectures have a higher likelihood of failure compared to others? (3) What lessons can be learned from past AI system failures to inform the development of more robust intelligent systems?

A specific random Yang-Mills model is theoretically examined. By applying a different approach to conventional methods, it is possible to derive a key equation from the master BF equation, and this leads to a more comprehensive understanding of the BF master equation. It is then shown that this new master equation represents stochastic parallel transport, which leads to gauge-invariant formulations of Yang-Mills theory and general relativity. Using a specific example, it is proven that formulas from Yang-Mills theory and general relativity can be derived directly from the master equation, providing an elegant and unified source for these fundamental principles.

A monitoring approach is proposed that can handle situations where multiple process rules are in effect, even if there are conflicts between them. This approach develops a monitoring model capable of addressing conflicts and providing execution diagnostics for rules that deviate from the norm. To achieve this, the method calculates the degree of conflict between existing and active execution rules and defines diagnostic metrics based on this ratio. These diagnostics allow users to understand the degree of conflict affecting their process and how much that process diverges from the standard. This approach was tested in the context of a university course registration process and shows potential for application in similar systems.

This research presents a formal system, Proto-Quipper-M, which builds upon the existing quantum programming language, Proto-Quipper-M. By incorporating a sound interpretation within bounded quantum circuits and using an axiomatic approach similar to David W. Ball's Quipper, the study ensures that essential quantum principles like the non-cloning rule and superposition effect are reliably observed. To achieve this, the paper develops a specific framework that explicitly defines program semantics within bounded quantum circuits. This framework, in turn, serves as the foundation for deriving a set of properties specific to the language. Building upon this understanding, the research provides a comprehensive collection of principles, which enables the systematic verification that a quantum program adheres to its specified properties, thus securing the adherence to quantum principles.

We've developed a comprehensive theory for the collective behavior of eigenvalues and eigenvectors in large random-matrix models with specific constraints. By applying the concept of eigenvalue density, we've created a unified framework that captures the scale-dependent behavior of eigenvalues near the spectral edge, even in the presence of boundary conditions. This approach allows us to utilize finite-size scaling to analyze the perimeter-dominated behavior of eigenvectors and connect it to the density of bulk states. Furthermore, we've applied this framework to study the skin effect in a random-matrix model with an anti-unitary symmetry, successfully deriving a scaling relation for bulk eigenvectors and identifying the scaling behavior of "skin" eigenvectors. This analysis also reveals an anti-unitary-determined duality between the perimeter density of eigenvectors and eigenvalues.

We explore the use of two-mode squeezing in enhancing the sensing of an optical phase. Our research involves integrating two-mode squeezing with an optical phase shift, ultimately forming a quantum sensor that utilizes the interference between beam splitters and phase shifts to achieve sensing objectives. This integration results in a matrix transformation that can be interpreted as a combination of two-mode squeezing, phase shifts, and beam splitters. As genomic sequencing technology advances and becomes more precise, assembling large genomes demands efficient methods for dividing complex data.
