A specific approach to this problem, known as multiway number partitioning, can significantly improve the parts of the genomic assembly process that involve over-splitting. One implementation of this approach uses a method that incorporates overlap information to divide overlaps between genomic sequences across multiple processors. Although existing methods vary based on the type of overlaps used, our research shows that considering overlaps more accurately leads to better results. To address the variety of overlaps used in over-lap graphs, we developed a technique to combine overlaps and then applied a multiway number partitioning algorithm to evenly distribute the data among processors. Our results indicate that utilizing this method yields better load balancing and overall performance in over-lap graph based assembly algorithms.

The paper begins with a translation of Gabor Daly's 1957 work on the delayed logistic equation for describing cell populations with a delay in birth rates, caused by a previous threshold in cell proliferation. Following a new proposal by Akhmet and Piekarsky in 2019, we establish a more direct method to obtain a variation of this model that incorporates delay more seamlessly. Our approach enables the model to consistently converge to a positive equilibrium, in contrast to the proposed model, which may lead to the extinction of the population. Our findings are further demonstrated through the application of a delay-bounded integral method that ensures the population remains positive.

A point process, describing the Isometric Log-Ratio (ILR) transformation of a vector of event occurrence times, has been the focus of transformation-based parameter estimation using maximum likelihood. Statistical inference, including confidence regions for parameters, can be established through the transformation's inverse. A simulation study compared ILR analysis and conventional analysis, revealing potential benefits in variable selection and model interpretation.

Researchers in quantum information technology are developing novel types of hybrid quantum circuits known as quantum hybrid conductors to manipulate and generate entangled quantum states at will. These innovative devices can leverage the quantum properties of mesoscopic systems to perform complex quantum operations. Specifically, quantum hybrid circuits composed of superconducting and semiconductor materials are capable of producing entangled Cooper pairs and leveraging their spatial, momentum, and spin correlation properties to implement advanced quantum logic operations. This work provides an in-depth examination of the physical mechanisms behind the formation of entangled Cooper pairs in hybrid quantum sensors, circuits, and computers, and explores the potential for harnessing their quantum correlations to perform precise measurements and quantum information processing tasks.

Investigations into the intricate changes in the nuclear shell structure have been a central theme in the study of shell evolution. To uncover the driving factors behind these transformations, researchers examined the pairing and pairing-energy correlations within the mid-shell regions of nickel and germanium. A notable shift in the levels of single-particle states was observed as nickel evolved to germanium, with a significant discontinuity in the pairing-interaction strength emerging at neutron number 40. This region's transition from nickel to germanium also marked a shift from orbital $f_{7/2}$ to $g_{9/2}$ dominance, resulting in complex alterations to the $g_{9/2}$ level's pairing interactions. By analyzing the changes in pairability within the $g_{9/2}$ and $g_{7/2}$ levels, researchers were able to dissect the origin of this shell-evolution phenomenon.

Deficient-in-neutrons nuclei with high atomic numbers were studied using a combination of hyperfine interaction and isomer shift measurements at a rate of 10^12 per second. Specifically, we measured these values for short-lived, neutron-deficient isotopes such as $^{111}$In, $^{113m}$In, $^{204}$At, and $^{204}$Rn. Our findings revealed that theoretical predictions matched experimental results well for isomer shift measurements of $^{204}$At and $^{204}$Rn, while discrepancies were observed for $^{111}$In and $^{113m}$In.

A cutting-edge approach to generating complex distributions in high dimensions is provided by normalizing flows, yet these flows lack built-in support for the integration of fundamental symmetries. In our work, we introduce a novel framework that enables a more natural representation of $U(1)$ gauge theory, one that is both gauge invariant and efficient. Our framework has been designed to enhance understanding of $U(1)$ gauge theories through its integration into machine learning techniques, and our results reveal that this integrated approach allows for well-trained models to achieve excellent likelihood assessments with relatively few degrees of freedom per unit. Our methodology involves extending a standard affine invariant normalizing flow by introducing a term that enforces gauge symmetry. Our study focuses on demonstrating the efficacy of our flow for a $U(1)$ gauge theory in various configurations by comparing it to established sampling methods. Our findings show that this integrated approach yields well-trained models that are capable of accurately sampling gauge-invariant observables with very few degrees of freedom per system. Our work also highlights several promising avenues of research, one of which is exploring the potential applications of our framework in more intricate theories, and we anticipate that it may be adaptable to a broader range of theories, encompassing more sophisticated gauge symmetries.

We test various methods to recognize unstructured W3JAX forms via a comparative analysis of different datasets and strategies. A key objective is to identify if biased sampling and training enhances recognition performance on specialized forms, such as applications and consent documents. To evaluate different recognition models, we create a set of W3JAX forms to provide standardized input. Results show that biasing significantly improves accuracy in recognizing text following specific formats, but has a more limited effect on free-form content. While biasing and training on forms with known layouts yields the best OCR accuracy, this approach is not always feasible due to the limited number of available forms. We provide detailed findings on how to optimize OCR performance based on document formatting and content type.

The cross-section of top quark pair production is analyzed in a dataset, generated by proton-proton collisions, with an integrated luminosity of 92 nb-1 and a centre-of-mass energy of 800 GeV. The cross-section is estimated using both a direct and a nested method. The results are 1.36 ± 0.06 (statistical error) ± 0.06 (systematic error) nb for the direct approach and 1.36 ± 0.06 (statistical error) ± 0.07 (systematic error) nb for the nested method. The measured cross-section is consistent with predictions from perturbative quantum chromodynamics.

This paper introduces a novel quantum framework that ensures accurate outcomes even when database information is unavailable. We've developed a subroutine to retrieve the inner product of two vectors from a quantum database. By applying this subroutine and incorporating its outcome into a DBNQKR algorithm, we enhance execution precision and reduce errors to 0.000162, down from 0.024411 without database contents. Furthermore, we enhance execution speed by 1.12 times, primarily due to the elimination of two preparatory circuits required in the original DBNQKR method.

We analyze the angular distribution of 4833 LoTSS galaxies using an optimal estimator for the power spectrum of weak gravitational lensing and an estimator for the two-point correlation function, incorporating multiple hypotheses of the $\Lambda$CDM model. Our findings suggest a slight deviation from the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, with $2\sigma$ constraints on the parameter $S_8$ at $S_8 = 0.87^{+0.13}_{-0.11}$, which is consistent with other large-scale structure data sets. Our results provide a new constraint on the parameters of the standard $\Lambda$CDM model, particularly relevant for understanding the distribution of massive galaxies and the impact of evolutionary and mass selection effects on angular clustering statistics.

The Lasso technique excels in rank-one recovery for two-dimensional matrices by incorporating sparsity-inducing regularization, yet its application becomes impractical in high-dimensional settings due to computational complexity, which scales cubically with dimension. A novel predictive sieving method has been developed to efficiently solve the general low-rank sparse rank lasso problem for matrices, extending beyond low-rank regression to encompass various problem formulations. This method's effectiveness hinges on a fundamental property: the solution to the rank lasso problem can be obtained through thresholding the solution to its relaxed quadratic program. By leveraging a hybrid of convex relaxation and sparse approximation, this method significantly reduces the computational burden associated with traditional Lasso techniques, enabling its use in scenarios with matrix dimensions that have a quadratic relationship to the number of samples. In this paper, we propose an innovative adaptive-sieving-based algorithm to tackle the high-dimensional rank lasso problem, involving the iterative refinement of a initially overestimated solution to its relaxed counterpart through a fundamental thresholding principle. This algorithm combines a global Gaussian mixture model to maintain stability, with a localized linear regression technique that ensures convergence under a suitable sparsity condition. Furthermore, we establish an $O(d^2)$ complexity bound for computing an $\epsilon$-accurate solution to low-rank regression, which is not only dimension-independent but also achieves near-optimal performance in terms of the product of variables.

The rate at which entropy is produced in optimal global states has a unique characteristic: it can only be achieved by one specific protocol (up to reordering of its steps). This result is also applicable to the auxiliary rate of entropy production. Our findings complement earlier work on the minimal entropy production rate between nonequilibrium states, where any protocol optimizing the auxiliary rate is unique in terms of its first and last steps. Now, any protocol that minimizes the total entropy produced over a finite number of steps has a unique identity. This uniqueness holds regardless of a particular condition previously thought necessary for its validity.

We're seeing a surge in the use of AI across the network, which has the potential to significantly impact energy consumption. To better understand the environmental implications of AI services, we propose a novel approach that incorporates life cycle assessment and a functional method to evaluate energy consumption. By doing so, we can more accurately measure the energy usage of AI services by considering their complete life cycle, as well as the specific work they perform. We've developed a framework for evaluating the energy usage of AI services in a LCA context, which involves breaking down LCA inventory items into computational tasks and aggregating the energy consumed by each. We've applied this evaluation method to a neural machine translation service, which yielded promising results for now, but a more comprehensive study is needed to better understand the energy impact of AI services in more detail.

Prescriptive process monitoring method development often relies on simulations, yet a key issue arises due to the lack of awareness of a crucial assumption - that there is a connection between operational data and future defects. To address this concern, this research aims to evaluate the effectiveness of these methods with actual data rather than simulations, in line with the principles of evidence-based operations management. The case study focuses on prescriptive process monitoring for spot-welding in an aircraft factory, employing a neural network to predict defects and measure the reliance on defects for method performance assessment. The evaluation reveals that proposed methods can improve makespan reductions by up to 10% while avoiding holds, but these benefits are method-dependent and not guaranteed without the neural defect model's accuracy. By validating the methods with real defect data, the study fills a critical knowledge gap and demonstrates the significance of rigorous validation to prevent methods from being misled by inaccurate simulations. The study's findings and evidence-based operations management principles highlight the necessity of thorough validation and provide a novel approach for evaluating methods using real-world data.

The goal of this research is to develop an effective error estimation method for a coupled problem involving Navier-Stokes equations and a plastic model for quasi-brittle materials, leading to a reliable and efficient numerical simulation of material behavior. The proposed approach utilizes the duality method to provide an approximate error estimate, supplemented by the use of an adaptive algorithm that iteratively refines the solution. The algorithm incorporates the Duale Weighted Residual technique to effectively utilize approximate solutions within an adaptive framework that prioritizes a balance between accuracy and computational efficiency. The effectiveness of this approach is thoroughly evaluated through a range of benchmark tests, demonstrating its potential for resolving issues related to plastic and elastic contact between fluid and solid surfaces.

Graph packing problems, particularly those involving vertex-disjoint paths or cycles, are notoriously difficult to solve with tight bounds. This difficulty stems from the lack of effective methods to determine tight lower and upper bounds on the maximum number of such objects that can be packed. This paper presents a novel technique for establishing tight upper bounds on the maximum number of k-cycles in a graph, with a specified length k, based on novel novel path decomposition methods and new observations on divisibility and cross-terms. As a result of this approach, we successfully derived tight upper bounds on the maximum number of 6-cycles in graphs. Furthermore, we present path decomposition methods that yield improved constants compared to traditional methods for various values of k.

This work revisits the one-dimensional opinion dynamics model that considers agents' opinions as values on a continuous scale between -1 and 1, with neighboring influences pulling towards their own opinions rather than simply shifting them. As a result, the system exhibits complex, time-dependent behaviors where social cliques emerge over time, especially when considering interactions within a finite cluster of agents. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that for certain interaction strengths within a circular arrangement of the same-type agents, the system reaches a stable equilibrium in which the opinions within each clique follow a Gaussian distribution, even as the number of agents in the clique increases. It also confirms the presence of persistent differences in opinions between cliques.

We've discovered an extensive family of black hole solutions that exhibit scalar hair when paired with an electromagnetic field and a scalar field that's sensitive to both. These black holes display properties similar to holographic superconductors as they develop a scalar field's "hair" when a certain temperature threshold is crossed, much like a phase transition in materials. Furthermore, these black holes allow us to investigate quantum corrections in superconductoring black rings and observe how these corrections impact the critical temperature of these black rings. Notably, our analysis reveals that quantum corrections from the scalar fields contribute positively to the critical temperature, whereas corrections from the charged sector can either increase or decrease it, highlighting the complexity and distinct behavior of these black holes compared to other black hole solutions.

Our analysis of the time lag between transcription and mature mRNA is based on two key processes: the time it takes for a gene of a certain length to produce an mRNA that reaches maturity, and the time interval between individual transcriptions. By considering the variability in this lag, we found that the distribution of lagged transcriptions is widest at its center and decreases towards the extremes. Our model of lagged transcriptions is built upon earlier findings about the variability in transcription initiation times, which we verified experimentally by tracking the spacing between fluorescently tagged transcriptions in HeLa cells. Our calculations indicate that the variance in this lag is substantial and cannot be disregarded. Consequently, we developed a novel model for the age of transcriptions within a nucleus that incorporates these lagged events and alternates between them, revealing a peak at the lag's center and decreasing to the extremes. Our model of the distribution of lagged transcriptions is validated by a laboratory experiment, which tracks the production of transcriptions and mature mRNA in mice and reveals a peak at the lag's center that aligns with our model. Our model of the distribution of lagged transcriptions is adaptable and can be applied to any gene in any cell type to estimate the proportion of lagged transcriptions and mature mRNA. Our model also provides a new perspective on the age of transcriptions and mature mRNA within a cell nucleus, which is crucial for understanding the dynamics of gene expression and its impact on cellular function.

Investigations into the excitation energy levels within the nickel isotopic chain have been carried out using inelastic electron scattering, specifically targeting the even-neutron nickel isotopes with mass numbers 58 through 66. This research has revealed that as neutrons are added, the excitation energy of these isotopes decreases in a non-linear pattern. This finding has implications for understanding the shell structure of these isotopes, specifically regarding the gap at $j_{7/2}$ and their monopole interaction properties. This knowledge has been utilized to develop an updated interaction model for neutrons, which in turn has led to a revised understanding of the binding energies within these isotopes, consistent with the observed trends in their nuclear radii. This revision has closed some shell gap values in these isotopes, a closure that has been quantitatively assessed using the Landau-Migdal interaction in the context of self-consistent mean-field theory to determine the ground-state properties of these isotopes. This quantitative analysis has shown that our revised gap predictions are in line with the observed shell closure patterns of these isotopes, a conclusion that has been further supported by comparing our findings with the experimental and theoretical $Q_{\mathrm{ec}}$ values of these isotopes, which has led to a quantitative evaluation of these theoretical $Q_{\mathrm{ec}}$ values of these isotopes, which has led to a quantitative assessment of these theoretical $Q_{\mathrm{ec}}$ values of these

The Wilson loop, particularly its non-abelian behavior, serves as a fundamental concept in SU(N) gauge theories and has an enduring significance in the Abelian non-abelianization of the theory. In SU(N_c) gauge theories with additional Weyl fermions in the adjoint representation, an anomaly arises, contradicting expectations and necessitating an examination of the non-abelian dynamics within the theory's conformal window. Although this anomaly can be interpreted through the lens of the fermions' non-abelian dynamics, an anomaly formula is necessary to quantify these effects and be applicable beyond the conformal window. This paper derives such an anomaly formula, expressing it in terms of the non-abelian Casimir, the abelian T-gonoral, a universal coefficient determined by a universal function of the theory's parameters, and an anomaly coefficient of the non-abelian dynamics.

A new type of group code has been developed using a subgroup of the multiplicative group of a finite field. The code's parameters were determined, and the parameters of its duals, a linear code and a generalized Reed-Muller code, were fully characterized. The code's properties were compared with existing ones, and a complete classification of its duals was achieved. The code and its duals have potential applications in secure communication and key distribution.

Our model, which is based on Bucket Elimination, incorporates an ordering of variables in the Markov Random Field to efficiently perform inference and optimization tasks. This is achieved by partitioning the variables into buckets and their respective neighborhoods, resulting in a significant reduction in the size of the potential functions used for computation. To efficiently manage a large number of buckets, we've created a new data structure that can be extended to Gaussian fields. This model has the potential to be applied in a range of optimization tasks, including the optimization of energy minimization problems and multi-objective optimization.

Our goal is to train a neural network to predict whether an object has been released from the hand based on data gathered from a camera and a microphone. To give the network a basis for making decisions rooted in physical principles, we have designed a comprehensive environment for simulating object interactions that produces and records audio and visual data. This setup enables the collection of annotated image-sound pairs, which we use to train the network. By defining physical characteristics of hand and object models, as well as interaction dynamics, we can calculate interaction times and frequencies, as well as estimate the object's position in 3D space. These characteristics are essential for making predictions grounded in physical principles, which we employ to create and evaluate a dataset for object interaction analysis.

Our investigation into complex phase transitions in dry granular packs reveals both frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming exhibit characteristics of continuous transitions with distinct exponents. Notably, our findings show shear ordering below a unique control parameter threshold leads to an abrupt and unobservable transition type. Our study highlights that attempting to model shear jamming as a second-order transition leads to inaccurate predictions of critical behavior, such as pack densities at the transition point. Our research points out discrepancies between our results and previous studies on second-order transition models, such as the isotropic isotropy restoration transition.

This study employs a novel model called MS(2)-AR(4) to account for seasonality in electricity consumption, in contrast to a standard autoregressive model that assumes consistent behavior. We apply this to 15 months of electricity data from the first month in each of 15 consecutive years. Our analysis uses a maximum likelihood method for parameter estimation and a likelihood ratio test to check for seasonal patterns. The results show that the MS(2)-AR(4) model offers a substantial improvement in model fit and forecast accuracy over the autoregressive model for all electricity demand time series. We also develop a confidence region for the mean electricity consumption under the MS(2)-AR(4) model, utilizing the Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix of logarithmic electricity demand.

Public sector workers should be aware of algorithmic biases in Web search results, given that search engines are integral to their decision-making processes. To investigate the extent of these biases, a study involving 184 participants was conducted. The study aimed to assess whether professionals from various public sector organizations who utilize search engines for their work are influenced by biased search results. To that end, participants were asked to perform real search tasks and were provided with a link to the corresponding search results bias. Approximately half of the public sector workers involved completed this survey. The findings revealed that search results bias indeed affects public sector professionals. The study further demonstrated that search results bias influences how these professionals interpret and make sense of the information on search results pages. Interestingly, the research showed that search results bias also impacts how these professionals utilize search engines in their work. The study's results highlight the significance of addressing and mitigating algorithmic bias to ensure fair and equitable decision-making within public sector organizations.

Our research introduces a novel, versatile program synthesis framework that excels at generating high-quality C code for arithmetic-logic-expression benchmarks within a wide range of user-defined constraints. The framework's efficiency and adaptability are demonstrated through its swift average performance of less than two seconds per synthesized program and its capacity to incorporate user-specific requirements within its core design. The underlying architecture of our framework is rooted in a innovative, highly expressive syntax called NLV. This syntax NLV combines a compact set of constructs with an advanced parsing system to produce an extensive and diverse program space. To further enhance program synthesis, our research introduces a sophisticated evaluation metric that accurately assesses the correctness of synthesized programs without incurring any performance degradation, and a novel evaluation protocol that enables users to preview and select the most promising synthesized programs. The effectiveness of our framework is substantiated by a set of benchmark evaluations, which reveal its capacity to generate programs equivalent to industry-standard solutions in terms of speed and reliability, and its ability to consistently produce synthesized code that outperforms state-of-the-art models in zero-shot settings by an average of 20%.

Climate reduction techniques are increasingly being used to interpret complex climate simulations, a process that is being facilitated by the development of novel statistical methods. This work presents two such design-level reduction approaches, which are PDE discovery methods aimed at uncovering the structure of an underlying system of partial differential equations. These methods are tested on a comprehensive climate-reduced model of the Earth's climate, involving 36 variables, and demonstrate their efficacy in accurately identifying the structure of the governing differential equations. However, these discovery methods are found to be less effective at reconstructing the full set of differential equations. In response, an adaptive discovery method is introduced to iteratively refine its findings and successfully identify the differential equations driving the reduced-order model. The results of this study pave the way for applying reduction techniques to diverse climate models and serve as a blueprint for discovering the structure of complex differential equation models within a reduced-order modeling framework.

Gravitational wave events that also involve matter can lead to the formation of material similar to that produced in supernovae. These events can create extremely bright stellar explosions known as kilonovae, which emit strong light in specific lines within the electromagnetic spectrum. The James Webb Space Telescope, with its advanced capabilities, is capable of detecting these lines, which fall within its infrared vision, even in distant galaxies. The movement of these lines due to the expansion of the universe shifts them into observable ranges for the NIRSpec instrument on board the JWB space telescope. The stellar explosions following a neutron star collision can appear bright enough to be detected by the space telescope at great distances. The data that the space telescope can gather using these observations will help scientists understand the fundamental processes behind these stellar explosions and how they change over time.

When delivering an X-ray beam, oncologists face significant challenges from external interference, including incoming light and natural daylight, which can impair their ability to accurately aim the beam. To address this issue, a novel sensor was created to detect various forms of distracting light and transmit it to the X-ray beam's imaging system via a camera. The performance of the sensor was evaluated by collecting and processing data from diverse light sources to train and assess its efficiency in transferring the images to its intended application.

In the analysis of high-dimensional compositional data, log-transforming each vector component is a common step, yet it can be challenging to apply due to the presence of zeros or near-zeros. A computationally efficient method is proposed to mitigate this issue, drawing from the theory of high-dimensional statistics. By utilizing this approach, a novel closed-form solution is developed to perform a multi-parameter log-normal transformation on complex compositional data, taking into consideration the influence of sparsity.

A statistical examination of exoplanets discovered via radial velocity observations is conducted to assess the accuracy of the core accretion model in explaining planet formation. To achieve this, an analytical description of final planet masses and separations resulting from the formation process is proposed. By comparing this model with existing exoplanet data, it's observed that the model correctly predicts the tendency for runaway gas accretion to occur at greater orbital distances, but fails to accurately predict the distribution of massive planets, which is found to be more broadly distributed than the model suggests.

A novel AI model, called Agent2, has been created that operates within a deep reinforcement learning framework. Agent2 is capable of its own initiative in identifying crucial environmental states. It uses a unique memory system with distinct memory cells and employs dynamic weighting to focus on relevant memories. During decision-making, Agent2 integrates its memory with deep reinforcement learning techniques. We demonstrate that Agent2.1, the simplest version of our model, outperforms state-of-the-art AI models in predicting partial observations, and we show that Agent2.2, the most complex version, successfully follows a rational strategy to monitor hidden states. Furthermore, Agent2.2 consistently discovers and retains essential memories, which it uses to improve its decision-making and policy choices.

We examine spin-independent dark matter-nucleon interactions resulting from the exchange of a scalar mediator that has a non-zero vacuum expectation value. The non-Standard Model scalar we consider includes the Higgs, a singlet in an extended scalar sector, and components of a complex bi-doublet from a minimal Majorana fermion dark matter model. When the dark matter candidate is considerably lighter than the mediator's mass, commonly observed in direct detection experiments, contact approximation is appropriate. Conversely, when dark matter and mediator masses are similar, this approximation breaks down. We analyze how this approximation influences predicted rates for several direct detection experiments and find that it can lead to substantial differences in predicted signals. We also investigate how signals from nuclear recoil and ionization are connected. Additionally, we investigate how signals from nuclear recoil and ionization are related. Finally, we map out how direct and indirect signals for dark matter are related.

A diverse collection of cognitive tasks is essential for creating intelligent systems 
capable of adapting to changing objectives. This study proposes Mod-Cog, an 
expansive and balanced set of 25 tasks across 5 cognitive domains, surpassing 
existing sets with its complexity and versatility. Each task is carefully chosen 
from well-established literature, incorporating simpler variants of well-known 
tasks and providing an array of task characteristics for effective research. 
Mod-Cog encompasses tasks ranging from very high complexity, akin to the TAC 
(CAR) task. A comprehensive benchmark was established by determining task 
similarities using multiple criteria, uncovering both established and 
previously unexplored task domains. The study presents a range of battery 
configurations, utilizing task complexity and similarity to generate 
unforeseen scenarios suitable for evaluating adaptable learning systems. 
Mod-Cog's extensive nature enables the examination of multi-task learning in 
novel and demanding contexts, opening avenues for further exploration within 
this area.

We investigate the geometric characteristics of nilpotent algebra varieties. 
Given a commutative symmetric algebra $A$, which is a nilpotent algebra with a m-times square equals zero property, where $m$ is a non-negative integer, we denote by $\mathcal{N}$ the variety of all nilpotent algebra varieties that can be formed using tensors over $A$. 
This variety $\mathcal{N}$ consists of various algebra varieties that can be represented as $A \otimes_{k} M$, where $k$ represents the field of scalar coefficients and $M$ is a $m+1$ dimensional space of multilinear maps. 
It is established that $\mathcal{N}$ has specific properties: it is an irreducible variety with a field of definition that can be extended, and its dimension can be calculated based on $m$ and the number of elements in $A$. 
Furthermore, it is shown that the nilpotent algebra varieties that can be formed using tensors over $A$ are a dense subset of $\mathcal{N}$. 
Additionally, we prove that for a finite dimensional field of definition that can be real or complex, it is possible to find a nilpotent algebra where the product of certain elements equals zero, and which cannot be obtained as $A \otimes_{k} M$ for any $A$ and $M$. 
This has significant implications for the dimension of $\mathcal{N}$ and

The primary reason for the observable light from large cosmic radiation jets is the emission of photons through Compton interactions of fast-moving electrons with photons from the Cosmic Microwave Background. To better understand the effects of this process, we developed an efficient and precise numerical model for simulating Compton scattering, by combining relativistic velocity transformations with the Doppler shift. The new model compares positively with established methods and is now available for integration with other radiation hydrodynamics codes.

To achieve an analytical post-Newtonian expansion in general relativity, a specific parameterization that's neither pre nor post-relativistic facilitates expansion. We introduce a new post-non-relativistic parameterization, enabling smooth post-Newtonian expansion while maintaining well-defined, well-behaved Schwarzschild coordinates at the zeroth order. This novel parameterization does not rely on a post-Newtonian series but rather on the post-SPR (slowly moving particles in the non-relativistic limit) one, in accordance with the philosophy of general relativity.

This research introduces a novel method of image registration called SIFT-CPD, specifically designed for use in whole-body MRI and abdominal CT scans. The proposed method combines the robust feature matching technique of SIFT with the robust point-based CPD algorithm. To address the limitations of existing feature-based methods, which can be sensitive to variation and noise, the authors leverage CPD's robust estimation. The authors implement their method by first registering keypoint features using a bipartite matching approach to create feature-to-point correspondences, and then refining the matches with CPD. The authors evaluate SIFT-CTP on synthetic images and real CT and MRI scans of lungs, pancreas and kidneys. The results indicate significant improvement in image overlap and feature overlap when compared to existing feature-based and point-based methods. The authors attribute this improvement to the robust CPD optimization of feature-to-point correspondences.

We examine a rapidly rotating binary star system formed by two white dwarfs that undergoes periodic eclipses, originating from the SDSS data. Its unique characteristics include a non-uniform light pattern caused by the rapid rotation and the presence of a magnetic field evidenced by strong magnetic star markings. By analyzing the light variations and a specific type of emission known as the He II lambda 2280 Angstrom, which signifies that one of the component stars is of the DA type, we determined that it consists of a slow-rotating, magnetically weak DA white dwarf and a fast-rotating, magnetically strong DA white dwarf. Furthermore, a detailed analysis of the shape of the light variations enabled the calculation of a precise distance between the two components and their size. What's more, a three-dimensional model of the system was developed, which also indicated the presence of an accretion disk. Finally, we also calculated the period derivative of the system and determined the rate at which it is changing, which might eventually lead to a merger of the two components.

A newly introduced layer, the UOT-Pooling layer, can be integrated into existing
convolutional neural networks to boost their performance without altering the
network's overall architecture or parameter count. UOT-Pooling layer utilizes optimal
transport theory to determine the most effective mapping between feature maps from
different resolution channels. This approach effectively consolidates multiple
channel features into a single lower-resolution feature set by assigning each high
resolution feature a unique weight to the lowest resolution feature. This unique
weight assignment minimizes the transport cost between features and effectively
prevents information loss during the pooling process. Because of its beneficial
effects on neural network performance, UOT-Pooling layer can be utilized across a
range of networks and tasks, ultimately leading to significant improvements in the
accuracy of neural networks for applications such as image classification and
segmentation.

This study examines the alignment of 209 Seyfert  nuclei from the NASA/IPAC Infrared Astronomical Observatory's Seyfert Research Archive in galaxies from the 2MASS Point Source Catalog, and relates their orientation to their host galaxy's morphological class. We discovered a significant trend where the orientation of Class 1 nuclei varies depending on their host galaxy's morphological class, but Class 2 nuclei show no such pattern. Class 1 and 2 nuclei from spiral galaxies are more likely to be oriented towards us, whereas those in other galaxy types show a more uniform orientation. We propose that this pattern might result from the active galactic nucleus being obscured by a disk structure in spiral galaxies, specifically for Class 1 AGN. We also found that the degree of nuclear obscuration decreases as the morphological class of the host galaxy progresses from Sc to Sd/ir. We also noticed that Sbc/ later and Sc/ir galaxies have a higher proportion of class 1 Seyfarts, suggesting that this type of AGN is more likely to be found in these galaxies. We propose that this pattern might be due to a relationship between the fueling of the AGN and the global star-formation rate of the galaxy, and that the Seyfert unification model might need an additional absorbing element to fully explain the observed patterns.

This paper examines the relationship between flat general rotational surfaces and their pointwise 1-Gauss maps, establishing a precise connection between these concepts and providing clear characterizations and associated maps for these surfaces.

A key benefit of unsupervisedly estimating scene geometry from image data is
that it could serve as an effective way to pre-train neural networks without the
need for extensive labeled datasets.  In contrast, commonly used approaches like
self-supervised image classification pre-train using large yet relatively small
datasets with weak self-supervision signals.  To address this issue, we
introduce Deep CIFR, a novel novel representation that enciphers flat images into
3D CIFR volumes, which can be applied universally across various scenes and
estimates geometry self-supervisionally by minimizing the temporal discrepancy
between successive CIFR volumes in video data, thus providing a more robust
self-supervision signal.  To supplement Deep CIFR's weak geometric self-supervision,
we incorporate an additional strength by pre-training with additional
self-supervised tasks that do not rely on labels.  Our results demonstrate that
Deep CIFR yields a 100% improvement in performance and superior generalization
capabilities in 3D reconstruction and rendering compared to state-of-the-art
techniques.

TCube is a Time-Cube Analysis Base that facilitates the examination of a single time-series and two other metrics represented as cubes. By utilizing a straightforward and efficient data structure, TCube enables the rapid comparison of multiple dimension combinations. In this paper, we describe the TCube data structure, our approach to data acquisition, and a simple but effective annotation tool we developed to mitigate the issue of finding annotated training data. We also present a time-series analysis method based on a single time-series and two other metrics represented as a cube and the effect it has on detecting significant changes, which we demonstrate using real-world data.

We have calculated the standard model predictions for the $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay and the $B^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay with momentum selection rules, taking into account chromomagnetic penguin corrections. The $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay prediction is $3.154^{\pm 0.034}\times 10^{-40} \textrm{cm}^3$, $b^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ prediction is $2.14^{\pm 0.04}\times 10^{-63} \textrm{cm}^3$. The results are in line with the experimental data for $B^0_s\to \mu^+\mu^-$ but $B^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ requires a higher significance. The findings indicate that the $B^0\to \mu^+\mu^-$ decay may be a candidate for a new physics process.

The Ising model on a Cayley tree based on the free product of two groups of order $l_1$ and $l_2$ is studied, where the Cayley tree's fundamental group is considered. By applying a spin action that turns the Ising model into a dynamic process on a tree, an expression is derived for the tree's dynamic condition using the tree's basic group. This result allows the determination of the model's equilibrium states and confirms the existence of at least one equilibrium state. An investigation into the uniqueness of these equilibrium states is also carried out.

The geometric characteristics of the phase space in hyperbolic equations offer a deeper insight into the phenomenon of smoothness loss, which enables us to establish precise conditions for this to occur by leveraging the metric defined by Christ. By demonstrating that the $L^2$-phase space for the wave equation is equivalent to the set of functions with compact support, we provide more comprehensive conditions for the preservation of $H_{loc}^{s_0}$, particularly in one spatial dimension, and extends to a more general class of linear equations, and also to non-linear equations like the $L^2$-subcritical Klein-Gordon equation.

This research paper outlines a novel application of Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks to enhance Japanese word segmentation accuracy. By integrating feature lattices, we have successfully addressed the challenges inherent in Japanese word segmentation, which has historically relied on complex morphological analysis. Our approach has yielded a significant reduction in segmentation errors, specifically a 31% decrease in Average Segment Error Rate, compared to the conventional method based on force-directed segmentation.

Stack Overflow, a widely utilized platform for programmers and software developers, features more than 225,000 publicly accessible questions answered with 1,100,000 external shared resources. Our analysis of these shared resources reveals the most frequently reused URLs to be those belonging to specific online courses, particularly those offered by Coursera and Udacity. A notable finding is the heavy reliance on course materials, especially assignments, test cases, and sample projects, leading to the conclusion that students and professionals heavily depend on course materials for resolving complex problems and implementing code features. Our research also highlights the need for students and professionals to develop essential skills to avoid over-reliance on external resources and to foster original problem-solving abilities.

N-body simulations of a wide range of galaxy masses and sizes are conducted to analyze the differences in dark matter halo densities. We examine the distribution of the dark matter halo density at specific distances from the halo center, focusing on a core region containing approximately 100 particles to ensure thermal equilibrium. We find that the initial conditions have a significant impact on the central density, but after the dark matter halo reaches a state of thermal equilibrium, the effect is reduced to a minimum. We conclude that this equilibrium state, or 'isothermal core,' can lead to the diverse rotation curves of galaxy halos through the expansion of this core as the galaxy halo grows.

To inspire action against climate change, it's essential to grasp the connection between individuals' personal values and their behavior. This relationship has been explored through qualitative research, yet a value system that captures the diversity of value influences on climate change attitudes and actions remains unclear. This study aims to fill this gap by conducting a comprehensive analysis of climate change activists' and defenders' values in three nations - the US, Germany, and India - via in-depth interviews. The results reveal a universal value system comprising ten components, whose combinations in various subgroups correlate with their climate change actions. We will discuss how these findings can be applied to promote climate change mitigation and provide practical examples of leveraging these insights to nudge individuals toward adopting a pro-climate lifestyle, ultimately contributing to sustainable actions within our community.

In this research, our primary objective is to enhance the accuracy of clinical text analysis using advanced NLP techniques and advanced computer vision. Our focus within clinical NLP lies in accurately identifying symptoms and classifying their severity, which are critical components for medical diagnosis. Text data is inherently diverse and subject to significant variation based on individual writing styles, making this a particularly complex task. Our proposed solution involves employing a domain generalization approach to improve model performance across a wide array of patient demographics. Complementing this, we introduce a novel framework that employs self-supervised pre-training on an expansive, unlabeled dataset of patient responses, prior to fine-tuning on a smaller, annotated segment of the diverse population. Our experiments reveal that combining domain generalization and self-supervised pre-training significantly enhances the effectiveness of symptom recognition and severity assessment across various medical conditions, despite their complexity and variability.

Autonomous vehicles present a complex challenge due to their partially observable nature. It's well-documented that Hidden Markov Models have limited effectiveness in this context. Recent advancements in Reccurent Neural Networks seem to offer more promise. To test this hypothesis, we developed a novel framework integrating Recurrent Units within a Particle Filter used for localizing vehicles in partially observable environments. Our findings indicate that using Recurrent Units within the Particle Filter allows it to learn a mapping between a hidden state and observation space, thereby improving performance even in difficult partially observable situations.

We introduce the concept of a distributed and collaborative classifier called ADP-CDC, which is a type of spiking neural network (SNN) that is energy-efficient with the potential to be used in edge computing. The classifier's distributed memory is filled with data that has been received through a balanced input stream of random spikes, and its hidden layers consist of adaptive threshold linear support vector machines (adSVMs) that are adapted to function with inherent temporal characteristics. The adPDC model and its learning algorithm are optimized in terms of their hyperparameters as well. The SNN classifier demonstrates comparable performance to conventional ANN classifiers in terms of accuracy while also exhibiting low power consumption. As a classifier with distributed memory, our proposed model is highly suitable for edge computing applications where a data stream is distributed across multiple spatial locations. To showcase the classifier's efficacy and versatility, we evaluated its performance using two binary classification problems: one to identify handwritten digits and the other to classify sea mammals from recorded audio recordings. The results indicate that our proposed model outperforms state-of-the-art ANN and SNN classifiers in terms of accuracy and energy efficiency. The SNN classifier's distributed memory also allows it to be applied to multiple support vector regression problems as demonstrated using an open dataset of sea level rise time-series data, and our model is able to accurately predict sea level variations while also being robust to noisy input data.

This article examines the soft theorems for a strongly magnetic field alongside the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter, specifically considering both non-relativistic and relativistic conditions. Our findings demonstrate that for a strong magnetic field, the soft theorems for polarized strange quark matter result in significantly softer equations of state compared to neutral matter, particularly as it pertains to spin-up and spin-down states, majoritarian, and minoritarian quark matter. Furthermore, for a very strong magnetic field, we computed the speed of sound for polarized strange quark matter and discovered that it can decrease to nearly zero in a majoritarian quark matter scenario. These theoretical outcomes align with recent data from gravitational wave observations and suggest that for such scenarios, a strong magnetic field could facilitate spin-polarization in strange quark matter, thereby softening its equation of state.

Social platforms like Pantheon enable users to contribute their idle processing power to a distributed network, allowing them to share the load of resource-intensive tasks such as image classification. We evaluate the effectiveness of our social microgrid, Pando, in harmonizing the synchronization, input, and output operations of user devices to form a unified system that can efficiently execute distributed computing protocols. By enabling multiple personal devices to collaborate, Pando enhances computational efficiency beyond the capabilities of a single device, while maintaining flexibility in terms of computational tasks, communications, and resource management. Tests demonstrate that in scenarios involving data transfer limitations, collaborative devices achieve a 2.5 times faster data processing rate, and in scenarios with rapid transfers, they reach a 6 times higher throughput compared to a single device. Additionally, user surveys indicate that collaborative computing has significant potential in the field of IoT, with over 90 percent of users showing interest in applications such as IoT and edge computing.

We integrate an adaptive sampling technique into a novel numerical method for estimating eigenvalues and their corresponding functions. This method, based on a stochastic variant of the Nystr\"om algorithm, leverages the Quadrature-Tree to dynamically adjust its sampling and reduce computational costs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this hybrid approach in a several-dimensional case, showing how it achieves faster numerical performance.

We describe the intermediate beta-transformations whose survivor sets have a Lebesgue measure zero, which happens precisely when the associated set of badly approximable numbers from certain non-integer bases also has zero measure. For these transformations, we provide necessary and sufficient conditions for their unique codimension-one ergodic measures to be smooth, which in turn gives rise to an abundance of examples of non-ergodic measures with smooth local graphs. Our results demonstrate the versatility of codimension-one ergodic measures in the context of these transformations, which can be utilized to identify badly approximable numbers in non-integer bases that fail to satisfy specific Diophantine properties. Moreover, our approach enables us to verify Conjecture \ref{conj} for a certain class of vectors, while supporting the broader claim stated in \ref{prop} with notable examples.

This work investigates Dedekind sum-related identities originating from one-loop Dedekind zeta functions in $SO(N_c)$ gauge theories with $U(N_{F})$ chiral symmetry, given the theories lack real quark flavors and zero topological charge. Refined zeta function Dedekind identities are also examined for their relevance to super-Dedekind zeta functions from $SO(N_c)$ super Yang-Mills theories.

Evaluating the impact of individual time series features on time series time series is a highly practical goal in various applications such as understanding personal activity patterns from wearable devices or predicting bike-sharing usage from weather data. In this paper, we introduce a new approach called Disentangled Attribution Courts that can detect and isolate distinct patterns of high impact within a target time series by analyzing multiple high impact periods. We first show the efficacy of this method through experiments on real-world data, and then extend it to uncover long-term high impact trends by analyzing the characteristics of disentangled impact patterns. The proposed method has been tested on several real-world case studies and has consistently outperformed baseline attribution methods, and we further extend it to identify notable impact patterns over time.

In the context of federated learning, various approaches have been proposed to ensure client anonymity, yet existing methods suffer from several drawbacks such as requiring substantial modifications to standard FL procedures, relying on a trusted third party, or incurring considerable computational and communication overhead. To overcome these limitations, we have devised a novel solution that requires minimal changes to the existing FL framework, does not depend on a trusted third party, and significantly reduces additional computational workloads and communication costs. The efficiency of our solution is demonstrated through theoretical analysis as well as empirical results, which reveal it to be at least 5 times more efficient than the current state-of-the-art approach in terms of communication costs.

We suggest a novel approach for implementing Test Drivers on user-friendly microcontrollers within a particular region of interest. The solution involves creating two key elements: a Test Driver Interface (TDI) microcontroller that generates predefined signal patterns, and a Pattern Analyzer (PA) that compares these patterns to a predefined list, taking into account a certain tolerance level. The outcome of the analysis is then transmitted via a digital protocol to a host computer for further processing. The effectiveness of the solution was verified through the use of several microcontrollers, including ATmega328P, ATmega2560, and ATmega1280.

Code emulation is becoming a vital tool for preventing applications from triggering security threats. By predicting system calls and avoiding those not made in the original program, emulation builds a customized filter for every application. Previously unfeasible for interpreted languages like PHP and Python, this process is now feasible due to their distinctive system call patterns and predictable behavior. We have developed a technique called Timeloops, which uses system call traces to automatically prevent system calls in interpreted language programs. We have evaluated Timeloops' effectiveness on various benchmark applications and found that our method accurately filters system calls not only when targeting known malicious inputs but also unknown zero-day inputs.

Single-cell RNA sequencing identifies cell types by measuring gene expression, but the sparsity of these measurements poses challenges for accurate classifications. Techniques like dimensionality reduction and clustering have been used to improve performance, but formal comparisons of these methods are lacking. We conducted an experiment comparing various methods for two-dimensional European and American data sets as well as simulated scRNA sequencing data sets. We found that by performing classification in a low-dimensional product space, we achieved four to five times faster processing and superior accuracy compared to classifying in the original Euclidean space. Our approach combines KNN classification with dimensionality reduction using principal component analysis or a novel method called quantile transformation of PCA, which transforms negative eigenvalues to positive values and reduces the influence of large eigenvalues. This method outperformed PCA, t-SNE, and PLS in most instances and enabled efficient storage and processing of transformed low-dimensional spaces for multiple datasets.

For a supermassive black hole that is surrounded by an equal number of Neutron stars and White dwarfs, we analyze how three different initial stellar mass functions affect the White dwarfs and Neutron stars over a period of up to 10 Hubble times, using a code that sim gravitational scattering near a supermassive black hole. The simulation shows that, due to the conservation of the number of Neutron stars and White dwarfs, a core that has been formed and that consists of supermassive stars, will naturally consist of four massive stars of equal mass. The simulation shouls that, with a population of Neutron stars, a core that consists of four massive stars, will reach a maximum of ten times the mass of the black hole, with ten Hubble times, whereas a core that consists of four four-solar mass stars, will reach ten times the mass of the black hole, with ten Hubble times. The simulation shouls that, with a population of White dwarfs, a core that consists of four massive stars, will reach ten times the mass of the black hole, with ten Hubble times, whereas a core that consists of four massive stars, will reach ten times the mass of the black hole, with ten Hubble times. The simulation shouls that, with a population of Neutron stars, a core that consists of four massive stars, will reach ten times the mass of the black hole, with ten Hubble times, whereas

This article introduces a novel approach to stochastic Model Predictive Control of linear systems with uncertain parameters, modeled as random variables with known distributions. The proposed method, which accounts for uncertainties, is implemented through a stochastic affine policy, and its implementation is facilitated by a affine system, the parameters of which are optimized to minimize performance deviations. The objective, which considers uncertainties, is addressed by implementing a affine control policy and evaluating its performance in relation to the nominal trajectory and future reference signal. The performance is quantified using an expected value of a quadratic cost function that measures the deviations in a generalized sense and is dependent on the distribution of uncertainties. The proposed affine control law, which considers uncertainties, is optimized using an iterative algorithm that minimizes the expected value of the cost function. The effectiveness of the proposed model is demonstrated through simulation of a cart-pole system with uncertainties.

The primary goal of this research is to introduce novel Compressive ICA methods that necessitate minimal memory usage, reducing it to just a few multiples of the size of the mixture matrix. By integrating Compressive Sensing principles with the fast ICA algorithm, our compressive ICA approaches can identify significant directions of variance without storing the full covariance matrix or eigenvectors of the mixture matrix, yielding a considerable memory efficiency gain. Moreover, by applying a novel compression technique to the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck process, we enable compressive ICA to converge quickly and converge in a manner nearly proportional to the target dimensionality. Both theoretical analysis and numerical experiments confirm that our compressive ICA algorithms achieve rapid and reliable results in scenarios where the number of target directions is much smaller than the number of available measurements. Consequently, these algorithms hold great promise for applications in the analysis of massive datasets generated by high-dimensional sensors, such as those employed in genomics, neuroimaging, and climate science.

In an $n$-dimensional integer grid where two species initially occupy adjacent sites with different species on all surrounding sites, we examine the dynamic between these species under the asymmetric noisy voter model. As the competition between these two species evolves over time, it may result in an outcome where one species eliminates the other, or both species persist in a prolonged coexistence that could theoretically last indefinitely. Our research focuses on an irreversible model that always ends in a draw. Introducing a modification to make the noisy voter model symmetric at a specific site leads to a transition from prolonged coexistence to species extinction occurring abruptly at a critical threshold.

We investigate von Neumann algebras generated by network states, specifically focusing on a model where the Hamiltonian $H$ satisfies the condition of being a ground state without frustration, given that $H$ acts locally on the Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ and commutes with the corresponding local operators. Under this condition, it is demonstrated that the time evolution, constrained to these local operators, forms a von Neumann algebra with two-dimensional factors for each element of the discrete set $\Lambda$. It is further demonstrated that, in one dimension, all Type II local algebras from such network states are equivalent. The findings can be applied to quantum circuit states, one-dimensional quantum network states, and the ground states of one-dimensional quantum systems with local Hamiltonians that have gapped spectra.

A system consisting of two oscillators connected by mass-spring connections of various types is analyzed in an investigation into quantum correlations. One link operates under consistent conditions, while the other experiences random fluctuations due to thermal effects or loss of energy, all within a system isolated from external influences. By studying a model that initially shows entanglement in the absence of loss, we find that these internal effects on the connectors have significant impacts on the system's ability to resist entanglement loss due to heat. It's also discovered that these effects have similar effects on system correlations as do external influences, provided there is no heat in the environment. Furthermore, we identify an optimal level of loss that maximizes system correlations for certain combinations of heat and heat.

The novel approach to creating subtraction terms for massless QCD cross-section calculations at the one-loop level is based on a fundamental splitting operator that captures the behavior of partons coming together in a specific, extremely collinear configuration. We have successfully calculated a specific complex configuration of three colliding partics at the one-loop level and verified our results against theoretical predictions from another approach to these calculations. Our calculated splitting operator is consistent with other parton interactions and can be used as a building block to derive other splitting operators through mathematical transformation.

We extend Greenberg's strong approximation theorem to a broader class of rings: one-dimensional local rings with an infinite residue field. For such a case, we develop a analogous approximation theorem based on Greenberg's original ideas. Furthermore, we explore the applicability of this theorem to specific instances, including its potential use in Greenberg-Straub's Iwasawa theory for general formal schemes.

This study explores the utilization of sundials in scientific research, particularly through citizen science initiatives, to enhance documentation and understanding of these timekeeping instruments in Indonesia. By combining approaches of archaeoastronomy and geographic information systems (GIS), we developed a system to map and analyze sundials' locations and orientations across Indonesia. As part of the ISOTIA project, we collected data on 329 sundials through online resources and citizen science programs, aiming to fill in knowledge gaps and facilitate further investigation into sundials' historical and cultural significance. Our analysis highlights the potential for archaeoastronomy and GIS integration to enrich the study of sundials and their associated cultures in Indonesia.

This study introduces a novel data and energy transfer approach called DED2D (Data Enable Device to Device), which is an innovative solution to address limitations in simultaneous wireless information and power transfer techniques. DED2M devices act as energy and data relays, first being enabled by a base station through wireless power and data, and then enabling other device through wireless energy and data in the second phase of a two-time slot system. A specific enabling method, TFIET (Traffic Enabled), is introduced, which allows a DED2M to be enabled by a base station through wireless power and data in the first phase of a two-time slot system, and then enable other device by forwarding the data it was enabled with in the first phase, along with additional data from a base station, through wireless energy and data in the second phase. A detailed theoretical model of the DED2D approach, which incorporates the TFIET scheme, is developed and the effects of key parameters on the achieved data and energy rates are examined in the context of a two-dimensional scenario. A numerical example is provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed data and energy simultaneous wireless information and power transfer approach, which outperforms an alternative approach that solely transmits data and energy to the relay nodes.

The growing need for automation of experimental setups, driven by increased remote work opportunities, can be met by implementing techniques such as computer vision, robotic vision, and computer-aided design (CAD) assistance for task completion. A proposed partial automation approach, tailored for vacuum systems, is presented, which can be applied to other setups as well. The system, developed using CAD, executes a specific task, such as opening a vacuum valve, via a computer mouse, when prompted by a position change in the virtual CAD setup, without requiring any image processing. A proposed image-based automation approach, involving the imaging and tracking of a valve, is also presented, which can be applied to other value-added tasks as well. Experimental validation of the automation methods has been conducted using an actual vacuum setup, which verifies their effectiveness and confirms their potential for enhanced development to accommodate more complex tasks.

We can expand P's definition to include all undirected bipartite graphs with unique edge lengths, allowing for a broader interpretation of Asker's idea that every such graph represents a concept similar to the set of pairs of integers that can be computed by a deterministic Turing machine. This concept is more wide-ranging than that of spectra, which represent only those deterministically-computable sets of integers. Building upon previous work, our findings in [arXiv:1909.01044] and [arXiv:1909.01044] show that this idea is local in nature and leads to a new, relaxed version of Asser's conjecture. This new version states that every concept similar to the set of pairs of integers that can be computed by a deterministic Turing machine can be characterized by a local rule on bipartite graphs without direction. This revised version of Asser's conjecture is more likely to be true. This outcome is significant because it demonstrates that even if we can't prove Asser's idea directly, we can find a more lenient version of it involving undirected bipartite graphs that is more plausible to be true. This revised version of the idea is, in fact, equivalent to a modified version of the famous L versus P problem. This revised version of the idea is, in turn, equivalent to another modified version of the famous NP versus P problem, which involves directed bipartite graphs with direction

A new method is proposed that combines quantum simulation and analytical models to design complex patterns within electrostatic phase plates, ensuring minimal distortion of electron beams while achieving a desired phase shift. This novel design approach considers fill-factor and pixel arrangement, resulting in significantly improved probe size and current density compared to conventional circular phase plates. Two distinct types of square-based phase patterns are designed: one with varying fill factors to test feasibility, and another with a highly symmetric pattern to minimize probe size and current density. By employing a Wigner function method, the proposed design can yield a 10-15% reduction in probe size and recovery of approximately 70% of lost current density compared to traditional designs. Furthermore, the underlying design principles are applicable to electrostatic lenses and other beam manipulation devices.

We introduce a physical implementation of quantum computation based on stable flux qubits and Josephson junction circuits. This mechanism relies on a stable structure that can be manipulated through magnetic fields, which enables efficient scaling and control of the system. By exploiting this property, we developed a protocol for performing universal quantum computation via inductive loading and fine-tuning magnetic fields. Moreover, we found that even minute adjustments in the frequency spectrum suffice to accurately evaluate any computation within the quantum framework. This computational approach also exhibits exceptional resilience against decoherence and code errors due to the stable structure of the system and the precise parametric modulation technique. Notably, we found that the quantum computation's precision can be enhanced by optimizing the frequency spectrum, which is influenced by the system's qubit properties and the applied magnetic field. This feature allows for the possibility of achieving highly accurate quantum computation.

For a continuous random walk in space, starting from the origin, the average time it takes to visit or start the $d$-dimensional space one step further away, is calculated when the walk has reached a point located at a point $d$ dimensions away, is calculated. We then compare this average time for a walk in $d$ dimensions with the average time for a similar walk in the $d+1$ dimensions space. We establish a relationship between these two average times and express it in terms of a hypergeometric function. We also derive a differential equation that the this average time satisfies and use this to obtain an explicit expression for large $d$. Finally, it is shown that the average time for a walk in $d$ dimensions has a maximum when $d=4$.

In our investigation, we explore a novel polymer black hole model, which is characterized by a quantized, discrete structure at its event horizon, in contrast to the singular nature of traditional general relativity black holes. This model is applied in a vacuum setting, where the vacuum is replaced by a discrete energy-forming quantum, leading to a 'horizon fluid' with properties that allow us to analyze its effect on the black hole's geometry. We utilize this model to recover some key features of wormholes, such as their smooth spatial appearance and plastic-like behavior, but with a key distinction being the absence of an escapeable exit. We examine how this structure influences the black hole geometry, especially at the horizon, where the effects of quantum discreteness become most pronounced. We also investigate how these properties affect the black hole's thermodynamic stability and its loss of information. Notably, we found that the energy conditions are satisfied by the horizon fluid, allowing us to maintain the energy's positive energy density and non-zero pressure, which in turn results in a smooth structure at the horizon. This novel model offers a promising approach to understanding how quantum discreteness could prevent the loss of information and provide a quantum structure for black holes, which may one day unify quantum mechanics and gravity.

In a series of experimentally verified graphene-like sheets with various lattice distortions, we examine the low-energy properties of doped graphs, focusing on their relevance to high-temperature superconductivity. Utilizing numerical data and analytical calculations, we determine how quasiparticle velocity and interaction parameters influence thermodynamic attributes. Specifically, we investigate the quasiparticle velocity's impact on specific heat and magnetic susceptibility, and analyze its distribution. Furthermore, we demonstrate that doping alters the logarithmic mass renormalization, and this effect is sensitive to underlying lattice structure. Our findings indicate that, for an optimized Fermi liquid, the renormalized quasiparticle velocity decreases with doping level. Consequently, this leads to a reduction in specific heat, and our prediction aligns with recent experimental observations.

A novel system called MaskedSpeech is developed to fine-tune speech synthesis models on small datasets, yielding synthesized speech that is more natural and expressive than what is typically achieved with traditional training methods. Unlike traditional training, MaskedSpeech employs a cutting-edge approach known as mask-based pre-training to train the speech model. This innovative technique allows the model to develop a deeper understanding of speech features by learning which acoustic elements to retain and which to mask during the training process. MaskedSpeech incorporates this pre-trained model into a final tuning stage and produces synthesized speech that is more faithful to the training data and yields improved emotional synthesis results.

High-dimensional regression analysis often deals with scenarios where the number of potential variables far exceeds the number of available data points. In such cases, we need to identify a subset of variables that accurately represents the underlying model while also capturing the uncertainty associated with each variable. Due to the complexity of many variables, we cannot directly apply standard model selection techniques that rely on comparing the fit of the entire dataset.

We introduce a new approach that leverages neural networks enhanced by a specialized quantum-inspired variational family known as the Havrili\'{e}-Wagenmann model. This method incorporates neural networks to perform feature engineering and utilizes the Havrili\'e-Wagenmann distribution to conduct selection of important variables.

We test the efficacy of this approach on two well-known datasets and compare it with other popular methods such as Lasso, Generalized Lasso, and a specialized neural network approach. The results indicate that our method surpasses the existing techniques in two crucial aspects: retaining uncertainty associated with each variable and accurately representing posterior uncertainties from the original model.

This paper examines different types of attacks and defensive strategies against deep learning networks, focusing on how they manipulate predictions and how this can be utilized in Man-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. While adversarial examples are typically created by altering inputs, MitM attacks involve direct modification of a deep learning network's output or a target's input. This investigation delves into the feasibility of using various input attack and restoration techniques against text-based NLP systems, including using generative models and autoencoders. A key innovation proposed in this research allows an attacker to launch effective attacks against text NLP models without needing to know their architecture or parameters. The outcomes reveal that while restored input attempts can successfully fool a model's response, a restored input is often necessary to guarantee the attacker's desired prediction. Ultimately, this research shows that deep NLP models can be manipulated through multiple methods, some of which can be equally or even more effective than creating adversarial examples.

To effectively combat climate change, understanding the spread of related conspiracy theories is crucial. Our research identifies climate change deniers as the source of a majority of conspiracy-related content, with organized efforts driving a considerable portion of the discourse. Furthermore, we develop a novel, automated system for detecting conspiracy-related climate change attitudes in general social media posts, enabling a broader analysis of the issue's prevalence online.

Researchers have been studying dark matter, particularly within the mass range of 10 to 100 MeV, using a highly sensitive method that involves searching for its nuclear recoil signals. No notable differences from standard model predictions were found in multiple data sets collected by a highly sensitive experiment between the years of 2013 and 2018. New constraints on dark matter interactions were established and found to significantly improve on previous limits by two orders of magnitude, particularly against certain types of dark matter interactions with nuclei. Observed data did not show notable deviations from expected backgrounds.

In this research, we investigate exangulated categories with specified properties. First, under the condition that certain conditions (C1) and (C2) are satisfied, we determine the requirements for the existence of Serre duality in such categories. Specifically, (C1) states that an endo-full subcategory $\mathcal{S}$ of an exangulated category $\mathcal{E}$ leads to a well-defined duality.
