Meanwhile, (C2) states that $\mathcal{E}$ has an endo-full subcategory $\mathcal{S}$ such that the inclusion morphism $\mathcal{S} \to \mathcal{E}$ admits a right exact adjoint functor $\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{S}$ and an exact adjoint functor $\mathcal{E} \to \mathcal{S}$ respectively, under the condition that certain conditions (C1) and (C2) are satisfied, we determine the requirements for the existence of Serre duality in such categories. Furthermore, our findings generalize the results obtained by Chen and Zhou in their study on exangulated categories with a right exact adjoint functor $\mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{E}$ (where $\mathcal{C}$ is an exangulated category with a tilting object over a finite tensor product of number fields). Additionally, we derive the necessary and sufficient conditions for the existence of a right exact adj

We are interested in the returns on different fields of study. Our post-secondary fields of study are relatively homogeneous. We compare actual and predicted earnings payoffs to post-secondary fields of study in post-2002 Denmark and Norway, which are similar in size economies with significant cultural and institutional differences. Our results show that, in general, there is underinvestment in high-pay fields of study, which is more pronounced in Norway. Post-secondary fields of study have lower pay than those in higher education. There is little variation in the payoffs to fields of study, which is more limited in Norway than the US, Canada, and Denmark. Institutional differences in Norway and Denmark do not significantly affect the underinvestment in post-secondary fields of study.

In 2020, the BESIII collaboration started operating the BEPCII super $J/\psi$ factory at a center-of-mass energy of 5. GeV, accumulating $3.09~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$ of data, equating to $10.07~\mathrm{fb}^{-1}$. This dataset allows for a detailed study of various physical processes, and this paper outlines the data-taking achievements along with preliminary research outcomes. The enhanced brightness of BEPCII opens doors for exploring exotic states, precision measurements, rare decays, and the investigation of subtle parity violation and charge-parity violation effects.

We have simulated a single accretion disk interacting with a hierarchical triple star system, consisting of one massive and two lesser masses, to study how the accretion disk's two smaller stars behave. Our model reveals that the two stars' accretion patterns are similar to a single star of the same mass, with variations in their brightness. The accretion activity peaks when these stars approach each other and also when they are far apart. A dark shadow forms in the accretion disk due to a less massive outer star and rotates as a result. This shadow's intensity varies based on the angle at which it's viewed. Our model suggests that the two stars' accretion patterns could be recognized through their activity and light spectrum, and that the accretion patterns may be mistaken for a single star's irregular behavior. This type of system could be found by searching for stars with irregular and narrow-line features.

The inhomogeneous distribution of matter in space significantly impacts the overall structure of the Universe's formation and evolution.  To better understand this effect, researchers utilize perturbation theory to analyze fluctuations from a background model, such as the Friedmann-Lemaître universe.  Employing a weak-field approximation and low-frequency conditions, the derived equations from relativistic quantum mechanics and gravity can be compared and their similarities and differences explored.

We introduce a novel method for image segmentation, specifically designed to effectively clean up and segment corrupted images by combining the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model with a total variation regularizer in a piecewise structure, drawing inspiration from the Chambolle-Pock algorithm for constrained convex optimization duality.

Ultralight fermions and bosons can constitute all or part of dark matter, and understanding their mass limits is crucial. For fermions, Pauli blocking limits their density, and we examined how their mass and abundance impact their suitability as dark matter. We found that if each fermion species has a density greater than 10^-9 of the total dark matter with a mass above 38 eV, no single species can have a mass above 3.8 eV. We also explored how bosons, which can be made of multiple udderly indistinguishable particles and their combinations, are affected by indistinguishability. We found that if each boson species has a density greater than 10^-7 of the total dark matter, no single boson can have a mass above 1.25 GeV. We found that the limits for bosons are more restrictive as the symmetry of the particles increases. We used these constraints to investigate the possibility of bosonic axion dark matter, which is only possible if individual component or mixed particles have masses less than 10^-7 eV. We also examined the possibility of bosons made of five massless particles with different internal symmetries. We found that if there are more than five particles, the resulting boson mass would fall below this threshold.

In the field of computing on neuro-morphic hardware, novel training techniques have been introduced to adapt to this cutting-edge technology distinct from conventional learning methods.
This work presents a clear summary of the most prominent on-chip learning algorithms applicable to spiking neural networks by summarizing their working principles.
Specifically, we detail the global learning methods DL-to-SNN conversion and Dawis and the local learning techniques GLIO and three variants of Legan, as well as the semi-local learning approach DLIO.
We highlight the merits and limitations of each on-chip learning approach HNN and provide a practical guide for programmers aiming to implement these techniques in their own projects.

We employed a two-dimensional FDTD code that incorporates stochastic noise to simulate complex noise storms. This simulation revealed that the intensity of the noise storm is directly proportional to the amplitude of the noise input, as well as the size of the region affected. This phenomenon is known as the "evolution of the sausage mode." It is inferred that this effect is a result of a positive feedback loop between the storm's intensity and its spatial extent. Our findings are relevant to understanding noise storms in various contexts, including coronal loops and geomagnetic-polar mesosphere, and they suggest that a similar mechanism could be at work in these systems.

We present a novel maneuver to expand the application of optical molasses technology to miniaturized devices and intricate integrated systems with complex integrated waveguide designs. Our innovative design offers a significant efficiency gain without an increase in the number of required components, making it suitable for integration with any optical buffer mode converter or any free-space design. This novel design can be applied to develop a variety of integrated devices and circuits based on different atomic or molecular species.

A theory is proposed to address the low luminosity of supermassive black holes such as Sgr A* and M87*, with a root cause linked to their accretion disk's inability to supply sufficient gas to the black hole. This shortfalls in gas availability is attributed to the black hole's large size relative to its host galaxy. Building on this concept, a mathematical model is developed to predict the evolution of black hole mass within galaxies of various types and sizes. The analysis reveals that massive galaxies in an $\Lambda$CDM universe should house larger supermassive black holes, with M87*, residing in a galaxy smaller than expected, standing out as a distinct exception. Moreover, the power of jets produced by these black holes is found to correlate with the velocity dispersion of their host galaxy, with M87* and Sgr A* representing opposite extremes of this relationship.

We examine the impact of a moving neutral atom on a confined photon field within a Lumumba-Lange experiment setting, using a second quantization method to model atomic movement in three dimensions relative to a reflective surface. This relative motion generates an effective inhomogeneous laser field, enabling photon emission even when the atom's energy transition is below the photon energy threshold. The method can also be applied to other dynamic processes such as the loss of momentum by the atom and the dynamic Laporte rule.

Our 2018 30m telescope observations of the Westerlund 2 cluster have uncovered 113 sources in a highly concentrated field. Sources 1 through 7 match the spectral characteristics of massive stars found in other young star-forming regions. By comparing their spectra to those of standard star templates, we calculated upper limits for atmospheric impurities, excluding dust. Stars 1 through 6 match the spectral types O9.5V-O7.5 I, Obs9.5Ve, and Star 7 is a blue O7.5 star with significant H-alpha absorption, resembling the massive star HD179794. Based on our spectral analysis, we estimate the cluster's age at 3.1 million years. Assuming our complete member sample represents the cluster's population, we derived mass functions for the cluster and concluded that the mass of the cluster remains constant beyond 30 solar masses. Stars 1 through 7 have masses of 26 through 40 solar masses. We derived a birth velocity of 60.5 km/s for these massive stars, observing that their positions relative to the cluster center align with the young cluster members. We estimate the cluster's natal ejection efficiency at 28-36 percent, comparable to other massive star populations. We conclude that the mass limit of Westerlund 2 is likely 70-80 solar masses, similar to that of the young cluster NGC36

The solutions to a modified version of the classical  $\inf \, \operatorname{crit}$  problem have been reconstructed using the $\operatorname{argmin} \, \operatorname{crit}$ operation. This modified operation can be viewed as an oblique projection of the set of critical points onto the set of minimizers. We demonstrate that a significant portion of the solutions to variational problems can be recovered through $\operatorname{argmin} \, \operatorname{crit}$  applications, even in cases where the standard $\operatorname{argmin}$  operation fails to find a solution. This finding supports the idea that minimax theory's existence guarantees can be translated into concrete algorithms for discovering solutions. A modified variant of the $\operatorname{argmin} \, \operatorname{crit}$  operation, which incorporates the least upper bound and lower closed property of the minimizers set, is also introduced. Furthermore, an iterative algorithm for calculating minimax solutions is proposed based on the new $\operatorname{argmin} \, \operatorname{crit}$  definition.

This research paper introduces a novel system that integrates a handwritten text recognizer with Generative Adversarial Networks in a feedback loop to enhance the input of degradation models. By alternating between training the Adversarial Network to enhance images and a specific handwritten text recognizer, the proposed method aims to enhance the recognition performance for severely degraded document images. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this system through enhancement and handwritten text recognition experiments on a Chancelleria image dataset, and introduce a written form restoration model that ADR is particularly suited for.

Text extraction from id cards has been an area of study for OCR technology, 
with various approaches implemented by different organizations idiosyncratically. 
In this paper, we break down the id card OCR task into a well-defined 
problem framework and incorporate a natural language processing technique to 
enhance text extraction accuracy. 
To validate our proposed method, we created a id card dataset consisting of 
various id card types along with annotated information and utilized it to 
train our model. 
Experimental results show that the output of our pipeline is more precise 
than conventional extraction methods, 
with the intermediate outputs facilitating subsequent tasks such as entity 
identification and relationship mapping. 
A source code for the proposed pipeline is publicly available at https://github.com/zhenghanlin/ID-Card-OCR.

A key challenge in orthogonal frequency division multiplexing (OFDM) systems is channel estimation, which is complicated by time dispersion and multipath fading channels. This issue is further complicated by high mobility, which causes a rapidly changing channel state. Traditional approaches model the channel as independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.), which fails to capture its actual state in fast-changing scenarios. This limitation can be overcome by leveraging the long short term memory (LSTM) technique, which uses previous observations to predict the current channel state. This results in improved channel estimation performance for fast-changing scenarios. The use of LSTM also reduces the number of training symbols required for accurate channel estimation. This article presents an innovative approach to channel estimation in single-user OFDM systems by combining the projection-based approach with an enhanced projection term and utilizing an over-sampled channel estimator. The channel estimator is then employed to develop an LSTM model for predicting the changes in the channel state. The results obtained through simulations confirm that the proposed method surpasses conventional channel estimation techniques in terms of performance.

Astronomical images are becoming increasingly essential for research, but their clarity is often compromised by various factors, making resolution enhancement a top priority. This study aims to improve astronomical images by leveraging deep learning techniques in an unsupervised setting, where only low-resolution images are available as data. Drawing on recent advances in image restoration through self-supervised learning, we introduce a novel, weakly-supervised approach that utilizes both low-resolution images and their hypothetical high-resolution versions. The method employs an encoder to generate a latent representation from the low-resolution image and a decoder that produces a high-quality counterpart. We then present a network architecture capable of accurately mapping realistic high-resolution images back to their low-resolution counterparts. This framework was tested on a diverse set of non-astronomical images and successfully applied to images of the Milky Way and Andromeda galaxies, demonstrating a significant ability to resolve their features.

A novel algorithm is introduced to extract and evaluate the input's influence on a neural network's predictive performance by training a secondary network to estimate input-subset dependent importance scores without compromising the original network's performance.

In 2019, the ECFA established a new "Early Career Researcher's" working panel with a specific aim to support early career researchers within the community. The panel was later renamed the EECR's. Its first meeting took place in 2020 and has been held annually ever since. The panel has been gradually building its structure and has initiated some projects in its first two years. In this year's meeting held in 2022, the EECR's presented a comprehensive update on its work along with a plan for the future. Several presentations focused on specific projects the panel has been involved in during its second year including: the IPNIF initiative, ECFA IP education program, MCAS project, MCAS workshop, MCAS report, MCAS second phase plan, MCAS second phase launch, peer mentoring scheme, early career promotion task force, climate action group, ECFA second gender diversity report, ECFA third gender diversity report, ECFA EECR's survey, and a study on diversity within committees and early career researchers. The panel will now move into its third year with several proposed projects for the coming year including: launching the EECR's newsletter, establishing a digital archive, commissioning studies on EECR's retention and climate diversity, launching the ECFA early career promotion task force, creating the climate action group, commissioning the ECFA early career diversity report, launching a peer mentoring scheme, establishing a promotion early

Domain-specific patches on graphene demonstrate exceptional efficiency in line-wave propagation within the optical spectrum.
Consequently, they fit perfectly for integration into an envisioned graphene-based optical communication system.
We present a novel approach to modulate line waves by exploiting the Fano resonance in graphene patches.
Through simulations, it has been demonstrated that this modulation mechanism can be effectively realized using an electric field.
Notably, the required voltage to achieve significant modulation is merely a few volts.
The implemented strategy paves the way for implementation of high-performance optical modulators and integrates it with junctions to facilitate functionality in optical transmitters.

In multi-human multi-robot interactions (HxR), several challenges arise due to safety, privacy, and the diversity of human behaviors. To address these issues, we present a novel approach to address three problems simultaneously. Firstly, we employ Federated Learning (FL) to create a secure environment for learning from multiple human-robot interactions. By keeping local data on individual robots, FL ensures privacy and safety, while allowing a global model to be developed through collaboration. Secondly, we develop an efficient communication protocol that minimizes unnecessary exchanges between a central server and distributed robots. Our simulations reveal significant reductions in communication costs between 2 to 10 times, depending on the early stopping threshold. Lastly, we employ Reinforcement Learning (RL) to generate a collaborative policy for cooperative tasks between humans and robots. Through co-reinforcement, a collaborative policy is developed that maximizes shared rewards and ensures effective task completion. To demonstrate our approach's efficacy, we conducted co-writing tasks on a co-zoo interface and Co-writing simulations, yielding satisfactory results that demonstrate the potential of our system to address the challenges associated with safety, privacy, and diverse human-robot interactions.

A novel method of bias-reduced estimation is introduced, improving upon existing techniques by addressing the issue of non-smooth bias-reduced estimators. This estimator employs a flexible bias function estimate derived from data, unlike prior work that necessitated nonparametric series estimations. By avoiding over-parametrization, the nonparametric approach often leads to inefficient bias reduction. Utilizing a robust M-estimator framework, our method effectively tackles complex issues such as selection bias and sample dependence, broadening the applicability beyond that of the Augmented IPW estimator. This bias-reduced estimator exhibits asymptotic normality with nonparametric rate convergence, and simulations demonstrate that it achieves bias reduction with minimal loss in efficiency. Ultimately, our method offers a simplified yet effective solution for bias reduction in various modeling scenarios.

A novel approach called knowledge graph based link prediction is used to find
connected nodes within a graph and the resulting links are presented as suggestions
for data enhancement and gap identification in large databases.  A specific
implementation of this technique has been developed and tested using a subgraph of the
Wikidata database, where predictions of missing entities in the dataset were accurate
at a 70% rate and able to identify the relationship between the target entity and its
associated data source.  When applied to the task of discovering new data entries,
this link prediction method achieved a 60% accuracy in correctly identifying the
properties of the entity and was also capable of determining its value.  Unlike
previous approaches that focused on the entire knowledge graph, this
implementation uses a simplified graph for increased efficiency.

In the context of a strongly-coupled N=4 super Yang-Mills theory, we have derived the Debye mass under conditions excluding a baryonic chemical potential. Upon introducing the baryonic chemical potential, we have determined the Debye mass's heavy and light mass limits. Our findings indicate that the heavier Debye mass is related to the lighter Debye mass through a specific mathematical expression, which is also validated in the limit of a vanishing baryonic chemical potential.

A study of the magnetic properties of Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 was conducted using neutron diffraction, and both compounds were found to have a unique magnetic structure, consisting of two distinct Ru ions (Ru1 and Ru2). While Tb3RuO7 exhibits simple ordering patterns for both ions, Nd3RuO7 displays more intricate structures, particularly for the Ru2 ion. Additionally, the results indicate that the magnetic structure of Nd3RuO7 does not perfectly align with a magnetic structure predicted by a G-type model.

A novel local-functional model is proposed to enhance the performance of Kernels on lower-dimensional signals by exploiting its parametric structure.
The model combines a set of local functions with a product basis that is specifically tailored to the dimensionality of the input signal.
By leveraging this structured approach, our experiments indicate that the kernel can achieve better generalization and reduce overparameterization compared to traditional methods.
Additionally, our analysis of the model's capacity through a specialized measure and a corresponding growth function reveals how the local-functional structure enables efficient generalization for low-dimensional signals.

A new type of semi-generative model has been introduced that can capture the intricate connections between the root causes and their impacts on a given variable of interest. By assuming a unique set of latent variables that represent the underlying causes, each target variable is now dependent on both its corresponding cause and the common cause, which is also referred to as the effect node. The efficacy of this framework has been demonstrated through varational inference and further enhanced by the incorporation of graph structures within a specific context. This framework is capable of identifying patterns in data by leveraging a combination of generative capabilities and analytical methods based on linear regression. Extensive numerical evaluations have confirmed the efficiency of this model in handling real-world datasets containing missing information and closely following a causal structure. This framework is now available for use through our open-source GitHub repository.

A growing interest in understanding the geometric properties of deep learning models has emerged, as insight into their geometry can guide the design of algorithms and structures. Recent research has focused on modeling these geometric patterns within the data cloud and has suggested that their insights can help model training dynamics. In this context, we investigate how these geometric patterns evolve during training, as guided by the gradients of the objective function, to understand what aspects of the geometry are most beneficial for learning. Our analysis of geometric patterns within the data cloud and its boundary in Euclidean and projective spaces, respectively, reveals that objective functions should preserve the geometry of the data manifold and its boundary, especially the folds resulting from data transformations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that maintaining the geometry of the feature manifolds created by neural networks is also crucial for effective training, with our findings in stochastic gradient descent, momentum-based methods, and adaptive gradient algorithms like Adam and RMSProp. Notably, we found that while gradient descent with a small learning rate can benefit from momentum, adaptive gradient methods are essential for large learning rates. Our geometric perspective on training deep learning models, validated by theoretical results and empirical evidence, opens up a new area of study that combines deep learning with differential geometry, offering a comprehensive understanding of the geometry of learning itself.

By substituting a specific quadratic irrational with another in the continued expansion of a cubic field's fundamental unit, the behavior of the lattice's minimum values can be controlled, and this can be repeated an arbitrary number of times to further reduce the lattice minimums.

Grasping the underlying nature of deep neural networks is crucial for their effective application. In response, various approaches have been devised to measure a neural unit's response to specific input features. This paper reviews and compares three key methods - activation maximization, surrogate gradient models, and layerwise relevance propagation - that successfully uncover the behavioral activations of hidden units. Through a systematic evaluation, our study highlights the strengths and limitations of each technique, ultimately offering recommendations for future research and practical implementations.

We introduce the concept of r-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted by $\left\langle\begin{matrix}n\\k\end{matrix}\right\rangle_r$, which represent the number of ways to partition a set of $n$ elements into $k$ non-empty subsets, with the condition that no subset can contain more than $r$ elements. 

The corresponding numbers of the first kind, $\left[\begin{matrix}n\\k\end{matrix}\right]_r$, represent the number of signed cycles of the set $\{1,\ldots,n\}$ divided into $k$ blocks of size at most $r$. 

The paper examines their properties, including a recurrence relation, identity, and representation using $r$-associated Stirling numbers of the first kind.

We introduce a set of coherent invariants, known as multipliants, to detect irreducible domains in materials with reduced symmetries due to strain. By leveraging group-subgroup relationships in materials with low-dimensional layers, we establish a comprehensive framework for classifying domain orientations. Our theoretical findings are corroborated by observations of iron-oxide interfaces, thereby validating the introductions presented.

The concept of non-local observables on a specific type of Lie group is explored, allowing for non-local definitions of physical quantities such as angular momentum and energy without requiring a particular point in space. This concept is limited by a maximum resolution of available momenta, which is estimated by comparing the size of a manifold to a particle's de-Broglie wavelength. A mathematical framework for bounding these momenta is provided, specifically utilizing Gevrey classes and a topological theory of distributional symbols. This approach yields precise estimates for the maximum allowable momenta based on the properties of a de-Broglie type action.

We introduce a modified approach to affine coupling layers that accommodates complex numbers. This layer can be integrated with neural networks, which operate in the complex domain. This feature enables a novel application: performing Monte Carlo simulations more efficiently. Currently, such simulations are often conducted by transforming samples from normal distributions through a series of randomized operations. Our method adds these operations within a neural network that processes complex values. As a result, we achieve more accurate distributions with fewer iterations or access to a wider range of distributions with the same number of iterations. We also demonstrate that our layer improves Monte Carlo simulations for neural network likelihood evaluations and variational inference.

In a top-color assisted See-Saw model featuring a flavor $U(1)_F$ symmetry from the Moore-Valle framework, we investigate the origins of the top quark's mass, muon neutralness, and see-saw mechanism. By combining the symmetry's U(1)_t and U(1)_b, we break flavor symmetry to generate a substantial top quark and bottom quark mass difference, thus resolving their mass disparity. Furthermore, we find that symmetry breaking produces the required large Yukawa coupling of the third generation of fermions to a vector boson $Z'$. The see-saw mechanism in our model arises from the coupling of the Higgs doublet to a fermion triplet via a fermion Yukawa coupling. Also, we demonstrate that the model can reconcile experimental constraints from electroweak precision tests and the muon $g-2$ while maintaining the model's capacity to resolve the muon's neutralness issue, thanks to its long-lived vector boson $Z'$.

Virtual validation and protection platforms (VPPMs) serve as a trusted foundation, allowing the creation of virtual machines with installed software and preconfigured applications that can be accessed by users without verification of safety. As VPPMs gain popularity due to their convenience in scenarios such as web browsing, they present a potential vulnerability if an attacker exploits a vulnerability in the VPPM, leading to an unsafe state that users might mistakenly trust. We've developed a system called FlowValidation, a trusted middleware system that monitors network traffic and identifies applications with potentially malicious network activity, detecting anomalies and violations of network policy within VPPMs. Through manual analysis and an automated fuzzer, we've found multiple VPPMs contain hidden applications with policy-violating network activity, including one VPPM containing an application with traffic 100 times larger than expected. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of network monitoring in detecting malicious activities in VPPMs.

The performance of a language model on various languages has historically been considered consistent. Nevertheless, fine-tuning pre-trained models like mBERT and XLM-R on specific languages can significantly enhance its accuracy in those languages. Our study examines the adaptability of language models to 117 languages by examining two key issues: (a) the factors contributing to a language model's performance variations across different languages; and (b) the degree of fine-tuning required for different languages to achieve optimal results. Our analysis reveals that fine-tuning a language model on a particular language does not necessarily guarantee improved performance on another, indicating that language models are more susceptible to fine-tuning in certain languages than others. Our results also highlight the importance of fine-tuning language models on target languages to reach their full potential.

In a by-product of their analysis of the role of rotation in suppressing binary formation and its connection to the Faint Early Type galaxy debate, a team of researchers performed an extensive examination of a model of a binary system's surrounding environment. This model was initially studied in a preceding paper of their series and involved both binary and surrounding material dynamics under the influence of significant rotation. By running over 1,000 simulations with the Gadget model and exploring the interplay of key physical processes and parameters such as angular momentum and efficiency of binary interactions, the researchers modelled the outcome of these interactions. Their model's findings show that the binary's mass decreases as the kinetic energy of rotation increases in relation to the system's gravitational energy. This is because the angular momentum in these binary systems is predominantly derived from the kinetic energy of their surrounding material. Additionally, the researchers modelled how the binary's mass is influenced by factors such as the rate of its mass accumulation and found that, when the mass increase is high, the binary's mass is comparable to that of non-rotating systems due to the effect of mass conservation. This suggests that, in regions with high rotation and low rate of mass accumulation, the binary's mass is less developed than in systems with significant mass accumulation and less rapid rotation.

This study introduces an innovative approach to unsupervised dimensionality reduction, a crucial task in diverse fields, such as pattern recognition and data mining. Our approach is grounded in a set function, akin to the Radchalicki kernel, but with enhanced robustness. We demonstrate that it can be computed in linear time, making it particularly suitable for kernel methods in dimensionality reduction. Unlike traditional methods that focus on maintaining symmetry, our approach prioritizes robustness. To illustrate the efficacy of the new method, we conducted comprehensive experiments comparing it with other approaches, notably the radial basis function.

A recent finding by Bortz, Buss, Furzer, Leutheusser, and Williams established that a significant limit on computational power would a consequence of resolving the long-standing question of whether CPT is the same as PTIME in the context of first-order logic with full permutation invariance (EPC). We show that the converse implication holds as well – a super-polynomial limitation on the expressive power of EPC a consequence of CPT being distinct from PTIME. This development leaves a substantial gap between feasible and infeasible problems solvable using first-order logic with full permutation invariance.

A finitely generated ideal in a commutative ring with unity can be expressed as the intersection of primary ideals, specifically those that are $\tau$-elementary in nature, where $\tau$ refers to a large cardinal number. It has been demonstrated that $\tau$-elementary rings possess a unique property as intersection-prime elements within the set of all such rings, occurring at a high cardinality and exhibiting certain minimal characteristics for rings with unity and unit. Furthermore, an investigation was conducted regarding $\tau$-elementary local rings and those that are primary, revealing specific properties and requirements associated with these categories of rings, specifically regarding their unity and unit elements.

Social media platforms like Twitter provide social and political groups with a platform to voice their opinions on social issues, making it possible for researchers to analyze their online presence and engageability by examining the group's social media activity. Identifying the group's influence on social media requires a deeper understanding of the content they create and how they utilize online spaces to participate in social debates. Our research focuses on extracting and categorizing the social issues mentioned in posts from specific social media groups to create a framework for analyzing their engagement in online discussions. This framework is complemented by a system that predicts a social media group's likelihood to create content related to a particular topic based on their group's social presence and influence. This approach enables researchers to gain insight into a social media group's content creation patterns and areas of online engagement.

We introduce a novel deep learning-based system for event detection in free-standing objects within multi-resolution sequences, where each sequence comprises diverse, unaligned sequences of depth frames. This framework is specifically designed to account for the varying spatial dimensions of occurring events. By treating each sequence as a unified entity in a group convolutional neural network, our system preserves information across various spatial resolutions. Through thorough experiments on a newly created dataset consisting of depth sequences at various spatial scales, we demonstrate that our approach outperforms current single-resolution detection methods. This framework is particularly suited for applications like non-contact gesture analysis and robot interaction, leveraging depth sensors' advantages of robust lighting adaptability and viewpoint invariance.

The distribution of galaxies is not uniformly affected by matter fluctuations, 
with large-scale deviations having a disproportionate impact on certain galaxy 
populations, thereby influencing their relationship to the overall matter distribution. 
Since we cannot directly observe the fluctuations of matter itself, measurements of 
CMB lensing, which indirectly maps this fluctuation, are not sufficient on their own to 
determine the effect of imperfections in the galaxy probe's bias. To address this issue, 
researchers have developed a new method for calculating lensing bias using the underutilized 
information in lensing measurements themselves. By simultaneously considering the underestimation 
and overestimation of fluctuations by different galaxy probes, these measurements can be 
leveraged to constrain possible forms of lensing bias. The research shows that current 
weak lensing experiments will be unable to effectively restrict these forms due 
to the limitations of lensing signal-to-noise and systematics, suggesting that 
future experiments should prioritize other aspects to maximize their cosmological potential.

The rapid advancement of neural networks has led to a surge in applications in AI, but there are significant concerns regarding their reliability and security. Adversarial attacks on machine learning models can lead to severe safety hazards, financial losses, and a compromised trust in AI technologies. To enhance the reliability of deep learning models, we introduce a novel framework that fortifies them against the harshest possible perturbations. This framework utilizes a combination of functional interpolation and functional differentiation to establish reliable bounds on how models respond to such perturbations. By utilizing these bounds, we devise an optimization procedure that effectively balances model accuracy and robustness. Our approach, applied to classification networks built on CNNs, yields state-of-the-art models with exceptional robustness against various types of attacks. Additionally, we develop theoretical guarantees for general performance that are independent of the specific dataset distribution, thereby reducing biases and promoting fairness in AI systems.

The rapid dissemination of false information on social media poses a significant threat, necessitating the development of an effective method to predict and control its growth. In this study, we approach this problem by treating false information as a system of reactions between interconnected entities. We propose a novel neural network that utilizes unique identifiers and location data of individual users to refine prediction and reduce computational complexity. Furthermore, we demonstrate that adding these features allows the model to accurately classify active user segments based on their susceptibility to false information, and that different behaviors of various segments result in distinct growth patterns and characteristics of false information.

A significant problem in hyperspectral image analysis is accurate classification of individual pixels. The performance of conventional methods often hinges on the effectiveness of a preliminary step: dimensionality reduction techniques. Various methods, like PCA and LDA, have been previously employed in this context, primarily for classification purposes. Our research delves into the capabilities of various dimensionality reduction methods from a novel standpoint - their ability to recover and reconstruct signals. Our analysis reveals that PCA and LDA exhibit limited signal reconstruction capabilities, suggesting that their inherent properties also hinder their ability to preserve data structure. In contrast, methods like autoencoders and t-SNE demonstrate improved signal reconstruction capabilities. Our findings further revealed that certain features of dimensionality reduction methods, such as their ability to identify and preserve critical spectral bands and enhance structure nonlinearity, correlate positively with their performance in classification and signal reconstruction tasks. Based on these discoveries, we propose a general framework for evaluating dimensionality reduction methods, enabling their application in scenarios beyond classification where preserving the original data structure is crucial. Our research ultimately demonstrated that a dimensionality reduction method achieving high classification accuracy would perform even better in signal reconstruction applications.

Several methods exist for reducing the size of deep neural networks by employing 
pruning and quantization techniques that decrease computation costs, memory usage, 
improve efficiency in inference and transfer learning. Despite these efforts, most 
approaches only target one of these objectives at a time, neglecting the potential 
benefits of addressing both efficiency and expressiveness simultaneously. Our novel 
method, named PqNet, incorporates both quantization of weights and activations and 
pruning of the network structure. By employing the Advanced Model Compression 
Framework (AMCF), PqNet efficiently performs joint quantization and pruning with a 
single cost. The effectiveness of PqNet is demonstrated by its ability to achieve 
sub-1MFlops models on ImageNet, as well as significant memory savings and high 
accuracy rates in the Cifar-100 dataset.

We introduce a novel approach called ProCS that leverages conditional variational autoencoders to condense a vast number of 3D protein coordinates into a significantly smaller set of conditional features. By learning this conditional representation through VAEs and using it to reconstruct protein coordinates, ProCS enables the efficient refinement of protein structures while maintaining structural integrity. Experiments on the binding modes of small molecules to proteins demonstrate that ProCS not only reduces the number of variables in the protein structure optimization process but also enhances the accuracy of the binding modes. Compared to a more advanced method called REINFORCE, ProCS achieved a substantial 40% improvement in root-mean-square deviation and a 20% decrease in the computational cost of the optimization process.

This study introduces a novel method to improve weakly-supervised visual localization by leveraging unique attributes of vimap-based loss functions. We enhance their effectiveness against weaker alternatives by applying a under-fitted optimization approach that deliberately restricts their potential. This under-fitted approach can be replicated across various loss functions by incorporating the inverse Fenchian-Young conjugate constraint, derived from a weakly coupled convex optimization problem. Since the optimization problem spans a convex set, partial replication is possible, yielding consistent performance gains with minimal computational cost. As a result of this improved training, we achieve state-of-the-art outcomes on the KITTI benchmark, surpassing more traditionally used loss functions.

The parquet amplitude is distinguished by its adherence to both conservation and crossing symmetry. This concept has been expanded to relativistic many-body theory, which often fails to exhibit these symmetries to all orders. A new, from-first-principles-derived amplitude alternative to the standard parquet amplitude is proposed. This new model amplitude exhibits enhanced stability, as evidenced by a modified energy equation that remains consistent to any order of approximation. While the standard parquet amplitude lacks conservation, the new model amplitude preserves it and differs significantly in numerical terms. This model amplitude also lacks crossing symmetry but shows improved approximate adherence to the symmetry compared to the standard parquet amplitude.

Experimental examination using high-resolution resonant inelastic x-ray scattering has been conducted on exfoliated monolayer TiSe2. This research reveals that excitation energies are substantially enhanced when TiSe2 exists in a two-dimensional form compared to its bulk counterpart. Furthermore, the seismograph patterns of seismographic data show that seismographic responses are lost when TiSe2 exists in a monolayer form, indicating that seismographic phenomena in multilayer TiSe2 originate from multilayer seismographic phenomena and are not simply a result of monolayer seismographic phenomena repeated in three-dimensional space. This finding has been further supported by theoretical calculations, which suggest that exciton-seismographic interactions can occur in monolayer TiSe2 without multilayer seismographic phenomena and that seismographic phenomena are lost due to the Seismographic Critical Point. This implies that Seismographic phenomena in monolayer TiSe2 are driven by Seismographic criticality rather than simple three-dimensional repetitions of seismographic phenomena and that this is significant for the study of two-dimensional exciton-seismographic phenomena.

In text-based risk reporting systems, dispatchers receive various categories of event reports from users and gather essential information to effectively allocate responsibilities.  While data collection guidelines exist, there is a lack of standardized information collection across different categories leading to uneven data availability.  To address this issue, we conducted a study to identify which variables are commonly collected by dispatchers within specific categories of event reports.  We analyzed 1,552 conversations between dispatchers and callers to extract 1,000 essential variables and discovered that variables such as type of incident, location, and type of report are consistently collected, whereas others like the type of armed individual, nature of incident, and call time are category-specific.  Based on our findings, we recommend dispatchers to consistently gather key variables and suggest potential tools to do so.

We have computed superconducting properties of Mo$_{5}$Al$_{2}$ along its non-circular Fermi surface segments. Our studies incorporate both the influence of the Fermi surface topology on the magnetic susceptibility and the impact of nodal structure on the superconducting transition temperature. By comparing results from different pairing interaction models, we found that both s-wave and d-wave superconducting phases are capable of occurring in Mo$_{5}$Al$_2$.

A novel, semi-supervised active learning algorithm based on minimax entropy is proposed to address its uncertainties and diversity limitations. The algorithm selects unlabeled samples with maximum uncertainty and diversity for labeling, by minimizing conditional entropy and entering diversity among selected batch samples. The resulting selection criterion results in minimal mutual information and entropy for selected batch samples. To enhance diversity selection in unlabelled samples, an innovative graph-theoretic minimax cut-based entry divergence measure is devised. The resulting method achieves a remarkable improvement in labeled sample coverage and model performance in various real-world and synthetic scenarios.

In the digital age, vast repositories of music enable research into the evolution of song styles across periods. We analyzed over 500,000 copyrighted songs by more than 10,000 artists from 1988 to 2018, examining their timbre similarity. Our findings reveal that songs within the same decade exhibit a cluster structure, characterized by distinct high-similarity groups. A closer look at this phenomenon shows that songs by artists sharing a genre demonstrate greater similarity, particularly among hit songs. Furthermore, this analysis sheds light on how songs with similar characteristics have emerged and evolved across time, genres, and languages.

Consider a continuous-time stochastic process with reinforcement on a countable set that may be affected by randomness. Under certain reasonable assumptions, we establish non-random bounds for the number of elements visited at least once over a period of time t. As t increases, the process exhibits subdiffusive behavior, characterized by the number of elements visited growing more slowly than linearly with time. The relative error in the number of elements visited over a period of time t grows at a rate slower than the square root of that relative error in the number of elements visited, thereby confirming the accuracy of the established bounds. Additionally, we derive both a lower and upper bound for the relative error as time tends to infinity, thereby narrowing the range of possible growth rates.

This paper delves into the concept of containment, its converse known as the converse property, within the framework of proof-theoretic semantics. Contemporary PTS adheres to the idea that a compound's meaning is formed by the constituent meanings of its components, thereby embodying the containment principle. Conversely, the converse property posits that a component's meaning is incorporated in that of the compound. While initially proposed by Barendregt and Piterman in relation to lambda terms and PCF, the property remains contentious among modern PTS advocates due to its apparent counterintuitive nature. Nevertheless, certain compounds such as Sch\"uttz's biconditional demonstrate containment as well as the converse property. Moreover, a model based on directed biordered sets reveals that the meaning of Sch\"uttz's biconditional incorporates the full meanings (biomorphs) of the components, rather than being confined to their intersections as contended by some. Additionally, we demonstrate that a broad class of biordered sets ensures the applicability of both containment and the converse property across all G3c-terminating sequent calculus proofs.

Reward learning for reinforcement learning agents often relies on human feedback, but current approaches have significant efficiency issues due to their sequential nature. By batch-processing human preferences, however, parallel interaction and learning can be enabled, improving overall efficiency. While existing methods handle batch comparisons effectively, they necessitate a strict preference format that necessitates comparing all elements of a given batch, leading to an unfeasible number of preferences when dealing with large batches. A novel approach called ValueMax is presented that accommodates a more flexible preference format, enabling flexible batch sizes. This allows for manageable and manageable human feedback even in batches with a large number of elements. Furthermore, the relative nature of ValueMax's loss function provides theoretically and empirically evidence of its benefits over current valuation-based and policy-gradient-based methods, showing superior performance on relevant benchmark datasets.

The Smyth powerspace construction, a dual to the Hoare powerspace construction, applies to any core-compact lattice. It is shown that this construction does not always maintain core-compactness, though it does keep of finite rank lattices core-compact. It has been proven that for a lattice of finite rank $n$, the Smyth powerspace has a rank of $n-1$. We identify a class of lattices where the powerspace under Smyth's construction remains core-compact.

Gaussian random pointed vortex loops of fixed length are studied in three-dimensional space, considered as submanifolds with a boundary of the configuration space of these loops in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The configuration space does not include configurations allowing self-intersections. The loops are modeled as directed closed paths in three-dimensional space, where the direction is achieved by designating a specific point on each loop as an arrowhead, effectively making the point where the loop starts and ends distinct. The general configuration space of unpointed loops can be understood as the direction-specific configuration space of pointed loops, divided into two components corresponding to the loop's orientation, and these two components are equivalent in measure. The probability distribution of these loops is given by a version of the Geman-Jones distribution specifically tailored for pointed loops, dependent on the point where the loop's entire geometric configuration is determined by distances between all points and their associated weights. The method involves a 3D version of the Edwards model for polymer physics but applied to vortex behavior. The Geman-Jones distribution is known to be weakly admissible for sufficient loop lengths, according to recent research by Geman-Jones and particularly strengthened by additional analysis in our paper. The method involves transforming the configuration space into a area-based configuration space where the directed loop is divided into $N$ segments, labeled as islands, each contributing an enclosed area to the total area of the loop's projection on a two-dimensional surface. The double machine learning approach has gained popularity for achieving accurate causal inference in machine learning, thanks to its ability to mitigate model misspecification and prevent overfitting. Despite these benefits, our research finds that using a regularized AIPW estimator can lead to suboptimal results, particularly for sample sizes of 2000 or less. Notably, we observe that excluding regularisation in this estimator may enhance performance. Our analysis combines theoretical and empirical methods to explain these observations. Consequently, we propose an alternative approach for obtaining doubly machine learning estimates that incorporates regularisation effectively.

In particle physics, lattice calculations can be particularly insightful for processes involving the Higgs boson and its couplings to fermions, especially given the absence of experimental data on the tau lepton. Its modest mass makes lattice studies feasible, and its detection in崩灭 processes involving the bottom quark and the $H\rightarrow\tau\tau$ reaction is a focal point of current experiments. This paper presents a summary of the $H\rightarrow\tau\tau$ reaction on the lattice and its application to the $H\rightarrow\tau\gamma$ reaction, with results from the lattice calibration already providing the shortest path to the standard model standard for these崩灭 processes.

In a rotation-dominated environment, weak thermal differential expansion causes baroclinic waves to form in a narrow annulus, resulting in a characteristic surface pattern of 'zonal jets' interrupted by wave activity confined to the 'equator'. This setup allows for a clear comparison with a slightly less weak differential expansion, where the annulus transitions into a state that supports 'meridional jets' and wave activity at both 'equator' and 'poles'. By using time series data and spectral analysis on the 'meridional velocity field', we can identify and track individual waves in both scenarios. This method reveals that increasing the weak differential expansion strengthens and shifts the location of the 'meridional jets', causing them to appear at both 'equator' and 'poles', and shows that these transformations occur gradually and are linked to a continuous modification of wave properties. This finding demonstrates that a gradual transition can occur between two rotation-dominated states with distinctly different behaviors.

This research introduces a prior on regression coefficients in the context of a Bayesian model that handles various types of extreme value distributions with an unspecified number of parameters. The number of parameters, denoted as 'm', is crucial in tuning the pre-defined normal scale mixture representation of the prior. A crucial aspect of implementing this approach is selecting an appropriate 'm' value, which significantly influences estimation. This paper investigates the impact of different 'm' values on estimation accuracy, suggesting the use of pre-defined 'm' values based on data characteristics, including the desired accuracy and data dimension. Simulation studies demonstrate the efficacy of this approach, particularly for Pareto and Gumbel distributions, while also examining the computational implications. A real-world application to a dataset of insurance claims further illustrates the utility of this approach.

In this reinforcement learning setting, we acknowledge the presence of a certain level of environment corruption within a Markov decision process. Since the type of environment degradation is unknown, we modify standard algorithms by incorporating an adjustable parameter. This parameter allows us to determine the degree of susceptibility to a corrupted environment without needing to know in advance how much the environment has been corrupted. Our goal in this research is to investigate the sensitivity of reinforcement learning algorithms to potential saboteurs who may be introducing environmental degradation and to develop algorithms capable of operating effectively in environments with an uncertain level of corruption.

This study investigates the impulsive heat equation with varying support in space and time, focusing on its approximate controllability in a short timeframe. By dividing the short period into multiple sub-intervals, we approximate the impulsive equation with a large system of zero-impulse equations defined on different spatial domains. The approximate controllability of the impulsive equation is then derived from the properties of the zero-impulse equation system. Our findings provide a positive answer to the existence of impulse approximate controllability, particularly for cases where the final state is non-zero.

Current methods for out-of-distribution detection struggle with certain types of challenge data, such as strong perturbations and strong out-of-domain data. As a result, accurate OUDD methods have been developed, but they often rely on threshold selection using validation or OUDD evaluation data. To address this, a neural network-based method is proposed that learns both scoring and thresholding in a single step, using a cross-entropy loss on evaluation data. The approach is evaluated against established baselines and other OUDD methods on four common benchmark datasets, including CNNMNIST, OUDUD, OUDND and OUDGD. Results show that the proposed method excels compared to other tested methods, particularly on the OUDND benchmark. Additionally, the OUDND dataset is introduced as a formidable challenge due to its complexity.

This paper applies a simplified model of a molecular motor's dynamics to develop a theoretical method for controlling the motor's behavior through electric currents. The model incorporates the motor's structural details and forces induced by electric currents to derive its equations of motion. The results indicate that small, time-dependent currents can significantly impact the motor's dynamics, potentially causing substantial conformational changes. This is supported by the calculation of the probability distributions of the motor's states and its average position as functions of time, which are found to be consistent with single-molecule experiments.

Consider an input string, and let its two copies move bidirectionally along a tape, controlling a transducer that reads their contents, potentially rewriting them as $\gamma_i$ and $\delta_i$. This setup can be modeled as a non-deterministic two-way word transducer, which we show can be converted into an equivalent one-way transducer, using a regular resynchronizer that maps every position in the input to one of its copies with the same origin. For this resynchronizer to exist and remain size-bounded, however, the equivalent one-way transducer must be able to process both tape ends simultaneously without moving them.

A novel, efficient algorithm has been developed to calculate key components of f-Convolution with reduced computational costs, significantly lowering the operations required from $O(N^3)$ to $O(N^2)$. This innovative approach leverages the properties of Gaussians and a tailored tail integration technique, enabling the computation of individual components to be roughly equivalent to performing a standard d-dimensional box tail integration using a hybrid algorithm. As a result, the new algorithm offers a substantial computational advantage, with a speedup of at least a factor of $N$.

Our knowledge of the intermediate objects that arise from planetary and stellar formation processes is extremely limited due to their cool temperatures, short cooling times, and the inherent challenges in studying them. The only object of its kind that was thoroughly studied until very recently, is the giant object, GJ 229B, which has a cool atmospheric temperature of 450-500 Kelvin. As a result, it became the benchmark for understanding these intermediate objects. Recent high-resolution observations at multiple wavelengths have provided new insights into its atmospheric composition. These observations have confirmed the initial model that identified water and methane as the primary molecules driving the atmospheric temperature structure. However, these analyses have also revealed the presence of unexpected features, including unexpected pressure-broadened methane and a significant discrepancy between the methane and carbon monoxide abundances. Although the former is a relatively straightforward aspect of the atmospheric physics, the latter poses a substantial puzzle. One possible explanation for this phenomenon is the presence of an unusual nuclear reaction that produces an excess of oxygen in the atmosphere. To investigate this unusual possibility, we have performed a comprehensive review of the chemical processes that take place in the atmosphere of GJ 229B, which has led us to conclude that this unusual scenario is extremely unlikely.

Our investigation into spectral density in meson-meson scattering processes
yields a striking result: it is possible to discern tetraquark states within
the spectral density, but only under specific conditions. By examining the
spectral density at very low energies, we found that its presence is heavily
influenced by two key factors, namely the inclusion of three-gluon interactions
and a non-zero value for the gluon condensate. We further demonstrate that the
structure of the spectral density can be theoretically linked to the properties
of the effective Lagrangian, allowing us to establish a direct relationship
between the coefficients of the spectral density and the Lagrangian's constants.
As an application of this relationship, we were able to show that the
gluonic bound state $\eta_g$, previously identified in $\eta\eta$ and $\eta'\eta'$
scattering, cannot exist in the form of a tetraquark.

With the $C\Gamma$-violating angle in the Standard Model now predicted with high accuracy, low-energy searches for physics beyond the Standard Model become even more sensitive. In particular, a proton target is optimal for discovering such new interactions due to its solid-state nature, enabling a more thorough exploration. A proton target also has a well-defined value of $\bar{d}_E$, a crucial parameter that governs the sensitivity to $C\Gamma$ new physics. This paper proposes a novel $C\Gamma$-sensitive search using spin-polarized protons, where the new physics signal would manifest as an alteration in the CP-violating electron-electron scattering rate.

When a contagious person coughs, sneezes, or speaks, these actions release an aerosol cloud, increasing the concentration of infectious droplets in the immediate vicinity. This increased concentration, detected by a detector, is modeled as the output of a system where the cloud behaves like a stirred tank, allowing us to calculate concentrations using residence time distribution theory. Under specific conditions, the detector will register a peak concentration that's proportional to the infection rate. These conditions, along with the advantage of detector mobility, make the well-mixed model a powerful tool for locating an infected person in a confined space. This advantage is demonstrated through agent-based model simulations, which reveal that detection methods using complex airflow patterns can often be accurately predicted using the well-mixed model. This is particularly evident when detectors have a tolerance for measurement errors, as seen in various scenarios where different airflow patterns produce similar concentration signals that fall within a specified error margin. This similarity holds true even when detectors have zero measurement error tolerance, as revealed by a more detailed analysis involving singular perturbation analysis and the method of characteristics. This analytical approach also identifies areas of inaccurate prediction when extending well-mixed results to scenarios with complex airflow patterns.

Isotopes of tellurium with mass numbers of 112 to 139 have been studied via $\beta$-decay in an experiment conducted at the Tantalum target facility of the GISSO beam line at GANIL. Following the dissolution of the irradiated target, Te samples were separated and analyzed using $\gamma$-ray spectroscopy. Specifically, certain $\beta$-decay transitions were observed in $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te, allowing for a detailed comparison between $\beta$-decay and $\gamma$-ray transitions. This comparison revealed $ eta$-decay transitions of high spin in $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te, and additional $\beta$-decay transitions were found in $^{133}$Te, $^{133}$Se, and $^{131}$Se. Additionally, some newly observed $\beta$-decay transitions were found in $^{127}$Te and $^{125}$Se. New $\beta$-decay $Q$ values were determined for $^{133}$Se and $^{125}$Se. Additionally, some $\beta$-decay properties were found in $^{127}$Te, and these in $^{133}$Se were found to be in agreement with theoretical predictions.

In our study, we introduce a novel method for identifying and confirming
violations of the exchange program, grounded in the introduction of a
comprehensive uniqueness result. Our approach also encompasses the
generalized free disposal monopoly problem and its application to determining
unique market equilibria. We then extend the scope to markovian models of agents
and their potential equilibria, before concluding with an examination of the
uniqueness of markovian equilibria.

This study presents a computational framework for heavy-light mesons, utilizing the quark model with an interpolated bottom meson. By applying the quark model to predict the masses of $F$-wave mesons, a Trajectory, much like the Regge trajectories, is established. The predicted masses align with existing experimental data, and a trajectory analysis indicates that the $F$-wave trajectory lies above the $P$-wave trajectory. Furthermore, this framework is extended to incorporate an estimate of the wave functions at the origin. The calculated results align with experimental data, and a predicted value of $\sqrt{s_{\Lambda_{b}^{\prime\prime}}} \approx 1.36$ GeV is obtained for a previously unobserved state.

Building on this result, we focused on a particular case of Szabados's conjecture, which states that for any n elements, a valid pattern of length 2n exists if the patterns of length 2n-1 and 2n-2 exist. The pairs of patterns that satisfy this relationship are those where the second pattern is formed by repeating the first pattern. The proof involved a specific case in which the first pattern is repeated to create the second pattern. Our current work expands upon this finding by considering all possible valid pairs of patterns for the second pattern, consisting of at least n but at most 3n-2 elements. The proof relies on a mathematical argument that can be applied to any valid pair of patterns. A versatile technique has been developed to identify dynamic modes in complex nonlinear systems, often applied in various fields like meteorology and engineering. In contrast to the standard method that relies on a specific distance between system points, this technique uses a flexible method to determine that distance. By employing this method, the system's behavior can be accurately analyzed even when it involves significant interactions between distant points. To illustrate its effectiveness, the method has been successfully applied in two different ways: one to decode a model of atmospheric circulation and the other to solve a complex problem in the dynamics of a type of material known as a Bose-Einstein condensate.

Chess openings can be analyzed in great detail, with databases containing thousands of games. This paper presents a new method for evaluating player skills and chess opening quality based on frequency of game repetitions. The Economic Fitness and Complexity (EFC) approach was adapted to select the best of 11 popular chess openings. We compared the EFC results with expert opinions from Strong 09 players, finding a correlation for four openings. These findings suggest that EFC can serve as a useful tool for selecting openings and identifying player skills.

Our study investigates the phenomenon of Accretion Induced Collapse in a binary system comprising a neutron star and a massive star.  The massive star, which can be either a supergiant or a red giant, is modeled as an n=1.33 polytrope with complex convective mixing.  The accretion of mass onto the neutron star causes the neutron star to exceed the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff density limit and transform into a massive neutron star or even a black hole.  The numerical simulations, which are carried out with the CoCoNuT-Fcode, demonstrate that the behavior of the binary system is highly sensitive to the rate of accretion and the angular momentum loss.  The evaporation of the binary system, which is a long-term outcome, is influenced by the neutron star's mass and the orbital parameters.  The mass of the neutron star has a significant impact on the binary's long-term evolution and evaporation time.  The binary system, which is initially in an orbital period of approximately 10^4 days, can experience significant changes in its orbital parameters and the neutron star's mass, ultimately leading to evaporation.

A systematic approach is developed to calculate integrals for higher-order Euler-Lagrange ordinary differential equations, including the fourth-order Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator as a key example. This method utilizes the Helmholtz variational derivative and the properties of perfect derivatives to derive a set of first integrals, which are then employed to obtain a nonlocal transformation reducing the original second-order system to a pair of first-integral ODEs. Additionally, an intrinsic formula is provided for the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator's conserved energy.

Recent advancements in retrieving 3D shapes using a set of point clouds as a guide have been achieved, but the current state-of-the-art methods are based on assumptions that may not hold true for more complex and complex 3D shapes. It has been observed that these methods struggle to effectively reconstruct complex shapes due to their inherent ambiguity. Nevertheless, using a polygonal framework as a guide has led to promising results with other tasks, prompting an investigation into how to improve shape retrieval based on point cloud proposals. Our study introduces a novel algorithm called FC-GM, which employs a graph neural network to create a circular shape representation from a set of point clouds. FC-GM achieves superior performance on the ShapeNet retrieval task, surpassing current techniques by a significant margin. It has also been demonstrated that FC-GM is more robust in handling complex and complex 3D shapes.

This study examines the effects of a planet's own thermal radiation and varying temperatures as it moves in a fixed orbit, and how these factors impact the planet's overall appearance. Researchers used a specialized computer model to simulate a rapidly rotating planet and observed its overall look under different conditions. They found that the planet's overall temperature changes significantly throughout its orbit, reaching an extreme difference of about 800 Kelvin in one case. They also discovered that the planet's thermal radiation varies greatly depending on its orbital position, reaching a maximum difference of about 300 Watts per square meter. These variations are particularly noticeable when the planet is closest to its host star, where its atmospheric dynamics and flow patterns are affected by the planet's own heat and reflected light.

Numerical simulations of collapsing fluids with smooth initial conditions consistently produce numerical singularities in finite time. To investigate this phenomenon, we analyze small perturbations to the mass profile in a 1D gas cloud collapse scenario. These perturbations do not affect whether a singularity forms, its location, or the moment of its formation. Instead, they only influence the perturbation pattern within the collapsing fluid. This suggests that the decision to form a singularity originates at the boundary of the cloud, implying that perturbations from fluid turbulence inside the cloud may not play a crucial role in determining the outcome of the collapse. However, it remains uncertain if all types of perturbations that can arise from a collapsing fluid are genuinely smooth in nature.

A code-based proof for the strong weak gravity conjecture in extremal asymptotically flat electric theories has been offered, establishing that in an extremal ensemble, the mass of each black hole must be able to diminish under non-extremal conditions, given that the conjecture's requirements are met. This was done without assuming any specific structure for the ensemble, though the proof's validity is subject to a constraint on the number of black holes it can accommodate, which is determined by the theory's parameters and a parameter $N$. This proof was initially based on an earlier code for extremal black holes in such theories but was enhanced by considering an extended code that allows for non-extremal black holes as well.

In reinforcement learning (RL), intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards are both crucial for a learner's growth in a variety of scenarios. However, integrating intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards in practice is a complex challenge. To tackle this issue, we introduce a novel method that combines intrinsic motivation and extrinsic rewards more effectively by introducing an intrinsic exploration bonus. This new method is efficient in training and showcases improved generalization when compared to multiple RL baselines, as demonstrated in a number of test scenarios. Furthermore, our method is adaptable and can be applied to various off-the-shelf RL models.

A newly developed coloured Poincaré gravity is positioned to explain the origin of coloured gravity. By employing a coloured algebra constructed from the oscillator representation of the Heisenberg algebra, this work leverages prior research by Wu and the authors on coloured Lie groups and generalised Coset models to derive a suitable generalisation of the Einstein-Hilbert action. The resulting action includes an infinite series of scalar curvatures coupled to specific density terms. Specifically, this generalised action includes the standard Hilbert-Palatini action for Lie groups, as well as a collection of higher-order curvature actions. Furthermore, this generalised action can be applied to the study of coloured gravity through a Coset model, specifically for a model denoted as U(3)⊗U(3)/SU(3). This application yields a total Hilbert-Palatini action that incorporates an additional gauge field, thus facilitating a pure gravity action with an additional field. Consequently, this generalised action can be used to derive a total Palatini action, consisting of a combination of Hilbert-Palatini actions and a Yang-Mills one, enabling a total Palatini action to be written down for coloured gravity. This result allows for a comparison of the total Palatini action with a cosmological constant, an additional gauge field, and an additional scalar field, mirroring the Standard Model + Cosmological Constant action.
