The calculation of particle emission from black holes formed in the early stages of the universe's inflation is performed taking into account the Hawking's exponential spectrum modification due to the finite time available for particle creation during the radiation-dominated universe. This leads to a finite flux of low-energy photons that can have a significant impact on various constraints related to primordial black holes such as their contribution to dark matter, evaporation events, and gaps in the cosmic microwave background. The findings show that the migration of the peak of the Hawking spectrum for lighter black holes can result in an order of magnitude increase in the photon flux for masses less than $10^{5}$ GeV.

We assess the circuit assessment capability of our proposed Reconfigurable Field-Programmable Gate Array-Processor (RFGP) by comparing the circuit evaluation speeds with state-of-the-art Prolog interpreters and an open-source FPGA. By integrating a customized hardware description language with a processor architecture featuring pipelined operations, a single instruction can utilize up to four Field-Programmable Gate Array cells. The resulting speed improvements allow the RFGP to process a set of 32,768 instructions in 0.008 seconds, allowing it to surpass the fastest existing software-based interpreters and the conventional general-purpose hardware implementation. Specifically, the RFGP exhibits significantly faster circuit evaluation performance than software-based solutions by 2 to 3 orders of magnitude, and faster than hardware-based alternatives by 1.3 to 2 orders of magnitude.

This paper presents an algorithm that allows for approximate solutions to be found efficiently within a time frame of $n^\mathcal{O}(1)$ for a broad class of problems, specifically those involving minimization of constraints without direction and any form of symmetry (crisp constraints). We establish a more general template for this algorithm, which can be applied to a more expansive set of constraints, and an important outcome from this is the verification of a polynomial-time approximate solution finder ($\mathsf{PTAS}$) in specific cases. To derive this result, we initially prove the intractability of exactly achieving the minimum value for these problems, generalizing a prior result on crisp constraints and revealing the first instances of valued constraint problems where the optimality of solutions is undecidable for any degree of approximation ($\epsilon$). Furthermore, we establish the intractability of valued constraint problems featuring only minimization constraints and constraints with no direction, generalizing a prior result on crisp constraints and having a more limited scope than the current PTAS result.

Previous research on few-shot parsing has often assumed a large training set of around a hundred annotated target trees. Our new model, FPIO, is the first parsing approach specifically designed for a few-shot setting. It is capable of learning from as few as twenty annotated target trees while still matching the performance of its competitors that use a larger training set. Our evaluation shows that FPIO is outperforming the existing methods in tasks involving new languages as well as new trees within the same language. Our approach integrates a novel syntax-augmented transformer model and a novel target grammar discovery method to improve the quality of derived grammars. Notably, our model is also capable of adapting to different grammatical structures by learning a single-layer syntax tree-togrammar translator that can be applied to a range of different target grammars.

In numerous real-world applications, such as detecting invasive species or
identifying pollutants, hyperspectral images are employed. By leveraging
classification results from end-members, we developed a method to label each
pixel with a high level of detail. These detailed labels significantly enhance
the accuracy of semantic segmentation compared to using standard labels.

Studies of the star KIC 6801014, previously identified as an example of evolutionary rotation changes, reveal an unexpected profile, featuring slow and nearly constant mid-section and a faster rotation at its poles. The star actually belongs to the red clump phase, a red giant with specific evolutionary characteristics. The likelihood of its unusual rotation being caused by evolutionary processes is low, and other possibilities include it being part of a binary system with the red clump cladding a blue straggler core, or the system being part of a triple with equal masses. The analysis of its rotation, mass, and other properties offers new insights into red clump stars and their evolutionary rotation changes, as well as their internal structure and the causes behind evolutionary rotation changes.

We create a modified version of the RAM model for computing with polynomial integers, by representing each as an array of words. It is shown that any function within NC^2 complexity can be computed using a circuit of size O(n^k) and a program of size polylog(n), with a total runtime of O(k * log n). A key component of our reasoning is developing a efficient "lookup" problem and designating a new problem as "division", by leveraging bit manipulation and fast arithmetic operations. Similar techniques are applied at a bit-level analysis. A subsequent paper builds upon this work to prove an NC^2 separation from P under a specific assumption related to matrix multiplication.

A significant challenge in session-based recommendation is the scarcity of data in training. To address this issue, we propose a novel data augmentation technique that leverages self-supervised pre-training to enhance the performance of session-based recommendation models. Our pre-training method utilizes an attention-based model to learn meaningful representations from unlabeled data without prior knowledge. We then use these representations to generate augmented sessions by modifying user affinities and session start times. This approach not only preserves session diversity but also enhances the representation quality. Through comprehensive experiments, our method achieves a 5% relative performance gain over baseline models on real-world datasets.

This paper investigates subfamilies of linear complementary code (LCD) types within group algebras. By employing a group algebra framework, different subsets of LCD types can be defined using specific elements. Our findings show that these subfamilies can be encoded in a systematic manner via matrix forms and in variable time. Various properties of these subfamilies are also established, including their rank and weight distributions. Experiments using MATLAB confirm that our proposed subfamilies yield a substantial collection of unique LCD type codes, which is an significant contribution.

Infinitesimal invariant differential forms play a key role in the stable cohomology of the group GL(n,R), allowing a connection between these forms and the stable real cohomology ring. Infvariant forms can be represented by polynomial expressions in invariant GL(n,R)- differential forms. Research into the stable cohomology ring focuses on finding invariant forms with non-zero application results on specific polynomial representations of GL(n,R). Our investigation reveals the application outcomes for certain invariant forms related to GL(n,R), specifically those with one or two blocks, and consequently, we derive the stable cohomology ring's polynomial generators.

We've developed a novel method for enhancing recurrent neural networks by incorporating auxiliary variables that improve categorization capabilities without necessitating additional training. The mechanism is grounded in a state-visitation encoding scheme for recurrent states, which enables neural states to be categorized into discrete objects automatically. We've integrated this method into a variety of neural network architectures and demonstrated its effectiveness through comprehensive evaluations on benchmark object categorization tasks that involve varied domain adaptation and generalization challenges. The results indicate that our method boosts performance across multiple object categorization benchmarks, consistently delivering state-of-the-art outcomes even under demanding conditions.

The skin effect exhibited by non-Hermitian Chern bands in the extended Hatano-Nelson chain is influenced in diverse ways depending on the type of correlation present.  In this research, we investigate the skin effect in this chain when subjected to both diagonal and non-diagonal correlations. Our findings reveal that diagonal correlations amplify the skin effect, whereas correlations stemming from a global mapping to a Hermitian system diminish it. Furthermore, we observe that the skin effect can be minimized through a skin depth formula applicable to diagonal systems.

This paper presents a novel method for constructing Golay complementary multi-dimensional arrays using quaternary bases. It demonstrates that feasible Golay complementary array pairs made from unit-quaternion numbers can be achieved at any odd length with unlimited power, while feasible constructions at even lengths are limited to powers of 2. We have developed a recursive technique to create GCAPs at any prime power length. We have identified a significant connection between Golay complementary binary arrays and quaternary arrays. We have derived a formula for the minimum power of unit-quaternion GCAPs at prime power length n. We have shown that GCAPs at odd lengths n can be made at power n, whereas at even lengths n they must be at power 2n. We have presented a novel construction of GCAPs at odd lengths n. We have found that the smallest known length for a GCAP with a power of n + 1 is 11. We have found that the maximum size of an orthogonal set of GCAPs at odd lengths n is 2, with an infinite supply of such sets. We have constructed sets of maximum power of 1, 2, and 3 at even lengths n. We have found that the largest known size for a set at length n = 10 is 3. We have developed a novel technique for creating GCAPs at any prime power length n. It is proven that the maximum power of GCAPs is 1 for odd lengths n

Recent data from the LHC's Higgs boson run has yielded interesting information about its interaction with vector bosons, particularly in the context of anomalous vector boson couplings. Analysis of the invariant mass distributions from 125 GeV Higgs boson decays to WW* and ZZ* in the 2016-2018 time period, along with predictions from the standard model, have led to a lack of significant deviation at a 95% confidence level. This analysis has imposed stricter constraints on couplings than previously established through similar analyses, especially for couplings to transverse polarization states. When considering scenarios in which the couplings to these states are equivalent, some of these constraints exceed the expectations of the standard model. A similar comparison with the standard model using an effective field theory also exceeded expectations in this scenario.

For a diverse range of applications, identifying and extracting changes from multi-temporal image pairs is crucial. While unsupervised change detection methods have been being developed, they are often limited by their ability to detect only simple changes and require the pairs to be near-identical except for the changes. In contrast, the proposed method leverages a generator based on a normalizing flow to produce realistic images for an imaginary reference time, thereby enabling the extraction of latent changes through a binary masking technique. By treating this as an autoencoding task and employing a generator that encodes the pair into a change indicator and a common time, the method enables detection without the need for labeled data. Furthermore, it has been observed that the method can perform well on non-identical images and even on data from different data sources. As a result, unsupervised change detection has emerged as a highly data-efficient approach, yielding results comparable to or better than those of supervised methods, which are limited by their ability to learn the distribution of changes from labeled examples.

We establish that for any positive integer $n$, there exist infinite sets of relatively prime integers $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$, comprising only non-zero digits up to $n$, such that their union is additively complete, with a corresponding set of relatively prime integers $\mathcal{A}'$ and $\mathcal{B}'$ up to $n+1$, such that their union is additively complete and contains $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$. This finding is an improvement on a previous result, changing the upper bound from $n+1$ to $n$. Furthermore, for any relatively prime integers $\mathcal{A}$ and $\mathcal{B}$ forming an additively complete set with all elements not exceeding $n$, there exist infinite sets of integers $n'$ and integers $n''$, such that $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$ can be extended to form an additively complete set by adding non-zero digits up to $n'$. Similarly, $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$ can be extended to form an additively complete set by adding non-zero digits up to $n''$, where $\mathcal{A} \cup \mathcal{B}$ only consists of even integers. This work generalizes a result from [arXiv:2009.0029

In a Heisenberg two-spin system within a silicon lattice, a gap exists for coupling between Heisenberg exchange interactions for specific energy gaps. The valence band's influence on this coupling is minor. The Heisenberg exchange interaction can be adjusted by the position and quantity of dopants within the Heisenberg exchange interaction's energy gap, which can be controlled by electric fields through accumulation or depletion of the dopants. The donor concentration can also be manipulated to adjust the Heisenberg exchange interaction, offering an opportunity for developing silicon-based quantum processors with controllable and scalable coupling.

This paper introduces LibOPT, a C library for global optimization that features
multiple algorithms and a broad range of benchmarking functions, as well as a
benchmarking suite, to evaluate and compare different optimization methods.

We have determined the transitivity degree for complete linear systems on smooth complete intersections within toric varieties of codimension one, along with examples illustrating the concept in toric surface bundles over other toric surfaces. Our analysis builds on a final example from Keel's theory of relative moduli spaces of stable pairs. Our concept of transitivity degree originates from Rosenzweig and Seshadri's work on relative Seshadri constants.

This brief note is a collection of quantum mechanics problems, primarily focusing on systems with multiple particles and their inherent symmetries, as well as fundamental conservation principles such as energy and momentum. The problems address both one- and three-dimensional systems, both bound and free, with solutions presented in a pedagogical format. The compilation emphasizes the principles of angular momentum and parity for single-particle states, and delves into the properties of total angular momentum and momentum in systems with multiple particles, especially within non-abelian frameworks. Problems also explore the principles of linear momentum, kinetic energy, and the Heisenberg uncertainty principle, utilizing single-particle Hamiltonians in various scenarios. The purpose of this compilation is to supplement existing textbooks and to provide an organized collection of quantum mechanics problems with multiple particle systems as a central theme.

The article investigates the two-photon absorption process in a quantum well structure composed of a QW layer sandwiched between a multiple quantum well and capita layers, using the continuity equation and detailed analysis of charge carrier dynamics. It examines the two-photon absorption coefficient in graphene and its given data to model the process, analyzing the resulting current density and examining how the quantum confined Stark effect influences the coefficient. The study reveals that two-photon absorption leads to the generation of two charge carriers simultaneously, with the probability proportional to the product of the incident photon probabilities. It further explores the impact of space charge on the quantum confined Stark effect. The resulting equations can serve as a foundation for modeling similar quantum well-based structures.

We introduce a novel framework in which we train the existing MARBERT model to learn the characteristics of a specific group. We use this model to enhance its ability to detect misogyny in text, by providing information about female representation in its training data. Our findings show that the model is capable of identifying detectable patterns of misogyny in text, and that its performance is linked to its exposure to specific groups of text during training. Through our analysis, we determine that the model is capable of text classification based on its exposure to misogynistic text. Our results also reveal that the model's performance in detecting misogyny is comparable to or better than other top-performing models. Through our fine-tuning experiments, we found that the model's ability to detect misogyny can be improved further, by fine-tuning it on a large dataset of text that contains examples of misogynistic language.

This research focuses on a novel backward stochastic differential equation that incorporates historical time intervals into its generator, along with an associated forward-backward differential equation system. A key finding is the development of a necessary and sufficient condition for the existence and uniqueness of a stochastic interval times' four-tuple that satisfies this equation. Furthermore, under certain conditions, the solution can be effectively characterized by a generalised Volterra integral equation that includes past time intervals, and the equation's differentiability is also examined.

Reinforcement learning techniques enable the creation of robotic controllers that can operate in varied settings without control adjustments. However, the reliability of these controllers when faced with operational conditions different from the initial one remains a concern. We investigate this issue from a novel perspective by modeling the transition from a controller's original operational setting to its current state as a time-varying process in a framework where the future state is uncertain and contingent on the current state. We propose a method to train a robust controller that can withstand gradual environmental changes by simulating environmental degradation in the dynamics model. This is achieved by introducing a lower bound on the noise level within the dynamics model. We demonstrate this method's effectiveness on a 7-DoF robotic task and observe that it not only yields a more robust controller but also leads to an improved control performance. Moreover, we find that setting a lower noise threshold in the dynamics model results in a controller with both enhanced robustness and precision.

We define a general framework for analyzing coded caching schemes and demonstrate its benefits. This framework is expressed as a function that takes a user count, file number, and specific users' demands, yielding the total data transmission required by the scheme. This data transmission rate can be described through a $\mathcal{R}$ function that maps combinatorial structures to data transmission rates. In this framework, various upper bounds on the minimum cache size are explored in detail, including schemes based on set systems, uniform set systems, and resolvable set systems. A notable achievement is the demonstration of a novel resolvable set system that yields an improved data transmission rate for the $\mathcal{R}$ function. Additionally, a framework-style proof is presented, showing that certain schemes achieve the desired data transmission rate, and this is applied to verify the optimality of a uniform resolvable set system that had been previously proposed. This discovery confirms the scheme's optimality in achieving a specific data transmission rate under given conditions.

We present a predicative Scott model of languages similar to LF, establishing a 
constructive and predicative framework that is consistent with proof terms containing 
classical reasoning, while also resolving issues arising from previous models attempting 
to interpret such terms through a single level of implication. Models based on Scott 
domains are particularly useful as they facilitate the inclusion of computation within 
proof terms, commonly seen in languages with proof irrelevance in mind.

A specific set of elements from the Weyl group, known as $W^{\vee}_{\mathbb{R},>0}$, consisting of matrices with non-negative diagonal entries, is utilized to define a unique decomposition of degenerate Eisenstein series for GL(n). This result relies on previous work with supergroup GCL(n+1) and establishes that the degenerate Eisenstein series, initially defined by Harish-Chandra, can be expressed as a sum of unique contributions from each coset within $W^{\vee}_{\mathbb{R},>0}$.

This research focuses on collision avoidance methods for mobile robotic systems, specifically utilizing neural network-based approaches that consider the spatial configuration of the arm's components to optimize avoidance strategies. By defining a collision function that accounts for the position of each link relative to the environment, training data can be created through a combination of sampling methods. A classification model is then developed to accommodate multiple constraints and optimize collision detection. To further enhance performance, various training techniques, including multi-class optimization and adversarial training, are investigated, leading to improved generalization capabilities without sacrificing accuracy. Experimentation reveals that techniques such as adversarial training significantly boost the system's robustness and reliability, particularly in handling unseen obstacles.

The rapid growth in the use of the Internet and digital communication has led to a significant shift in the way people express and communicate with each other, NLP's primary goal is to effectively process and understand digital text, which has become increasingly crucial to address the complexity of written and spoken communication.  Despite the advancements made so far, the field of NLP still faces challenges in fully grasping nuanced forms of communication such as sarcasm, double meanings, and cultural references.  Despite these challenges, the applications of this technology are highly beneficial to industries such as search engines, news and social media monitoring, and language learning.

Advancements in the precision of Ramsey interferometry on large-scale Bose-Einstein condensates are being propelled by the development of nonlinear quantum gates. Hadamard gates traditionally employed in Ramsey interferometry have been upgraded to nonlinear versions, enabling a fundamental shift from linear to quadratic phase accumulation and consequently improving measurement efficiency. These nonlinear gates can be physically realized through interactions with photon-matter systems or atomic collisions. An optimized quantum state preparation, combined with innovative readout methods developed by Resch and Kim, has been applied in our simulation of nonlinear quantum interferometry, demonstrating a quantum interference pattern with an enhanced contrast and measurement precision equivalent to that of classical interferometry using unstable oscillators.

This paper deals with the topic of value distribution theory for several complex variables. We have developed a novel estimate of the counting function for the intersection of meromorphic mappings with given subsets. Specifically, we give a precise bound on the frequency with which images of holomorphic mappings intersect with specified hypersurfaces and hyperplanes in complex projective spaces. Our estimate can be used to establish new inequalities, including a significant generalization of the standard Nevanlinna inequality in complex projective spaces.

This paper presents an innovative approach that adapts signature-based Gröbner basis algorithms to efficiently compute a generative representation of a Gröbner basis for a subspace of a polynomial ideal with fixed bounds. By having access to a generic software tool for solving systems of polynomial equations, we can calculate generative representations of solution spaces for certain polynomial ideals, specifically those representing algebraic constraints in terms of affine Gröbner basis elements. We demonstrate the utility of this method by applying it to two novel problems: containment testing between Gröbner bases and a solution approach to Kollár's effective Nullstellensatz.

The PHENIX collaboration has measured the yield of direct photons at midrapidity in Cu+Cu collisions at 47.6 GeV per nucleon-nucleon. In comparison to measurements of midrapidity charged particles, the yield of photons in Cu+Cu collisions exhibits a distinct relationship. Specifically, the yield of photons, when considered per unit of rapidity, exhibits a proportionality to the charged particle yield.

The extremal function $exco_2(n,H)$ defines the maximum number of edges in a non-4-partite $n$ vertex hypergraph that does not contain a specific subgraph isomorphic to $H$ with 4 vertices or fewer. This concept is extended to general extremal functions $exco_t(n,H)$ for any positive integer $t$. We establish a quadratic upper limit for $exco_2(n,H)$ in the case of $H$ being $K_4^2$, and this limit can be achieved in infinite cases for 2-partite $exco_2(n,H)$ functions. Our current proof only applies when the parts are of equal size. This result applies universally for any $H$ that can be formed from $K_4$ by replacing edges with complete particlizations. Moreover, for any 2-partite $exco_2(n,H)$ that does not have equal parts, there is an associated partite hypergraph that does not contain $K_4^2$. This proves that $exco_2(n,H)$ is not always achievable in its maximum quartic form. Our findings also apply to saturation functions $satco_2(n,H)$.

This paper presents an innovative technique for rendering fan-shaped line joins that surpasses a standard triangle cap approach, resulting in more authentic and precise visual effects. We propose an algorithm for generating high-quality triangle fan joins and an accompanying method for seamlessly capging arbitrary polygon trails. This method is paired with a novel, efficient technique for dynamically switching between vertex and triangle fan modes at a significant framerate. This new strategy for triangle/vertex switching is both faster and produces a higher level of precision in triangle coverage compared to a commonly used reference method. Our proposed methods have been integrated into a high-performance triangle fan renderer that can compete with state-of-the-art libraries in both speed and visual fidelity.

This note aims to develop a quasi-interpolation formula based on the novel regularized fundamental solution of the fractional Laplace operator, as presented in [17]. We demonstrate that this formula preserves both convexity and monotonicity properties, while achieving optimal approximation error and exponential convergence in the presence of smooth scalar-valued data defined over a sufficiently dense grid. Furthermore, we derive an alternative expression for the fractional Laplace operator that enhances its numerical stability.

The TeV gamma-ray and cosmic positron excesses observed in the Earth's vicinity may have a connection to pulsar TeV emissions and their resulting gamma-ray halo formation within the interstellar medium. Given the long-standing pulsar activity and the profound penetration of high-energy electrons into the Earth's mid-ISM, the characteristics of pulsar halos offer distinct signals that can be identified. This study explores the potential of pulsar halos as a novel class of TeV gamma-ray sources with unique properties. Through the incorporation of the galactic magnetic field and supernova remnant (SNR) interactions, the study presents a theoretical framework for pulsar TeV photon and interstellar photon-induced cascade electron-positron pair formation. The findings indicate that pulsar halos could account for the observed gamma-ray and positron excesses, and their detection within large angular distances from pulsars could offer valuable insights into the galactic magnetic field's structure and energy. The study further discusses the predicted signal intensity and detectability of pulsar halos by the HAWC and CTA experiments.

This study introduces a novel method of enhancing APNES (a dataset of images with various animal parts) and applying it to produce randomized super pixel delimitation masks for the entire dataset. This approach is employed to boost the performance of Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) in classification and multi-label learning tasks. We utilized several popular CNNs, including VGG16, Inception, and Inception-ResNet, for experiments. Our findings demonstrate that using standardized delimitation masks leads to more similar and reliable features across different methods and models.

Our analysis of English-language publications from 1994 to 2020, utilizing AI-driven topic extraction and clustering, involved 180k+ articles from 21 high-impact peer-reviewed journals. We investigated how the interest of various stakeholders in 30 distinct scientific disciplines evolved over time. We found that while the overall scientific community and general interest publications showed increased focus on climate change, the trend was less pronounced among general interest science journals and economists, and surprisingly, policymakers showed a relatively lower concern for the issue. Furthermore, our research revealed that although climate change-related discussions often revolved around a limited number of scientific fields, the number of fields addressing the topic among general interest readers and policymakers was comparatively lower. We also discovered that climate change-related publications showed fewer inter-stakeholder groups sharing the same 10 most cited references. Our study provides a framework for comparing the interest of diverse stakeholder groups in scientific and technical domains and can serve as a valuable tool for analyzing their respective focal areas.

Recent advancements in soft robotics have been facilitated by the incorporation of intelligent materials and the development of sophisticated modeling techniques. The complexity of the underlying physics, however, poses significant challenges in creating an effective observer or controller within a feedback loop. Research in soft robotics has recently gained momentum through the application of the Koopman operator theory, which has been shown in several case studies to facilitate the observation and control of systems governed by complex physics. This work introduces the application of the Koopman operator theory to soften robotic systems, building upon previous research. We develop a novel approach for state estimation in a 120-degree continuum robotic system that employs x-ray imaging, resulting in a parametric state that captures the individual bending of each spine. By defining a parabolic function to represent the shape of the robot, we create an observability map. Leveraging an eigenfunction basis derived from a parabolic PDE and data-driven methods, we carry out an empirical study and demonstrate that the resulting estimator exhibits a mean square error approximately 10% lower than the performance of a standard linear estimator.

Optimization in deep learning relies on gradient-based methods that adjust model parameters using the gradient of a loss function, but these methods may converge slowly due to their consideration of only first-order information. A new approach to optimization is presented in this paper, employing a technique called the natural gradient, which incorporates additional information about the loss function's curvature to adjust updates in a geometrically informative manner. To efficiently implement this method, we use an approximate Hessian inversion technique based on Krylov subspaces and the Conjugate Gradient method, allowing us to compute the natural gradient descent update without storing the full Hessian matrix. Experimental results on SOTA image classification models demonstrate that our method can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy with fewer iterations compared to traditional optimization methods. The proposed approach also has several practical benefits: the need for a learning rate is eliminated, and the method can converge directly to stationary points regardless of its initial position.

Recent X-ray observations by the Chandra satellite have revealed unusual, highly ionized metal features in two distant active galactic nuclei, associated with complex, variable spectral patterns. These peculiar features are thought to result from complex geometries and non-standard temperature conditions. As a result, existing models of active galactic nuclei outperform each other in explaining these phenomena. What is striking about these active galactic nuclei is that they exhibit a high X-ray absorption level, which is inconsistent with typical counterparts in nearby galaxies. We hypothesize that these active galactic nuclei exhibit a jet directed towards us, as interaction with the jet could explain both their unusual spectral characteristics and high X-ray absorption level. Jets from interacting with the surrounding medium release energy that ionizes the metal features, while also producing radio emission. We predict that absorption lines from a similar temperature range to a similar geometry will be present in a sample of active galactic nuclei that exhibit radio emission and high X-ray absorption level, as observed by the Chandra satellite and radio interferometers.

The NetLLM project, an initiative led by Samsung AI Center in collaboration with researchers and clinicians at Asan Medical Center in Seoul, Korea, is dedicated to developing powerful AI tools to address critical problems in the field of lung cancer. This paper describes the development of Lite-ProSENet, a computer-based model designed to accurately predict the duration of a patient's survival after their lung cancer treatment. Lite-ProSENet has achieved a performance level of 0.828 in terms of the AUC value, surpassing the existing best results with a metric called AUPRC. To accomplish this, Lite-ProSENet utilizes a combination of high-resolution, globally context-aware feature extraction, a more precise image-based patient grouping method called Clinical-NetGuided Stable ClusterNet (CN-SCN), and a training approach known as Clinical-guided Adaptive Loss (gAL), which places greater emphasis on samples that are harder to categorize. This results in improved accuracy and generalizability of the network. Additionally, Lite-ProSENet employs a Clinical-guided Adaptive Loss (gAL) technique that dynamically adjusts the weight of training examples in accordance with their clinical significance and complexity. This allows Lite-ProSENet to achieve better performance and generalizability in its predictions.

Recent studies have revealed that many effective learning methods create hidden representations of states that are predictive, yet most are not designed to be understood linguistically. Despite their effectiveness, these representations pose a problem because they can't be interpreted in terms of specific, meaningful states, making it impossible to generalize new learning challenges, combine or transfer existing knowledge, or understand the internal workings of these methods. We believe that creating transparent, linguifiable state representations is crucial for developing more robust and adaptable learning processes, even if these representations are slightly less effective than optimal ones. To test this idea, we developed a new approach using natural language to search for optimal state representations in reinforcement learning problems, resulting in representations that are both more effective and easier to understand.

Using a simulation, we've tested and refined methods for rebuilding the power spectrum from synthetic and from the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's data. We've found that non-Gaussian effects significantly impact the accuracy of the reconstruction process, with varying wavelengths showing distinct levels of accuracy loss. As a result, we've developed a more advanced method to rebuild the power spectrum, incorporating a 'cleaning' technique to minimize the influence of long wavelength contamination. We've verified our methods against the Baryon Oscillation Spectroscopic Survey's data and found a substantial improvement in statistical precision for certain scale ranges. We've also demonstrated that our methods can be effectively applied in a model-independent manner to study the evolution of structure in the universe.

This paper addresses the following questions for Lie algebras of type A: 
(1) Can we establish the irreducibility of tensor products of the form $U(\mathfrak{h})$-free modules with highest weight modules, and 
(2) Can we characterize tensor products of irreducible modules and establish their decomposition into simple components? 
Moreover, we provide general answers to these questions, encompassing all types of Lie algebras.

Neural networks, including those utilizing Quasi-Arithmetic (QALSTOM), have shown great potential in various NLP tasks, including sentiment analysis. However, standard LSTM models often struggle with the variability of sentiment words and their context-dependent meanings. To overcome this limitation, a new approach was developed that incorporates a three-way classification system for identifying whether a tweet expresses positive, negative, or neutral sentiment. By pre-training filters for sentiment words and their associated sentiment values, this innovative model effectively learns to account for the polarity of individual sentences and their influence on overall sentiment. As a result, the proposed QALSTOM and LSTM models demonstrate superior performance compared to a traditional three-way sentiment classification system.

In this study, we examine how role specifications affect dialogue system performance within the scope of the MultiDialog system, which is designed to engage users in natural, sustained conversations. While role specifications are beneficial for streamlining development and maintaining consistency, users may interpret them differently, leading to varied responses and potential conversational awkwardness. To assess the relevance of role specifications in real applications, we collected and annotated a dataset containing actual user responses to the conversations. For evaluation, we compared the dialogue systems using the same training data but varying role specifications, and the results indicate that extensive use of role specifications is unnecessary for effective human evaluation.

Current and upcoming ground-based detectors are sensitive to stochastic background signals from gravitational waves, but they are also sensitive to a different background signal known as "memory" background signals, which has not been fully investigated yet. In this study, an expression is derived to describe the background power spectral density of the memory signal and compared with the standard power spectral density of the noise in Advanced LIGO, Advanced Virgo, and the future Einstein Telescope. It is discovered that detectors can respond to both types of signals simultaneously, with the memory response initially appearing weaker but eventually becoming comparable at lower frequencies. This indicates a need for specialized analysis methods to accurately detect and distinguish between these two types of signals in the future Einstein Telescope.

A comprehensive theory of supersymmetry breaking in a gauge-mediated model, 
involving a single mediator and a multi-flavored right-handed neutrino, has 
been developed. The mediator's supersymmetry violation results in a multi-flavored 
chirality superpotential that enables a single-flavored right-handed neutrino 
to achieve neutrino masses via the see-saw mechanism, but fails to result in 
leptogenesis due to CP symmetry. In this model, we have found a solution to 
this issue - the mediator's supersymmetry breaking can lead to supersymmetry 
breaking at a PeV scale, an optimal scale for non-resonant thermal 
leptogenesis, as proposed by Schmitz and Schmidt. This has been achieved by 
introducing a multi-flavored right-handed neutrino and a rephasing right-handed 
chirality superfield that interacts with the mediator and the multi-flavored 
right-handed neutrino, and whose soft mass is generated through a radiative 
mechanism, involving a unique $U(1)$ symmetry, and whose scale is comparable 
to the mediator's scale, and whose scale is comparable to the chirality 
superfield's scale, and whose scale is comparable to the mediator's scale, and 
whose scale is comparable to the multi-flavored right-handed neutrino's scale, 
and whose scale is comparable to the mediator's scale, and whose scale is 
comparable to the PeV scale,

A cutting-edge communication system based on wireless energy and information signaling has gained considerable attention due to its high data transmission efficiency. We consider a multi-antenna setup with an Energy Signal Communication link, where multiple energy signals are transmitted from a base station to a user via multiple paths. We derive the Energy Signal Communication's spectral efficiency and demonstrate that increasing the base station's transmit power leads to better energy reliability. We also show that using a maximum ratio transmission scheme significantly enhances both energy and wireless power transfer efficiency. We then develop a green communication strategy by optimizing the base station's transmit power to achieve a minimum required energy reliability while minimizing total transmitted power. We then extend this approach by considering a scenario with multiple users and a more challenging wireless power transfer problem, where minimizing total base station transmit power subject to each user's energy reliability constraint is addressed. We then analyze the sum energy efficiency of a novel PDP scheme that combines wireless energy signaling and information data transmission. This communication model utilizes energy signaling to convey the data symbols and measures communication performance by the sum energy efficiency. We then derive a necessary and sufficient condition for the sum energy efficiency's optimal solution to exist and develop a low-complexity algorithm that achieves this optimum by iteratively updating the energy signaling and data transmission powers. This innovation may lead to a significant paradigm shift in future wireless networks.

This study focuses on creating a more accurate and efficient word suggestion model. By examining the performance of various models with different levels of complexity, we found that models which integrate semantic analysis with syntactic analysis produce better suggested words than those that rely on syntax alone. Furthermore, it was discovered that using a hybrid approach to analyze sentences, combining the strengths of syntactic and semantic analysis methods, yields similar results to those obtained from fully hybrid models that incorporate semantic analysis into their core components. These findings were used to develop a highly effective hybrid word suggestion system that employs an external parser and is incorporated into a live user interface for actual applications and easier evaluation.

This research proposes an innovative method using attention networks to enhance
recommendation systems by dynamically generating user profiles and gathering
context from all user interactions and surrounding environment features. By giving
more weight to relevant past experiences and excluding unconnected events, this
method increases the quality of the generated profiles. As a result, our approach
enables the system to prioritize the most suitable items and incorporate contextual
information to provide personalized recommendations. We evaluated this method on
two widely utilized datasets and observed a notable increase in the relevance of
recommended items, along with improved contextual understanding, compared to
standard recommendation models.

We investigate the behavior of active dimers driven by fluctuating "kicks" at their leading segment. Building upon earlier studies, which demonstrated a seamless connection between random and directed motion for varying particle aspect ratios, we focus on how shape influences the directed movement. Our analysis reveals that, similar to steering mechanisms in larger devices, the internal fluctuations effectively guide the dimer's motion. However, which direction the dimer moves depends on its size and flexibility. This movement can be understood through a connection to orientational changes, revealing distinct behaviors based on whether the internal fluctuations are weak or strong. These findings align with observations of certain biological dimers.

This research presents a novel method for simulating fluid flow in fractured and fractured/ matrix porous media by introducing a new physics-informed neural network approach. Leveraging the properties of the conforming Delaunay tetrahedralization and conforming mixed finite element method, we ensure that the numerical solution accurately captures the interface between matrix and fracture networks. Furthermore, we introduce strategy for training and accelerating prediction in this method. Our approach involves first training a model on a simple mesh, then using distance transformation to shift the model to a mesh with complex fracture patterns without retraining. The effectiveness of this method is demonstrated through its ability to accurately simulate fluid flow in various porous media configurations, including comparative analysis with traditional finite element methods.

This paper addresses the challenge of guiding a drone swarm from a dispersed arrangement to a compact, cluster-shaped formation while ensuring minimal deviation from its central point. By focusing on this key aspect, we enhance overall formation efficiency and fuel economy by reducing drone point deviations. Our proposed approach employs two key innovations: an optimal control strategy utilizing a potential function to manage individual drones and minimize deviations, and an efficient graph representation of the swarm that enables rapid computation within a reasonable time frame. Our simulation outcomes demonstrate the feasibility of our method in achieving dense, drone cluster formations.

It is established that -1 is always an eigenvalue of the Seidel matrix for a connected chain graph. Furthermore, we develop a method to determine when -2 belongs to the eigenvalue set of the Seidel matrix. By leveraging this approach, we derive a formula for the eigenvalues of the Seidel matrix in specific cases. Also, we identify a chain graph whose Seidel matrix has eigenvalues -2 and -1 with multiplicity 1 each.

This investigation explores the impact of delays in both state and control variables, as well as a moving target, on stochastic control problems with linear-quadratic objectives.  By assuming the delay in the state variable can be approximated by a Feller–Piskorsski–Vasicek process, we develop a series expansion for the Bohnenblust–Paley operator operator and use this to propose an efficient numerical method for obtaining numerical solutions.  Furthermore, we provide a series expansion for the optimal consumption plan taking into account delays in the system and demonstrate the convergence of these approximations with increasing order.  The results are validated by comparing them to open-end money market funds with varying durations.  This study also yields an efficient numerical method for solving stochastic control problems with time delays by treating delay terms as perturbations.  The method is illustrated by considering a specific problem with quadratic objectives and a random delay and yields closed-form solutions that can be expanded using Taylor series.  The results show that the approximation of the delay-optimal state feedback control plan converges monotonically to its instantaneous version.  This research is relevant to a broad class of problems in optimal investment with time delays.

A family of four-second-order banded tridiagonal block matrices is developed,
connecting the eigenvalue problems of the Dirac operator with non-constant coefficients
to a Heun's equation, while also providing explicit expressions for all entries of these
semi-infinite matrices. As coefficients decay exponentially, the corresponding
semi-infinite tridiagonal block matrices converge to four-second-order banded tridiagonal
matrices, enabling the calculation of approximate eigenvalues and eigenfunctions for
the Dirac operator with localized solutions. These eigenvalues relate to parameters in
four special functions, with the eigenfunctions expressed as products of special
function solutions and exponential functions. A numerical demonstration is presented,
using the Sunspot data set, and shows the localized eigenfunctions of the Dirac operator
producing approximations of the pitch-angle distribution function of electrons.

In this study, we examine a complex vehicular network consisting of multiple base stations, heterogeneous vehicles, and two types of relays, all operating within a powerful and expansive environment. A decision is made to utilize either base station or relay relay backhaul links in this setup. We employ a sophisticated model, the K-analytic Gaussian shannon queue model, to determine the average data transmission rate for each relay. By applying advanced mathematical techniques and approximation methods, we calculate key performance indicators: the mean data transmission rate for each user and the overall network capacity. A numerical analysis reveals the impact of various factors such as relay deployment, vehicle density, and connectivity on network capacity. Specifically, our findings show that network capacity increases with the deployment of relay vehicles, and this trend is significantly pronounced under challenging conditions. Additionally, we observe that both mean data transmission rates for pedestrian users decline under difficult environments, and this effect is more pronounced for vehicle users. However, we find that vehicle data transmission rates increase with the deployment of relay relays, and this improvement is most noticeable when the distance between vehicles and base stations is large.

Our goal is to enhance the quality of automatic sentence labeling on Wikipedia articles by employing a weakly supervised method. To achieve this, we utilize the modification patterns of human editors, who tag the sentences in the articles, to learn a automatic labeler. By applying these patterns to a large dataset of articles and edges, we can effectively train the labeler and improve its accuracy. The results of our experiments demonstrate that this method can match the performance of the current top-tier approaches on Wikipedia evaluation datasets and has several advantages in terms of ease of implementation and data collection.

A significant challenge in artificial intelligence (AI) cybersecurity is achieving a comprehensive understanding of black-box models. Traditional black-box modeling techniques rely heavily on data collection through model queries, but this often overlooks the operational principles behind the decision-making process of these models. In contrast, Decision-based Black-Box Knowledge Distillation (DB3) utilizes the target model's own decision outputs for data generation and model training, thereby circumventing the need for excessive data generation. Specifically, our work in DB3 addresses two critical aspects: (1) decision-based output interpretation to create an insight into the decision-making process, and (2) decision-based knowledge distillation for constructing a concise and informative student model. Unlike previous DB3 methods that merely replicate the target model's output, our approach leverages the original model's decision outcomes to develop a student model that not only reproduces these results but also provides deeper insight into the AI system. Experimental validation shows that our DB3 method yields a more informative and functional student model with superior adversarial robustness.

Using data collected by the LHCb detector at a 13 TeV proton-proton collision energy, the branching fractions for the rare decay modes $\bar B^0\to\bar K^{*0}\ell^+\ell^-$ and $\bar B^0\to\bar K^\prime s\ell^+\ell^-$ were investigated within the $q^2$ range of 1 to 13 TeV. The observed and expected significance of the observed $\bar B^0\to\bar K^\prime s\ell^+\ell^-$ signal was 3.1 standard deviations, and both the observed and expected branching fractions were  $(1.06\pm0.15\pm0.10\pm0.04)\times10^{-6}$. The $\bar B^0\to\bar K^{*0}\ell^+\ell^-$ signal was also examined in several subregions and was found to be consistent with the predicted branching fraction.

String theory's homological mirror symmetry has broader applications in various dualities. We investigate the extended Hitchin model for T-duality, which is founded on a specific type of algebra known as continuous-trace. The existence of a classical T-dual in this framework is directly linked to the presence of such algebra. We also examine the implications of this algebra's structure on the duality between Hamiltonian T-duality and mirror symmetry.

Current reinforcement learning methods focus on teaching agents by showing them examples of what to do, but this approach relies on having access to expert behavior, which can be difficult to obtain. As a result, agents are often forced to learn from demonstration data that may not be easily accessible. To overcome this limitation, we introduce Co-IMITATION LEARNING (CoIL), a technique that enables agents to learn through social interaction without the need for demonstration data. In CoIL, agents with varying levels of intelligence engage in a series of trials and errors, with more experienced agents guiding less experienced ones. CoIL has been found to outperform a baseline method in multiple social learning tasks, with better guidance from more experienced agents leading to significant improvements in the learning process.

We examine the probability of error for a sequential decoder utilizing polar codes, under the assumption that the message cutoff rate, specifically the polarized cutoff rate, serves as the decoder's message threshold. As block length approaches infinity, we show that such a cutoff rate results in a negligible probability of error for a sequential decoder, provided the channel error probability is sufficiently small. We utilize a recursive tree expansion approach to analyze the probability that a sequential decoder incorrectly decodes a message, and express this probability as the product of an exponential term and a negligible factor. We prove that for small channel errors, the negligible factor is also exponentially decreasing, thus lowering the probability of error. Notably, while previous research has established an exponential upper bound on error probability with arbitrary cutoff rates, we find that for small channel errors, the exponential term in our analysis with the polarized cutoff rate yields a lower probability of error.

This research introduces a computer vision technique to monitor hands and their interactions with nearby objects in a scene. By training a model on how to detect these actions, the created system can track hands and objects in real-time, even when they occur as videos. The model is built on a novel concept of hand-object interaction tracks, which are formed by connecting individual keypoint locations at specific time intervals. To enhance tracking accuracy, the model uses a self-supervised learning approach to refine its detection capabilities without the need for labeled data. The resulting model exhibits high resilience to obstacles like occlusions and noise in various environments. By integrating this model with traditional tracking methods, the system successfully maintains the ability to detect actions and keeps the model simple in structure. The model is particularly effective in detecting hand-object interactions when both the hands and objects are nearby, a condition commonly encountered in various applications. The model's performance was tested on a variety of datasets, which revealed its ability to accurately detect actions and retain simplicity in structure. The model's performance was found to be comparable to state-of-the-art techniques in detecting hand-object interactions, even when both the hands and objects are nearby, a condition commonly encountered in various applications. The model's performance was discovered to be even better when the hands and objects are nearby, a condition commonly encountered in various applications. The model's performance was found to be comparable to state-of-the-art techniques in detecting action recognition and keypoint localization tasks. In 1992, Gordon reduced groups over $G=\mathbb{Z}_p$ for a prime $p$ and classified them. This result was later extended by Li and Chen for over $\mathbb{Z}_p$ groups in 2016. Our study extends the classification of reduced groups over a finite field $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ and demonstrates that these reduced groups over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ can be completely classified. Furthermore, an efficient algorithm for enumerating these reduced groups has been developed. Algorithmic experiments confirm the efficacy of our approach. Notably, our findings reveal that the reduced groups over $\mathbb{F}_{q}$ for any prime $\mathbb{F}_{2} = \mathbb{F}_{q}$ consist of ${q^{6}} + 3q^{4} + 2q^{2} + 2$ distinct groups of order $2$, which factor into ${q^{6}} + q^{4} + q^{2}$ principal reduced groups and ${q^{6}} + 2q^{4} + q^{2}$ non-principal reduced groups of order $2$.

A reliable calibration method is crucial for end-effectors in collaborative arms, and using a depth camera as a vision system allows for more robust estimation of the end-effector's pose, and through integration with data from three non-collinear markers, achieves a precise calculation of the end-effector's pose.

Identifying and measuring network interference in experiments is complicated by the need to define a clear unit of interest. The spread of interference through networks often spans across different spatial or temporal boundaries, making it difficult to pinpoint which areas or times are affected. The choice of what constitutes a affected unit is crucial for accurately detecting and measuring interference in these situations. The process is further complicated when it is not yet apparent which network members will be treated and how this treatment might spread. We have developed a novel network interdependence metric that can effectively identify and quantify interference of various types and sizes by incorporating both focal units and the extent to which they are influenced. The utility of this metric is demonstrated through simulations of various interference processes, such as the diffusion of a virus and social media posts. These case studies highlight the benefits of using network metrics that can capture interference of different scales, and show how the selection of focal units can make it easier to detect and measure interference in specific areas. We have also found that different types of interference produce distinct patterns of interdependence across networks, and that larger networks are more susceptible to interference.

The formation of a neutron star triggers cooling and self-annihilating dark matter accumulation within the star. This accumulation and subsequent annihilation processes significantly impact the neutron star's thermal evolution. We have developed a model that incorporates dark matter annihilation into the equations governing the evolution of a neutron star's heat content. We have also determined the conditions under which dark matter annihilation within the star becomes a dominant heat source. We have further analyzed how the dark matter annihilation rate is influenced by properties such as the star's crust-averaged squared phonon deformation. These findings reveal that for certain types of dark matter, annihilating within the star can lead to a dramatic increase in its core temperature, ultimately causing the star to become a warm or even hot star. This annihilation process could also result in emission of high-energy gamma rays.

Public, galaxy repository archives contain detailed morphological information from visible light observations, which can be utilized by the Shapepipe pipeline to generate precise and efficient galaxy shape measurements for visible light weak-lensing analysis. It is possible to train the pipeline using existing repositories within a limited timeframe, producing select galaxy images with high-quality shape estimates within a few hours. When compared to the publicly available Code-MAP pipeline, which relies on visible-light data and deeper spectra, our cross-validation indicates that Shapepipe delivers substantially lower shape noise and superior efficiency in estimating galaxy shapes. Collaborations with other research groups have led to the creation of new, in-archive training data to further refine the pipeline's performance. A publicly released version of Shapepipe will enable other researchers to replicate our weak-lensing analysis with minimal effort.

A modified version of the Veech discrete 2-circle problem on a geodesic flow is proposed. This modified problem involves placing 2 circles on a modified surface, where one circle comes from the original surface and is preserved, and the second circle is introduced and can be located anywhere on the modified surface. The constraint is that the lengths of the circles must be in a specific ratio. This modified problem can be broken down into several key issues: determining whether all possible positions of the second circle are finite for any given ratio, classifying these positions up to homeomorphism, and understanding their distribution across a measured foliation on the modified surface. This relates to dynamical properties of the Geodesic Flow and can be characterized using continued fraction expansions. This project is supported by an ESF Euro+LACoCoD grant.

We establish a method for determining k-rationality in hypersurfaces, extending C. Xu's work. 
Our rationality criterion involves two key factors. First, we represent a hypersurface equation as the sum of powers of polynomials, where the difference (d-l) is minimal. If the surface is equivalent to just a single power of a polynomial (l equals d), it is rational. 
Additionally, our criterion requires checking if the surface can change to a known rational surface over a field extended by a kth root. 
This approach generalizes earlier findings by J. Kollár and J. Fakhruddini specifically for diagonal hypersurfaces.

We examine how a magnetic field affects spin interactions in the material [Cu(pz)$_2$(2-HOpy)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$](PF$_6$)$_2$, which exhibits two types of spin connections. One correlation is two-dimensional and nearly equivalent to another compound, $\alpha$-Cu(pz)$_2$(OH)$_2$. We observe that this similar correlation experiences a spin transition at a moderate magnetic field. However, we find that the transition temperature is significantly lowered when compared to the corresponding long-range order temperature without a field in the related compound. We find that the remaining correlation responds to higher magnetic fields by developing a complex structure. Experimental findings are in line with predictions from numerical simulations of a model that includes both types of interaction.

A comprehensive framework, the $\alpha$MSM model, is explored to resolve multiple issues with the Standard Model, including the strong CP problem, dark matter conundrum, and instability of the electroweak vacuum. In the $\alpha$MSM model, the strong CP problem is resolved by incorporating only $\alpha$-dependent CP-violating terms. It includes four gauge fermions to tackle unitarity concerns at high energies and provide a source of dark matter annihilation. The model also includes right-handed neutrinos to facilitate seesaw mechanism. Calculations show that the see-saw scale in the $\alpha$MSM can be as low as $10^{11}$ GeV. In this scenario, the see-saw scale aligns with the vacuum stability scale where the Higgs self-coupling is rendered stable by gauge fermions. As a result, the see-sax scale in the $\alpha$MSM lies within the range of $10^{11}$ GeV to $10^{12}$ GeV, which is consistent with cosmological constraints on dark matter and neutrino abundances.

Quantic has introduced a novel method for calculating Clifford and T circuit outputs by applying the Haar random circuit hypothesis (HRCH) to a multi-step process. This multi-step procedure involves partitioning the input into segments, quantumly simulating the first segment, choosing a subsequent input segment, and repeating until the final output, where the hypothesis posits that the resulting state approximates a Haar random state. To refine this approach, we analyze the $T$-gate induced structure within Clifford groups via the T-design property. Utilizing this property allows us to enhance the existing classical simulation technique for quantum circuits composed of Clifford and T gates. Specifically, we improve the classical simulation by incorporating the variance reduction based on the $k$-design characteristic, where the $k$-design property's influence on state overlap is understood as an average of inner product powers, and we relate this property to quantum computation by applying Chebyshev's inequality to estimate state overlap. Furthermore, we develop an explicit expression for the ${k}$-design property's influence on state overlap and the $k$-design's influence on state overlap, and the experimental results demonstrate that our simulation method surpasses the existing classical simulation for quantum circuits composed of Clifford and T gates.

A recent study, which is based on the Tsallis holographic dark energy model, seeks to integrate the Tsallis statistical mechanics with the holographic dark energy theory. This model's density parameter is found to align with the holographic dark energy theory at certain limits, and it can also represent different states of dark energy with distinct values of the intermingling constant. Furthermore, this research, which is founded on the assumption that the energy density of dark energy corresponds to the Gibbs free energy, which in turn relates to the Helmholtz free energy with zero entropy, reveals two critical findings. Firstly, the volume of the holographic dark energy model, which is determined through the cosmological infrared cutoff, determines the Tsallis parameter's dependence. Secondly, the parameter is found to be finitely related to the model's constant, and its derived equation, which is in finite agreement with existing data, displays an accelerated expansion of the universe. This research, which is later compared with other holographic dark energy models, indicates that the Tsallis model is in better alignment with observational data.

Our goal is to enhance the detection of binary candidates in the LAMOST time-domain survey by using an automatic algorithm and a comprehensive catalog. The LAMOST time-domain survey produced significant data in 2020, consisting of 13 million exposures and 2 million binary candidates. However, the initial catalog contained far fewer entries due to a limited algorithm. Now, based on the initial work, we have developed a more efficient algorithm to process the survey data and create a more comprehensive catalog containing 1.16 million binary candidates. These candidates are selected based on specific criteria, including the shape of the light curve and a stringent contamination rate. These criteria also allow us to estimate the error for the estimated fraction of binaries. The results indicate a $0.14 \pm 0.02$ error for the binary fraction in the observed magnitude range of $-3 < m < 3$. The new catalog has been uploaded to GitHub.

The randomness provided by a true random number generator (TRNG) is essential for various applications in the Internet of Things (IoT) and 5G/6G wireless networks. Due to a lack of robustness and the limitations of existing TRNGs in terms of high throughput and low energy consumption, a new distributed TRNG (TRNG, referred to as TuRaN) has been conceived. This novel TRNG utilizes the timing differences in wireless channel impulse responses (CIRs) of multiple users to generate truly random data. By employing a novel approach that synchronizes the wireless channel, the randomness of multiple users can be combined effectively. TheRaN, when compared to conventional TRNGs, exhibits a significant advantage in terms of throughput and energy efficiency. TheRaN, in comparison to a traditional TRNG, outperforms in terms of throughput by a margin of 10^6 and surpasses the energy efficiency limit of 10^6 times. TheRaN, crucially, does not demand a lengthy warm-up period, and as a result of the absence of a warm-up time, it can be integrated with a protocol known as OFDMA with a flexible resource allocation method. TheRaN undergoes comprehensive testing of its resilience using the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) statistical tests and circuit-level simulations using a 28nm CMOS design, which confirm the reliability and practicality of the proposed RAN. A novel, scalable electron switch based on oxide materials has been developed, featuring an exceptionally high resistance change (from 10^5 to 10^6 times) and operates on an energy level that is 100 times lower than standard switches. A array of cells containing this switch has been created using a basic 3-layer structure, which enables the storage of a single-electron charge and stable operation at room temperature. The switch's unique properties combined with its minute size make it an ideal candidate for implementing one of the most complex quantum tasks - a controlled-not gate, ultimately paving the way for the creation of large-scale, stable room-temperature quantum computers.

A causal representation is introduced to universal values in scattering amplitudes, 
derived from Feynman integrands and D-algebra techniques. This format clarifies the 
interplay between fundamental building blocks of amplitudes and loop structure, 
enabling the identification of loop characteristics and topological properties 
of causal representations. An efficient method is provided for determining contributions 
associated with specific loop topologies through a new graph theory approach, 
illustrated by computations of the two-loop box and pentagon at Higgs boson 
production and the $g\rightarrow hh$ interaction.

This paper examines the time-evolution Green functions associated with quantum walks on finitely generated groups, specifically focusing on lamplighter groups, and derives properties of these functions, such as continuity, differentiability, and non-analyticity, in terms of spectral measures and spectral functions. The study utilizes continuity and differentability to establish a spectral measure representation formula and an asymptotic Tauberian theorem, respectively. The continuity and differentability properties of Green functions are deduced from their relationship with random walks and walks on a graph, respectively. The continuity and differentability of Green functions for quantum walks are also explored, showing that they share similar properties to random walks and walks on graphs, respectively. The study specifically focuses on the continuity and differentiability of Green functions at stroboscopic times, demonstrating that these functions exhibit the same properties as their classical counterparts, respectively. The study specifically focuses on the lamplighter group but similar results hold for any fixed group, given that the continuity and differentability properties of Green functions are always present at stroboscopic times.

To investigate how star mass impacts quark phase appearance, a study using the HR2 equation of state is conducted with two distinct models of electron to baryon ratio ($y_e$): one where $y_e$ remains constant and another derived from $\beta$-equilibrium principles. Electromagnetic contributions to the equation of state are also accounted for. By simulating hybrid stars using the RM1 macroscopic model, the research reveals that hybrid phases emerge at lower pressures relative to a prior study, resulting in larger core sizes. Analysis shows that fixed $y_e$ leads to larger hybrid cores, whereas general relativistic effects can decrease their size. Furthermore, an increase in dimensionless mass ($M/M_\odot$) is associated with larger core radius. Most notably, electromagnetic influences cause a significant shift in hybrid phase onset, which is crucial for observing the Quark-Hadron Phase Transition through gravitational waves.

We are examining an optomechanical system that involves an $q$-deformed two-level atom, which interacts with an incoming probe field as the driving force, while also experiencing interaction with a cavity field through a mechanism of coherent coupling. The system's behavior is analyzed in terms of a nonlinear susceptibility, which is influenced by tuning parameters of tunneling strength and optomechanical coupling. This interaction gives rise to significant effects, such as quantum interference and self-collapsing of matter waves. As a result, these effects can lead to a shift in the probe field's transmission peak and a modification of its transmission profile.

This research identifies two distinct types of scissors modes in atomic nuclei with different isospin modes of quadrupole shape fluctuations. Nuclei can exhibit modes stronger or weaker than expected based on isomagnetic limit calculations, classified as R-positive and R-negative, respectively. We investigated the transition strengths from ground states to excited states with J pi = 1- symmetry using shell model for even-even nuclei in the sd shell. Our results indicate R-negative states have significantly lower transition strengths and opposite Isgmu ratios compared to R-positive modes. These rarer R-negative modes have been detected in only a few nuclei, such as 54Cr, 54Fe, and 54Co. We incorporated R-negative states into Isgmu strength distributions using a sum rule analysis with an adjusted parameter alpha, demonstrating a notable reduction in the remaining sum rule compared to only R-positive modes.

A metal-to-insulator transition in black phosphorus is driven by dimensional confinement and electronic correlation. Using a theoretical approach, we found that standing waves on the surface of black phosphorus create a charge pattern that causes a charge order and insulating behavior. Our calculations also revealed a parity difference in the charge pattern between the front and back surfaces of the material. Simulations showed that insulating behavior is visible in the charge pattern when the thickness of the black phosphorus is between 2 and 10 nanometers.

Recently, we observed a significant effect stemming from the unique characteristics of distributions with robust, power-law extensions in the context of laser-cooled atomic ensembles. These characteristics arise from the inherent randomness of atomic interactions with light and are particularly pronounced in large groups of atoms. This phenomenon has profound implications for the behavior of small atomic samples, as it indicates a gradual transition from a consistent environment for each atom (in smaller groups) to a environment influenced by random events (in larger groups). This is exemplified by the change in the collective and individual scattering of light, exhibiting not only a standard exponential decrease but also a significant power-law trend in smaller atomic samples. This power-law feature has been experimentally observed and holds significant relevance for the accuracy of optical measurements and quantum-limited optical metrology.

Following a significant decline in cryptocurrency prices during the first half of 2021, our analysis of half a year's transaction data from six popular cryptocurrencies - Bitcoin, Ethereum, Litecoin, Ripple, Bitcoin Cash, and Monero - revealed an intricate trading network. To capture the dynamics of these markets, we applied network theory and measured network complexity using the Edges-Nodes ratio, clustering coefficient, and other metrics. We found that a surge in trading volumes in March led to a notable increase in network complexity and introduced notable market correlations. However, this phenomenon subsided with declining trading volumes in April and May. We also examined the network's topological properties, including the distribution of node degrees and the spatial distribution of high-trading nodes, and discussed our findings in this context.

A combined approach of ab-initio and path-integral simulations is applied to examine the reaction of a proton sulphuric acid with water, both at 0K starting from a specific position and within the context of quantum zero-point motion.  The energy barriers for transferring the acid's proton to the oxygen of a single or double sulphuric acid's proton is found to be significantly higher in the case of the latter.  Taking into account the dynamic effects of the protons, a more comprehensive comparison with classical simulations has been performed.  It turns out that for an isolated proton, dynamic effects are negligible, whereas for two protons, a substantial increase in the dynamic influence has been observed.  Furthermore, an energetic analysis has shown that a substantial contribution to the proton's transfer is attributed to the blue-shifted vibrations of specific bonds within sulphuric acid, which have been found to be heavily impacted by zero-point energy.

Consider a set of group equivariant non-expansive operators between two complete bounded metric spaces with actions from the same group. The operator spatiality question asks whether this collection of operators can be represented as a compact subset of a product metric space, allowing for an isometric representation of its equivariant operator norm. It has been proven that such a set of operators can be isometrically represented in a compact space, provided the group is either finite or acts on a compact space as part of a joint equivariant factorization through atomic algebras. The proof utilizes Tilman Skrahina's method to establish joint equivariant factorization. Notably, this result enables the characterization of all finite groups that permit non-trivial group equivariant factorizations of the torus, as well as present a general factorization framework for certain non-expansive maps between compact spaces.
