When calculating entropy for an unknown distribution, using only sample data without a closed-form expression, a new approach is taken. This method, rooted in the Bayesian framework, employs entropy as the objective function to optimize the distribution parameters using observed samples. It draws on the generalized entropy formula for generalized logistic distributions and the information entropy of a generalized normal distribution. To maintain accuracy, the variational approach is used to approximate the required integrals. This method's effectiveness is evaluated through numerical experiments, which demonstrate its performance in entropy estimation by comparing it with other estimation techniques and alternative definitions of entropy.

Modeling meso-scale dynamics in semiconductor manufacturing systems requires a first-principles approach based on Borel measures and their flow equations. This approach enables a first-step analysis of the state and fluxes in these systems through rigorous mathematical methods. By applying the Liouville theorem for measures, we develop a theoretical framework that accommodates complete and partial information about the system's behavior. This framework enables the continuous-time, probabilistic description of evolving states and fluxes. Furthermore, we introduce a fundamental theorem that connects a system's past to its present and introduce basic assumptions characteristic of semiconductor manufacturing systems.

Malicious software poses a major threat to resources-constrained devices, such as the Internet of Things. New threats emerge regularly, making it challenging to develop a universal classification method, especially on devices with limited capabilities. In response, we designed a resource-efficient rule-based system, called NBcoded, to encode Naive Bayes models as customizable rules in any programming language, enabling deployment on resource-constrained devices. By streamlining the encoding process, NBcoded allows for easier model maintenance and efficient rule-based classification, as evidenced by our comparison with rule-based systems using rule extraction and soft learning.

For metabelian groups, a stricter upper limit on their growth rate has been set to 1.16. This rate can go as high as approximately 1.28 for those that are infinitely presented or contain infinite cyclic subgroups. Conversely, when a metabelian group meets specific criteria, its growth rate is capped at around 1.39. On the other hand, when a metabelian group follows a different set of conditions - being finitely presented and torsion-free - its growth rate is maximum at around 1.16. This rate can vary and reach as high as 1.28 in this scenario.

A new tracking method is proposed to differentiate biological entities from
non-biological objects based on their movement characteristics in time and space.
An automatic approach is developed to identify and remove non-biological entities
from images in a binary sequence. This method is applied to a set of test images
to confirm its correctness and efficiency. Furthermore, a model is formulated to
predict the movement of biological entities from one frame to the next. This model
incorporates a parameter to represent the variability in movement and is fit to
observe the entity's movement over multiple frames. Results from model modeling
of several biological entities from multiple families are presented.

A novel hybrid method is developed to tackle the complex issue of partitioning large networks, with significant applications in analyzing the stability and resilience of power grids. We tackle the NP-hard problem of minimizing cut edges within an irreducible framework. Our hybrid approach is adapted from the classical greedy strategy, but instead of selecting the optimal option at each step, it incorporates a probabilistic hybrid sub-routine to revert partition elements. We demonstrate through tests on various power systems that the hybrid strategy outperforms both the conventional greedy method and a well-known stochastic approximation technique known as simulated annealing in both computational efficiency and solution quality. Moreover, this method is efficient enough for real-time analysis of extremely large networks, thanks to its hybrid components, which can be executed on hybrid quantum computers as well as high-performance classical computers, and notably do not necessitate the use of quantum entanglement.

In this physics-based computational project, participants create a model that
simulates objects in motion while incorporating the Gaze API to track a user's
dynamics and stream data to the system. To improve the model's real-world
accuracy, participants also develop a system that simulates measurement noise
both from the Gaze API and from the drag force exerted by unsteady fluids.
Aimingly, this project guides students through the process of learning to fall
objects via a structured, step-by-step approach consisting of four distinct
modeling stages. Moreover, this project introduces a unique perspective on
computer vision-based physics instruction, emphasizing the integration of
measuring noise from computers and real environments to teach students how to
extract valid results from unreliable data.

To address the $750$ GeV anomaly, we explore a scenario within the Minimal Noncommutative Supersymmetry model. In the context of the noncommutative parameter $\theta_{\mu\nu}$, we find that the required mass for the hypothetical particle is around $100$ GeV to $3$ TeV. This particular model is characterized by the absence of $125$ GeV Higgs and a positive noncommutative parameter. With the noncommutative parameter $0.3-1.5$ TeV$^{-1}$, we satisfy the constraints imposed by the LHC, while the production of the hypothetical particle is primarily driven by the non-SUSY component. This solution appears to be consistent with the requirements set by the model.

A new, highly efficient single-photon source is presented, utilizing a nano-antenna design to interface a semiconductor quantum dot with a low-index tapered waveguide section. This source operates at an optimal wavelength of 1550 nm with a corresponding far-field extraction efficiency of 0.70000006, achieved without relying on a high-index component. It has been determined that a 0.60 micrometer long taper is required to reach this optimum. This nano-antenna based single-photon source can be effectively integrated with various technologies, including fiber, edge-coupling waveguides and split-pair waveguides for further processing. Additionally, it enables a quantum dot design that eliminates the need for a 30 nm broad active region. A brief comparison of the proposed nano-antenna based source and a photonic crystal based single-photon source is also included in the analysis.

This study explores the damping of longitudinal sound waves in a "soft potential" system, where a part of the potentials are weak or non-existent. The results show that, according to the standard "soft potential" theory, sound wave damping at low frequencies and higher temperatures follows a $T^{1/2}$ pattern, whereas at very low frequencies it follows a $q^{2}T^{1/2}$ pattern. However, we find that applying the $BQ$ approximation leads to $T^{3/2}$ and $q^{2}T^{3/2}$ patterns, respectively, even when most potentials are weak or non-existent. The $BQ$ approximation appears to be in place due to $1/q$ fluctuations in density, which is in turn caused by "hard" potentials being transferred to $1/q$ modes via "soft" potentials.

The accuracy of predictions made at particle colliders is crucial for assessing the capabilities of the Standard Model and detecting new physics. Enhancing this accuracy necessitates improved knowledge of parton distribution functions (PDFs), which can be obtained through various approaches. In this paper, we develop a novel method to numerically evaluate the impact of large logarithms on PDF evolution by employing a numerical solution to the DGLAP equations. This approach allows us to analyze the DGLAP evolution of PDFs for specific partons and scale ranges with greater efficiency. Furthermore, our method enables a more versatile and precise determination of scale-dependent PDFs by starting from an input scale to another desired scale. To demonstrate its effectiveness, our method is applied to PDFs derived from perturbative QCD and LHAPDF6-based sets using a NLO DGLAP evolution.

We've developed a theoretical framework to examine how waves that exist within a confined space interact with a discontinuous medium. These interactions give rise to specialized channels that control transmission, which in turn affect the overall transmission transmission matrix and the efficiency of transmitting various states of polarization. These channel characteristics correspond to specific patterns of wave propagation, which also influence the outcomes of related processes like adding and filtering various states. Under particular conditions, all channels become active, enabling the efficient transmission of any given state and facilitating efficient storage as a result. We've demonstrated these concepts through experiments involving the transmission of various patterns of light and have additionally explored how these patterns relate to processes like adding and error reduction.

A bar is thought to exist near the center of our galaxy, but its bar pattern speed is not well understood due to conflicting models and simulations. To resolve this ambiguity, scientists analyzed a region within our galaxy, comparing the effect of bar gravity to that of stellar collisions, against a backdrop of other potential influences. To do this, researchers used data collected by the Gaia telescope, specifically the motion of stars within the galactic center, bar, and a region away from these areas to eliminate the impact of stellar collisions. To validate their findings, bar-free and bar-containing galaxy simulations were created to test the accuracy of their telescopic analysis. The results indicate that bar collisions have a measurable impact on the motion of stars within the galactic center, as illustrated by their action-angle diagrams. Based on these results, the bar pattern speed of our galaxy is estimated to be approximately 39 ± 3 km/s/kpc, moving 6° faster than the solar orbit in a clockwise direction. This discovery provides a precise way to measure the bar pattern speed of our galaxy, as well as that of other galaxies with sufficient data.

Multi-objective optimization and multimodal optimization are similar yet distinct optimization techniques, with a key difference being that multi-objective optimization seeks to preserve a range of non-dominated solutions that excel at being comparable, whereas multimodal optimization seeks to maintain a range of solutions that excel individually. It's surprising to note, however, that many algorithms designed for multimodal optimization are also effective in solving complex multimodal optimization problems, despite the goal differences. This study builds on that discovery by exploring how methods for multimodal optimization can be applied to tackle multimodal optimization problems, which are often encountered in real-world scenarios where various modalities need to be optimized simultaneously. The research evaluates the performance of different multimodal optimization algorithms compared to methods for multi-objective optimization when it comes to handling multimodal problems with several objectives. The criteria for evaluation include final solution fitness quality and diversity, as well as the rate of convergence. The analysis reveals that algorithms originally designed for multimodal optimization generally outperform those for multi-objective optimization in achieving better fit quality and diversity of solutions, as well as converging faster to a set of optimal solutions characterized by a Pareto front.

We investigate the computational aspects of identifying stable matches in a many-to-one matching market where multiple agents can be paired with a principal, and valuations are either tied to utilitarian or priority-based criteria. Initially, we address the general scenario by proving that stably matching agents and priorities is an NP-complete problem, while utilitarian-related stable matches can be found in linear time. We then shift focus to specific situations and identify key differences in complexity. This includes an exponential-time algorithm for the general case and linear-time solutions for priority-related matches. We also delve into the binary valuation scenario, revealing that stable matches can be determined in polynomial time, while finding those that maximize total utility is an NP-complete problem. Ultimately, we make an crucial discovery that related welfare maximization problems are an extension of stable welfare maximization and can be solved in O(n3) time using a reduction to the maximum weight perfect matching problem.

In a system under strain, valley Hall transport is influenced by a gradient that deviates from uniformity. To address this issue, a key characteristic of nonuniform strain is the presence of quasi-localized mobile carriers. Carrier interactions are particularly significant in two-dimensional materials, where the long-range Coulomb interaction plays a crucial role, leading to the formation of correlated states. To explore the impact of interactions on valley Hall transport, we have developed models that incorporate interactions in systems under nonuniform strain. Our results indicate that strong long-range Coulomb interaction in two-dimensional materials may cause a comparable effect to strain gradient coupling.

We extend the concept of stabilizers for symmetries of metric spaces to introduce the notions of stabilizer clouds and their centers. A group of isometries forms a cloud with a nontrivial stabilizer only if it encompasses a center. We examine the relationships between these concepts and the previous idea of fixed point sets for group actions. We also analyze and contrast point stabilizers and central stabilizers for subsets of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish a key theorem: a cloud with a nontrivial stabilizer has a center if and only if its elements are all equidistant from it. This fundamental result provides a solid foundation for exploring the theory of stabilizer clouds and identifying the challenges and strategies to address it.

A dual circularly polarized patch antenna with an integrated defected ground structure is designed to operate within a 4.025-4.2 GHz C band frequency range.  To achieve broad bandwidth, three transmission resonances are facilitated by a single patch with an integrated defected ground structure and three additional antennas positioned at specific points.  This design results in a low voltage standing wave ratio and efficient radiation, with an axial ratio of less than 2 dB, a gain between 2.3 and 2.8 dBi, and a flexible half power beamwidth between 50 and 70 degrees.  Due to its compact and dual circularly polarized characteristics with broad bandwidth, this antenna is suitable for various applications including super-regenerative receivers and distributed phase array antennas.

Reinforcement learning has been successfully adapted to solve complex quantum error correction decoding problems that cannot be resolved analytically. We employ a specific type of recurrent neural network called the quantum error detecting long short-term memory to develop an optimal decoding strategy for the minimum-weight perfect matching method applied to the surface code. This approach effectively addresses situations involving multiple simultaneous errors and a non-zero error threshold. We demonstrate that our model learns efficiently through a simplified probabilistic model of noise learning and validates its performance on a variational quantum simulator with real, experimentally observed data.

Hadrons from Au+Au collisions at 3 GeV were examined using the FAIRLab's data. 
  The study focused on how yield changes with the momentum fraction carried by the quark, 
  which was discovered to have a declining trend as the fraction decreases. 
  The analysis also looked at how particle yields in collisions were affected by the size of the system, 
 with Au+Au collisions exhibiting a higher suppression than in smaller collisions. 
This pattern aligns with theoretical models and suggests how different types of collisions influence particle production.

In the digital-analog quantum computing method, a type of Hamiltonian is given the control it needs by applying a similar circuit design that matches the underlying physics of the simulated system. By utilizing this design, which can be implemented uniformly across an quantum computer, it enables the efficient simulation of complex time-evolution processes. This technique is illustrated by simulating the Fermi-Hubbard model, where a specific Hamiltonian evolution is replicated through a sequence of pulses that mirror the digital simulation. Following this process, measurements are conducted to observe various observable properties. By combining experimental results with initial conditions, it is possible to recover key information such as correlation functions. These experiments were conducted on a quantum annealer from a company called DWAVE, which was set up for universal quantum computing in this instance. Despite being an analog device intended for optimization problems, it was successfully employed to evolve the quantum state and was able to accurately reproduce the numerical predictions for correlation functions within the Fermi-Hubbard model.

A novel algorithm called Bonsai facilitates the creation of adaptive feature
representations to enhance a pre-trained model's performance on a given task, 
by developing an intricate structure of feature transformations organized in a tree-like manner.
These distinct nodes specialize in specific aspects relevant to a given task and are 
constructed using unsupervised techniques like k-means clustering to automatically discover features without the need for labeled data.
A pivotal aspect of the algorithm lies in its capability to assign a distinct purpose to each node, thereby producing features uniquely suited to various tasks.
Evaluations on multiple datasets have demonstrated that Bonsai not only rivals state-of-the-art methods employed in vision and language applications but also effectively utilizes unlseen data to adapt feature representations.

A MWAGA-based model, which is grounded in the RT equation and incorporates two-dimensional detection, offers a flexible approach to enhancing our ability to distinguish and locate objects within complex and light-scattering environments. By applying a mutation-assisted genetic algorithm, our method effectively addresses challenges associated with object lightness and spatial positioning. The proposed algorithm is optimized through weighted mutation, which accelerates its convergence and improves its efficiency. Simulation outcomes demonstrate that the MWAGA-assisted model excels in identifying numerous targets simultaneously, outperforming the conventional radiative transfer model. Furthermore, we show that the MWAGA-assisted model is able to accurately resolve multiple objects even when they are below the diffraction limit and intertwined.

The size of testing samples significantly impacts the accuracy of value function estimates, yet this issue is not a primary concern in the literature, where samples are often assumed to be infinite. This paper investigates the problem using cross-validation, developing efficient function estimators that minimize the number of testing samples required while maintaining low estimation error. Our approach enables a new class of algorithms to achieve the same performance as existing ones but with fewer testing samples, a characteristic crucial for offline policy learning and reinforcement learning with function approximation. Notably, we demonstrate theoretically and experimentally that our methods outperform competitors, especially as testing samples increase.

A simulation study is conducted to examine the performance of new monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors. These sensors feature a thick high-resistivity silicon bulk and a very thin collection layer. By analyzing the charge collection efficiency of these sensors as a function of their operation voltage, we determine the charge collection properties. Our findings indicate that the charge collection within the thin collection layer is highly efficient. Also, the charge collection from the thick high-resistivity bulk can be tuned by adjusting the operation voltage. Moreover, a higher proportion of the total charge is collected from the thick bulk as the sensor becomes thinner. This research has significantly advanced our comprehension of monolithic small collection-electrode CMOS sensors and facilitated the evaluation of their signal-to-noise performance relative to other detector types.

A novel technique called speckle tracking and subtraction has been proposed as a method for discovering exoplanets using ground-based imaging systems. We have developed a new algorithm to enhance this technique's performance in varying atmospheric conditions by following the evolution of speckle patterns over a short period and removing the corresponding speckle signal associated with the planet's signal. The planet's detached speckle pattern mimics the parent star's and can be produced through speckle evolution by pairing it with a speckle image representing the exoplanet. Speckle subtraction's ability to subtract the parent star's speckle pattern at a high level of accuracy while maintaining sensitivity to the exoplanet's speckle pattern makes it a suitable method for discovering exoplanets with various orbital inclinations. We have applied this technique to synthetic data from a hypothetical HabEx telescope and discovered that it surpasses other commonly used exoplanet detection methods in terms of sensitivity and discovery potential.

This paper presents a novel model that accommodates both positive and negative yield curves with smooth characteristics. Our model is a -term Ho-Lee duration model, but with a modified drift that is proportional to a nondecreasing function of the nondegenerate Cauchy distribution. This drift modification is made in discrete steps for each matURITY from 1 month to N months. The drift's step size is ensured to be non-negative, thereby preventing negative Cauchy distribution values, and as a result, our model avoids negative interest rates. By design, the model is robust against data anomalies, and the statistical properties of our model are also analyzed in a closed form.

Although the DUNE detector is primarily optimized for nucleon form factor measurements, its setup can also effectively detect sterile neutrinos, particularly in the mass range of 0.5 to 2 GeV. With a anticipated 1000 kb data collection over 10 years, DUNE's near detector is expected to be able to identify at least one sterile neutrino event with a 95% confidence level, assuming a specific benchmark model. However, despite this setup's sensitivity to sterile neutrinos, the primary goal of studying nucleon form factors may be compromised by background events. As a result, researchers may need to lower their sensitivity threshold in form factor searches in order to achieve the desired sensitivity for sterile neutrino detection.

We suggest novel, straightforward cluster-robust estimators for equating two items with respect to their difficulty levels, taking into consideration uncertainty in both difficulty parameters. To develop these estimators, we apply a reweighted likelihood approach that addresses over-dispersion through a random effects model, similar to methods used in robust statistics. Our estimators enjoy asymptotic normality and efficiency in large sample scenarios, and in simulations, perform well even in small samples and when assumptions are violated, outperforming existing cluster-robust estimators and maximum likelihood estimators. Our estimators have been successfully tested using real data from a large-scale exam, demonstrating good performance in various scenarios. The full report, including both numerical and analytical findings, is available online.

High fidelity CFD models that account for finite particle stresses and drag forces are crucial in studying particle-laden flows. However, their complex nonlinear interactions require small time steps and significant computational resources. To overcome these limitations, a novel multiple-time-step integration approach is developed, which utilizes a three-time-step method on a finest grid and a force matching scheme to synchronize the largest and smallest time steps. This scheme is applied in both a Lagrangian and a tree-based variant, which optimizes multi-time-steps for a given particle cluster. By comparing it to a traditional method, the scheme demonstrates up to 3.5 times speedup in computational efficiency and retains high levels of accuracy.

In process-dependent scenarios like black hole evaporation and cosmological expansion, defining the number of particles becomes challenging, particularly given that a particle's wave function needs to be localized to the horizon area to be counted, which is impractical for macroscopic black holes or the universe. In this study, we introduce a novel, self-consistent approach to particle number definition, incorporating an internal clock that naturally localizes the particle's wave function, eliminating reliance on the universe or horizon size. We then develop a quantum tunneling formula for calculating the emitted particle number, valid for any process, and apply it to model the Hawking radiation of both slow and fast evaporating black holes, yielding results consistent with traditional formulas while also deeming the counting of particles in such situations meaningless. Furthermore, we apply our approach to cosmological expansion, yielding a formula for particle number definition in this context as well.

Our study of nuclear broadening in high-energy collisions uses the T-RQCD model, which treats the color field between a quark and a gluon as a rotating string, modelled with the model parameter $r_0$. We have modelled this model with $r_0$ fixed at $1$ fm and modelled it as a string with an end-to-end fixed value of $1$ fm. We have modelled two different models for the dipole cross section, one from IP-GloSMC and Model 2 from BDMPSZ, modelled the nuclear broadening of jets in high-energy collisions. The results show that the predictions of nuclear broadening are highly sensitive to the dipole cross section model used, which suggests that the predictions of nuclear broadening should be more precise. The predictions of nuclear broadening should be more precise, as the predictions of nuclear broadening are more precise than the predictions of nuclear broadening.

We primarily demonstrate that there are infinitely many cases where the equation $a^3+b^3=7^b\cdot 7^n$ has positive integer solutions for a, b, and n. This finding leads to the largest verified value of n=19 for the conjecture $7^n<a^3+b^3<7^{n+1}$. To make sense of the proof, we use the natural parameterization of the cubic curve $x^3+y^3=7z^3$. In addition, we use three sequences of positive integers, derived using three specific values of n, to find suitable a and b values for the equation.

The presence of air that has been entrained within a liquid jet that forms in a channel significantly influences its behavior. Although prior studies have emphasized the consequences of this phenomenon on the liquid's dynamics, their entrainment of air at the channel出口remains underexplored. To investigate the interaction between the liquid and air phases at the出口, an experimental setup utilizing a liquid jet that forms in a micro-channel and breaks into droplets at the出口was developed. By employing various micro-scales channels with different aspect ratios and a fast imaging system, the dynamics of air that has been entrained within the liquid jet and its effect on droplet formation have been analyzed. The results indicate that the air that has been entrained within the liquid jet contributes to destabilization and delays droplet formation, while the air's airiness within the liquid increases due to phase separation that occurs after the jet's initial instabilities. By adjusting the airiness of air within the liquid at different locations along the channel, the coefficient of coexistence of air and water within the liquid has been found to approach the theoretical limit of nearly 1.

A growing number of applications are now utilizing non-volatile memory, leading to a significant challenge in ensuring data consistency in the event of power failures. Current approaches to address this issue involve algorithm-based knowledge, which is critical for applications to update their data structures safely. Although this approach has been successful for a long time with volatile memory, its performance significantly declines when combined with non-volatile memory due to increased reliance on less efficient hardware abstractions. Surprisingly, most computer architecture research has overlooked the impact of software techniques on system performance. In this study, we examine the interaction between software abstractions and hardware features related to durable storage. For this purpose, we have developed a framework that enables the systematic evaluation of various techniques. Using this framework, we have analyzed three key aspects: (1) the effect of hardware support on software design choices; (2) the impact of software techniques on system performance; and (3) the optimization of these techniques. Our findings indicate that the interaction between algorithm-based knowledge and hardware techniques can result in a performance improvement of up to 2.6x, effectively addressing the initial concern about using non-volatile memory.

Networks of documents can be structured into topics, which can be either flat or hierarchical in nature. Traditional techniques such as topic modeling are often too reliant on data and sensitive to it, while assuming no hierarchical structure exists in the data. To address these issues, we introduce the Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), a new method for modeling hierarchical structures in networks of topics. This model is capable of identifying topics without prior model selection or knowledge of the data, which is especially beneficial in analyzing large networks of spam documents. Experimental results on two datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of HDTM in comparison to other methods.

An in-depth analysis of three-body encounters in the solar galactic disk has been conducted through extensive direct integration of 1000000 three-body systems, complemented by a comparison with the major-axis approximation and the Mikkola and Kuchner (2000) formulae to understand their statistical properties.

Investigating the radial distribution of encounters, we discovered that the Mikkola and Kuchner (2000) predictions align well with our simulation results, particularly for short-range interactions. However, our data suggest a higher frequency of escape events for short-range encounters than initially predicted.

While the Mikkola and Kuchner (2000) formulae accurately represent the overall distribution of radial distribution of encounters and their derivatives, the Mikkola and Kuchner (2000) predictions based on the second and third derivatives of the radial distribution appear to overestimate the number of non-escape encounters in certain scenarios.

Our study recommends that the Mikkola and Kuchner (2000) predictions based on radial distribution, its first derivative, and its second derivative be utilized for modeling three-body systems, particularly for long-range interactions.

A study of quarkonium suppression, particularly focusing on $\psi$(2S) and J/$\psi$ mesons, is conducted using high-transverse momentum data from p+Pb and pp collisions at the LHC. The ratio of $\psi$(2S) to J/$\psi$ yield in high-energy p+Pb collisions to that from pp collisions at the same energy is examined across various transitive momentum ranges and at 0-10% and 30-40% most central nucleon-nucleon collisions. Additionally, this ratio is analyzed as a function of rapidity. Findings indicate that the relative suppression of $\psi$(2S) to J/$\psi$ is consistent with that of J/$\psi$ within the measured transitive momentum range and shows no rapidity dependence.

We establish that in a continuous logic framework, equivalence relations can be represented as sets of complete metric spaces with the property of being closed under the Tarski-Vazirani embedding technique. We also prove the existence of a uniform method for the construction of these relations, which we find to be of considerable utility in logical reasoning and set theory. The implications of this finding are extensive, one example being that there are infinite sequences of equivalence relations of high complexity that do not have a uniform construction. We also derive logical consequences from this phenomenon, which demonstrate the limitations of these relations within the context of the Borel and analytic sets in descriptive logic.

One effective approach to managing changes in a software system involves utilizing model-based techniques, which enable both graphical and formal representation of system models. However, as multiple stakeholders contribute to a project, the risk of significant model divergences arises, necessitating effective strategies for handling such divergences. This paper presents a new technique that leverages singular value decomposition to detect and control model changes within a software system. The proposed approach is enhanced with a technique that assigns weights to individual model elements, allowing for fine-tuned management of changes. Building on this, we have developed a method for projecting diverse model versions into a unified, weighted average version, which preserves the weight information and permits natural navigation between various project versions through a series of weighted model states. Empirical evaluation using multiple real-world software versions has demonstrated the efficacy and potential of this approach.

For time-series forecasting, recurrent neural networks and similar deep sequential models are commonly used. However, these models often struggle with long data sequences due to excessively long dependencies in their recurrent connections. Utilizing attention mechanisms in such models helps mitigate these issues, though they can be computationally intensive when applied to extended sequences. In order to enhance performance, efficient attention schemes are required. In this study, we investigate various attention structures used in attention-based sequential models, in order to improve their efficiency. By analyzing existing methods, we demonstrate how attention models can be simplified without significant performance loss, based on the characteristics of time-series data. As a result, we propose an attention module that utilizes a regression-based approach to pinpoint key temporal regions within the input sequence. This novel module exhibits superior efficiency compared to standard attention mechanisms while maintaining similar forecasting accuracy.

We've obtained the earliest wide-field X-ray maps of Cassiopeia A at a polarisation limit of 10 percent, corresponding to our most sensitive observations to date. The emission at 7.2 keV shows a high degree of polarisation, ranging from 30 to 80 percent, and exhibits patterns that align with a filamentary structure. Our findings suggest a connection between the K-alpha line and the magnetic field. Moreover, the overall polarisation pattern of maps with low contaminants matches a 45-degree angle, aligning with previous radio observations. However, areas with high polarisation show a 135-degree angle, associated with regions with synchrotron and thermal components. These pictures with polarisation provide a deeper insight into the synchrotron and thermal mixing, as well as the local magnetic field, and may help to distinguish areas with a strong the strong magnetic field from areas with a weak the magnetic field.

Distinct subset sum requirements for a subset collection of size at most $n/q$ of $n$ integers are examined through the lens of the knapsack problem. A new lower bound of $n/64$ is established for these requirements, a significant improvement over the previously known $n/3$ threshold. Consequently, there exist specific constructions of subsets that satisfy a distinct subset sum quotient of approximately $n/128$ when considering subsets up to size $n/64$ of $n$ integers, a notable increase from the longstanding $n/3$ record.

The phase transition from deconfinement in quark stars is examined, and its influence on the stars' properties is highlighted through the implementation of deconfinement phase transitions in the star cores is shown to significantly affect the stars' characteristics, much like a phase transition in ordinary matter alters its state. Moreover, a sudden deconfinement transition, resulting in a discontinuous change in quark chemical potential at the transition point, may lead to a "mismatch" between the inner core and the outer layers of the star, potentially resulting in instabilities and eventual division of the star into two halves.

We investigate the Fock state structure of the compact quantum field in one-dimensional spin systems with ferromagnetic interactions. These systems serve as a generalization of the widely used NISQ algorithm for preparing the compass state. Our analysis reveals that the variance of the number of particles in a given mode increases with system damping $\gamma$. This property makes the compact quantum field an optimal probe. Leveraging this, we develop a novel approach for estimating the damping parameter with high precision. Our findings indicate that variance-stabilized probes outperform their Fock state counterparts in certain regimes of the damping parameter. We also discuss the practical aspects of implementing our damping estimator by measuring the number variance.

A recent experiment has captured a liquid jet forming from a drop oscillating in a pool of the same liquid using high-speed imaging in an air-based environment. High-speed images have been used to develop a geometric model for the drop's deformation and jet formation. This model has been validated against the experimental data and used to distinguish between different geometries of the drop and its jets. The study reveals that the dynamics of a liquid jet depend on its specific geometry and provides the first classification of liquid jets, along with a theoretical explanation of how they become unstable and break apart into droplets.

Researchers observed in 2009 that certain types of bacteriophages exhibit movement on the surfaces of bacteria. This phenomenon is similar to a viral metabolism, in which the viral rolling on the host surface serves a functional purpose, rather than the virus undergoing any metabolic changes. New computational models have revealed the key factors enabling this viral movement. By applying basic biomechanical principles, we found that these phages move by flexing their bodies, which is similar to the motion of a rolling ball. This finding may provide insight into the evolution of viral genetics, helping viruses navigate across bacterial surfaces.

An extensive study of galaxy warps in nearby, non-interacting galaxies has been conducted using data from the MANGA survey. We analyzed a sample of 1,021 S-type and U-type warped galaxies with high-quality data. It was found that S-type warped galaxies experience greater environmental influence than U-type warped galaxies, particularly in regions with tidal forces above 0.0015, likely due to the influence of a single or double galaxy interaction. It is also possible that galaxies with significant warp amplitudes are more susceptible to this environmental effect. Although most galaxy warps are found in the outer regions of disks, it was found that deeply warped galaxies extend to larger radii with a radius limit of approximately 0.7 for S-type and 0.8 for U-type galaxies. We found no evidence that galaxy warps are more prevalent in certain galaxy types or orientations. However, it was discovered that galaxies in certain environments are more likely to exhibit significant warp amplitudes. Galaxies in regions with high tidal forces above 0.0035 are more likely to exhibit a 20% warp amplitude, while galaxies in regions with a density of 100 sq. arcmin are more likely to exhibit a 20% warp amplitude for U-type galaxies. We have found a form of bounded harmonic function on a $k$-dimensional key component of a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton with $L^2p$-finite harmonic functions, where the growth of the function is constrained. This discovery has lead to the conclusion that there are no finite $p$-dimensional $L^p$-finite harmonic functions for $p\in (1,\infty)$. No such restriction exists for functions with $p\geq\infty$. Our work also provides an example of a 3-dimensional key component for an $O(l^2p)$-growth $L^p$-finite harmonic function, where $p\in (2,\infty)$.

Doping is a widely used technique to study and manipulate the electronic, magnetic, and superconducting properties of materials. In the study of time-reversal breaking Chern superconductors, it was found that doping can affect the phase symmetry, leading to unexpected results. By employing a mean-field theory, researchers investigated the effects of hole and electron doping on two compounds, KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$, discovering that electron doping can break time-reversal symmetry while hole doping can restore it. Moreover, it was found that hole doping of KRbB_i_4 and electron doping of RbCsBi$_{4}$ both result in s-wave superconductivity. This phenomenon can be attributed to the distinct band structures of these materials near the Fermi level. By comparing with experimental results, it was deduced that time-reversal breaking Chern superconductivity may exist in KRbBi$_{4}$ and RbCsBi$_{4}$.

We investigate the characteristics of nonadiabatic Born effective charge in clean insulators, finite-size conductors, and disordered systems of various dimensions using ab initio simulations and quantum mechanical theories. Our results show that nonadiabatic Born effective charges in clean insulators converge to a finite value as wave vector grid spacing decreases, whereas those in clean finite-size conductors approach zero as the Bloch wave vector grid spacing diminishes. Conversely, nonadiabatic Born effective charges in disordered systems depend on the supercell size and exhibit anomalous behavior due to the absence of momentum conservation. These findings emphasize that nonadiabatic Born effective charge measurements should consider system-specific limitations and demonstrate that valence-band electrons can contribute significantly to this charge even in metals.

The fluctuating hydrodynamics (FH) model's effectiveness in HPC simulations is limited by a deterministic version of the Navier-Stokes equation used in the sub-kernel, which doesn't account for thermodynamic noise effects on turbulence dissipation. We examined three novel dichotomous Navier-Stokes operators that incorporate noise influences on turbulence dissipation and developed three corresponding kernels for FH models. These were tested using FH simulations of turbulent channel flow at a moderate Reynolds number. One of the kernels we evaluated performed well for all Reynolds numbers. The best-perming kernel we discovered achieved up to a 2.5 times speedup over a reference kernel with an equivalent level of accuracy.

When magnetoelectric coupling occurs between a magnetic monopole and a ferromagnet, the Witten effect arises, resulting in the monopole acquiring an effective electric charge that is proportional to the ferromagnet's magnetization. In our macroscopic approach, the magnetic monopole is substituted with a Dirac string, which when interacting with the ferromagnet produces an additional long-range dipolar interaction, characterized by a $1/r^2$ decay, that the point monopole would otherwise lack. Furthermore, we observe that this effect is not isolated to magnetic monopoles but also emerges when an electric charge or a superconducting fluxon interacts with a source of topological magnetic field, such as a $g$-tensor impurity or a topological theta-term insulator, which generates an effective magnetic monopole density. Consequently, these interactions result in the system acquiring a effective dipolar interaction with the same properties as the electric charge and effective magnetic monopole, which is characterized by a magnetic dipole that is proportional to the electric dipole through the effective magnetic monopole density, exhibiting an effective electric charge with a proportionality to the ferromagnet's magnetization, which is analogous to Witten effect itself.

The concept of delayed nonlinearity has been explored in a variety of settings, primarily through models with space. In this paper, a different approach has been taken by considering time-based delays and demonstrating that an increased rate of delayed nonlinearity leads to higher diffusion. As a result, the effective dimensionality of the system decreases to a manageable level, allowing for an approximation of the delay-differential equation as an ordinary differential equation with time-correlated coefficients. The validity of this method has been verified using an example delay-diffusion equation, where a matched rate of effective diffusion was identified. The methodology presented can be applied to other systems with delayed nonlinearity and likely improves convergence in numerical solutions for these models.

This paper employs a higher-order probabilistic lambda calculus as a case study to
investigate the relationships between denotational and operational semantics. We
define both a denotational and an operational framework within a lambda term
denotational structure. Within this framework, we identify instances where the two
approaches to modeling programs diverge in their interpretations of certain terms. 
Moreover, we outline the specific conditions under which the denotational and
operational models will be considered equivalent. We then establish a
completeness property by showing that any term leading to denotational model
discrepancies can be detected through standard terms testing procedures. To aid
this analysis, we also develop an interactive tool that facilitates the
examination of lambda calculus terms within both denotational and operational models.

Industrial designers play a crucial role in creating innovative products by balancing functional, technical, and aesthetic considerations. However, due to time constraints and the iterative nature of the design process, valuable design alternatives can be easily overlooked. Computational design mining techniques have emerged as a means to analyze existing designs and provide insight into more effective design choices. While current techniques show promise in improving design decisions within a specific project, their applicability beyond that context remains limited. To overcome this limitation, this study introduces a novel approach that leverages concept-driven semantic representations and similarity-based metrics in design mining. By incorporating this method into a case-study of a real-world design project, the paper demonstrates its effectiveness in ensuring concept-level stability and enabling meaningful cross-project design analysis. Additionally, the research highlights how this framework enables discovery of hidden design knowledge that transcends individual companies and domains, thereby proving its generalizability and universal applicability.

A novel, two-component model unifies the concept of negative pressure dark vacuum energy and the holographic dark energy's future de Sitter horizon with an intrinsic positive pressure energy density. The work, based on the assumption that the dark vacuum energy's density remains constant, shows that only a specific state of the model is capable of meeting the standard for cosmic flatness, which in turn necessitates a particular future holographic dark energy density characterized by a future de Sitter horizon. This leads to a more cohesive and physically plausible model, in contrast to the, at times, counterintuitive behavior of the, solely as a single component, future holographic dark energy models. By introducing an arbitrary constant for the state of the model, we are able to determine its expected and observable properties, which currently appear to be in line with current measurements. However, it is important to note that, due to the limited accuracy of the available data, the dark vacuum energy's constant state is not yet definitively confirmed, and a more detailed study is required to fully understand the model's potential and address any remaining issues.

This paper introduces a innovative optimization technique that integrates a differentiability identifier into existing black-box solvers, enabling automatic detection of function differentiability within a optimization context. By harnessing automatic differentiation and a local approximation of differentiable segments, the proposed method IDMan can accelerate convergence when encountering differentiable regions and continue using a given solver during non-differentiable portions of a function. An algorithm is formulated to systematically identify and adapt to these segments, with support for a wide variety of existing optimization algorithms. Thorough testing demonstrates the potential of IDMan to facilitate differentiability-manifold convergence and the seamless integration of automatic differentiation.

We investigate higher levels of 1-absorbing prime ideals, focusing on their connections to annihilator-primality and 2-absorblity, as well as the implications of taking the cube of a weakly 1-absorbing prime ideal. Specifically, if a weakly 1-absorbing prime ideal I of a ring A is not a 1-absorbing prime ideal, then the ideal generated by its cube, I^3, is both 2-absorbing and annihilation-prime in A. Additionally, if a ring A contains a proper principal annihilation-prime ideal P, then P^3 is 2-absorbing. Furthermore, if a ring A contains a weakly 1-absorbing prime ideal I, then its cube I^3 is 2-absorbing, implying that A/I is a field or a two-element field.

The fraction of uncertainty systematic is dominated by modeling in the signal and background.  A total of $2.063\ \text{fb}^{-1}$, obtained from $J/\psi$ decree, was utilized in this research.  The number of $K K \pi$ events observed is in agreement with expectations.  And  the calculated branching fractions for the two types of decree.

This paper outlines a technique known as cross-correlation lag measurement that enables rapid estimation of image similarities, whether full or limited in scope. Correlation strength and timing are both leveraged to enhance this approach, yielding improved accuracy. A modified version of FastCorr, leveraging a tree-based data structure and signal decomposition, has been developed and demonstrated with a 1000 times speedup over a reference implementation for specific use cases in Gravitational Wave and cross-correlation lag research. Additionally, FastCorr 2 is described, which incorporates a combination of legacy and innovative methods to calculate cross-correlations between two images, ultimately accelerating computations by a significant margin.

In recent years, researchers have shown significant interest in applying relational machine learning techniques to problems in pharmacology, including both chemical and pharmacological entities. To track and compare the performance of these models in a consistent manner, we have developed a new dataset of tasks and evaluation method. We have also conducted an extensive evaluation of models on this dataset, highlighting several important issues in the field that we believe will guide future work and further investigation.

To effectively track road conditions, which vary by location and state, large-scale data collection is essential. Our proposed method utilizes smartphone users to detect wet roads through a specific algorithm. As a result, we've gathered over 10 million data points across 45 countries, enabling comprehensive global road condition monitoring. This approach has successfully enabled us to map wet roads at a country level in five nations. Integrating this algorithm into navigation apps allows drivers to receive real-time warnings about potentially slippery roads. Moreover, by partnering with government agencies, it's possible to collect road condition data at a state or country level, supporting public policies and initiatives.

Current imitation learning techniques operate under the assumption that expert and agent environments are consistent with each other. Nevertheless, this assumption is often not met in practical applications, leading to a scenario where the policies being learned don't align with those of the experts. To address this challenge, we propose a novel method that accounts for and mitigates the effects of domain discrepancies. We do this by modeling the domain shift as a series of perturbations and designing our approach to identify optimal corrections for the expert actions within the agent's environment. This enables us to learn a policy that better aligns with the experts, even when they are not directly applicable in the agent's context. We experimentally evaluate the effectiveness of our method and compare it to existing imitation learning baselines across various tasks, including control and visual tasks, under both known and unknown domain shift conditions. Additionally, our method has a beneficial side effect of reducing the risk of overfitting that plagues current imitation learning techniques.

Our analysis of a new, isolated sub-arcminute millimeter-wave telescope's data has led to the identification of three dense clumps in the L1542 gas cloud, which is part of a gas cloud complex near the formation of the L1498/485 protostar pair. By analyzing the motion of these clumps, our research indicates the presence of a rotating, L-shaped structure within the L1542 cloud, which is consistent with the formation of a gas cloud and is supported by a dense central clump at a rate of one object per 100 years.
