Salient object detection methods using deep learning have been extensively studied, with a focus on detecting key objects in RGB and RGB-D images. Deep models are required to effectively utilize information from multiple channels in RGB-D images but often struggle when applied to RGB images with just three channels. This discrepancy has led to many models being developed separately for RGB and RGB-D images. In this paper, we address this issue by proposing a novel framework that integrates feature extraction for both types of images by introducing an additive channel fusion module within our unified structure. By sharing components processing RGB and RGB-D images, we enhance efficiency and adaptability to various input conditions. Additionally, we develop a novel depth-salience correlation module and an image-enhancement module to account for depth-salience relationships and mitigate image degradation caused by the Max-Salience DeSaliation (MSDS) loss. Experiments on six publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that our model outperforms existing methods adapted from other salient object detection techniques and excels on salient region detection tasks utilizing depth information.

This paper outlines ABUSI, a system that competed in the 2020 TwAb Challenge, an online data challenge focused on identifying and classifying harmful content in online spaces. ABUSI excelled among the top-5 systems in the competition, achieving a score of.7941 in detecting abusive content in tweets and .8109 in categorizing its severity. We will detail ABUSI's approach to detecting and severity scoring of abusive content, and then discuss how the model was fine-tuned to maximize performance on the competition dataset.

Ivanov and Karpenko investigated various types of palindromic numbers, including those that can be formed by reversing the digits of certain integers in a different base system. They found that unrepresentable palindromic numbers with these characteristics have a dense logarithmic approach-zeroing function. We built upon their work by investigating palindromic numbers that feature specific sequences of digits, or "atoms," in different bases. Their method can be applied to investigate "thin" sets of palindromic numbers, such as those that are divisible by a specific sequence of digits, or those that contain certain sequences of digits, $b^{k_1}, \ldots, b^{k_m}$, in base $b$. To understand the growth rate of unrepresentable integers with these characteristics, we developed general techniques for doing so that are not limited to logarithmic growth rates. These methods are particularly useful for studying growth rates of unrepresentable integers that do not grow logarithmically. We also modified Ivanov and Karpenko's ideas to establish corresponding results for integers with specific sequences of digits in their base-$b$ representations.

We introduce a novel, conditional generative model for reconstructing CT images from low-dose scans that's capable of handling a variety of noise types. The model takes a sparse projection as input and directly outputs a volumetric image in 3D space. A key aspect of our approach is its ability to condition on the degree of noise present in the input data, enabling it to adapt to different levels of degradation. The model is conditioned not just by a single type of noise but also by various degrees of that noise, which is achieved through a continuous autoencoder that maps a latent noise state to a 3D CT volumetric image from a low-dose CT scan. The conditional model is then used in a 3D GAN framework for image reconstruction. The model is able to accurately replicate the characteristics of the high-quality scan that produced the corresponding noise state. The ability of our method to condition on a continuous noise state allows for a more accurate reconstruction of the underlying high-quality scan, rather than simply producing a noisy output similar to the low-dose scan. The ability to control the level of noise in the input also allows for better image quality in reconstructions of very low-dose scans that would otherwise be heavily affected by artifacts.

We apply Bayesian Program Learning to the task of generating handwriting from as few as five samples per person. By modeling handwriting movements as a sequence of nested functions, our approach allows us to discover both the specific characteristics of an individual's writing style and the underlying components of each character. These components, in turn, are parameterized by a distribution that can be conditioned on to produce consistent, natural-looking instances. This model is particularly effective at capturing multi-modal variability in writing, enabling the generation of diverse but consistent handwriting. Our results demonstrate its ability to produce realistic, natural-looking handwriting even with the minimum amount of data available.

A new approach is presented for creating multi-nucleon matrix elements using an extended U(3) label system. This method enables direct creation of matrix elements without the need for an intermediate representation. By leveraging SU(3) symmetry properties, it also permits the reuse of matrix elements between different three-nucleon states. This scheme enables the generation of three-nucleon interaction matrix elements with fewer memory requirements and computational time, specifically reducing the need to ~50% and time, respectively, of previously observed values. Furthermore, it can be applied directly without modification for nucleon-specific matrix elements.

Quantum electronics is evolving into a leading field of research that requires comprehension of both classical and quantum electronic phenomena. By applying advanced entanglement methods to electronic systems, researchers can gain deeper insights into various quantum-electronic systems. This paper examines how these methods contribute to various applications, including multi-quantum bit circuits, single-quantum bit charge pumps, and measurement of quantum currents. The results demonstrate that modern quantum electronics can be effectively analyzed using principles from quantum information theory, thereby providing valuable tools for the study of this intricate field.

Let's consider a relatively well-behaved, bounded, three-dimensional space and another space where functions can be evaluated at points within this space. We're interested in understanding the effect of certain transformations, called composition operators, that map the first space to the second. Under specific conditions, we found that most of these composition operators have significant flaws when trying to maintain their injectivity, and even when they succeed, they still fail to preserve a key property known as compactness. We further explored how the complexity of functions that interact well with these operators on the edge of our initial space, and discovered that a non-trivial situation arises when functions create non-trivial 'platforms' right at the boundary, and this in turn influences whether the associated composition operators can be considered compact or not.

All-order estimates for two-loop corrections to twist-four operators in string theory have been found, specifically for operators with non-strange components, and this information has been used to calculate the anomalous dimensions associated with such operators in type-0 string theory, in the limit where the number of colors goes to infinity, up to twist eight. The findings are in line with previously calculated results for twist-five operators, in terms of the correction parameter.

In high-performance computing on GPU systems, efficient allocator design is vital. Existing GPU allocators, however, often lead to suboptimal use of coherient and unified memory types, resulting in increased latency. Moreover, they can cause the Bank Conflict issue, which hinders memory access efficiency. To address these limitations, we propose an in-house GPU memory allocator called DynaSOAr, which caters to the specific needs of AI workload acceleration. DynaSOAr optimizes allocation by using private and shared memory efficiently and can handle large allocations within shards. By doing so, it substantially reduces Bank Conflict occurrences. Furthermore, our system is capable of fast reset, leading to a 1.57x performance improvement. Compared to state-of-the-art allocators, DynaSOAr achieves a 1.11-1.57x performance gain.

We investigate a U(1)_X model that explains both dark matter and the muon anomaly, while also evading stringent laboratory and astrophysical constraints. With the introduction of two Isospin-breaking Higgs fields and one L_μ - L_τ fermion doublet, our model achieves dark matter explanation through fermion-mediated spin-independent scattering, while producing the correct thermal relic density via Coherent Destruction of Higgs portals. The model achieves evasion of stringent constraints from direct detection experiments by generating Isospin violation between dark matter and nucleons. It further explains the muon anomaly through Coherent Enhancement of muon-photon coupling at the loop level, a level of enhancement that could potentially exceed experimental constraints while satisfying muon anomaly fit requirements. We demonstrate Coherent Enhancement can be as large as ~10^4 without violating experimental constraints, a level of enhancement sufficient to explain the muon anomaly without needing large Isospin violation.

A crucial aspect of building straw tubes is pre-tension, which is directly related to the mechanical properties of the straw tube material. An essential step in constructing a straw tube detector involves determining the minimum pre-tension based on the straw tube's dimensions and material. Before final production begins, it is necessary to validate the pre-tension through rigorous mechanical testing. By utilizing a dedicated testing apparatus, this research provides an accurate measurement of minimum pre-tension in straw tubes. A mathematical model is developed to predict pre-tension, taking into account the influence of pre-tension on the straw tube's internal diameter. By applying this model, internal diameter and pre-tension can be treated as interdependent variables. After introducing the assumption that the straw tube's deformation is linearly related to pre-tension, this research provides a theoretical method for calculating minimum pre-tension, which is then verified by comparing model results with actual measurements for the K2K pre-fabricated straw tubes.

The effectiveness of deep learning models in real-world settings is heavily dependent on the accuracy of their assumptions about the world parameters. We've developed a method that measures how resilient a model's decisions are to uncertainty in those parameters. The quantity considered calculates the minimum confidence a model has in its choice when it encounters the most misleading scenario possible. We have established a connection between this measure and adversarial robustness by showing that the most misleading scenario can often be found extremely close to the model's training data. We have also created a method for computing this scenario using an inner-loop optimization technique. The method relies on approximating the model's behavior using tangent linear models and their duals. We've developed efficient algorithms for calculating these duals using techniques like Fenchel-Legendre transformation and stochastic gradient descent. These methods can be used to train models to resist uncertainty in parameters. We've tested our method on models predicting structure from images and models making decisions about object categories, and compared its performance to other methods that make models more robust to common data issues.

We investigate the impact of an oscillating impurity on a supersolid by numerically solving the damped phonon-boson impurity model with quantum Monte Carlo. As a result of the oscillation, phonon modes are no longer dispersionless but exhibit oscillatory behavior. In the long-wavelength limit, this oscillation occurs at a finite frequency. In the short-wavelength limit, this frequency converges to a non-zero value and matches the impurity oscillation frequency. Introducing an external driving force at the oscillation frequency amplifies all phonon modes and increases their response, particularly at the roton minimum. This enhanced response is analogous to light-matter coupling in optomechanics.

A generalised quadrangle is a specific type of neighbour-transitive code on a graph, consisting of all points and panels, where each panel connects two points. We will determine all possible weight distributions for this code type.

The central region of the Milky Way harbors numerous young stellar objects and exhibits numerous massive stellar clusters. These young stars share a common origin, as evidenced by shared ages and isotopic signatures. Observations using radio, optical, and infrared wavelengths have provided valuable insights into the central molecular zone's (CMZ) physical characteristics. The scale of the central molecular zone is around 100 parsecs. The zone's density structure is highly anisotropic, with varying anisotropy at different scales. The anisotropy is most pronounced on smaller anisotropies and decreases with larger anisotropies. The anisotropy is also observed in other regions of the Galactic plane. The physical, chemical, and temporal evolution of the central molecular zone is still not fully understood. The zone is thought to be the product of multiple, perpendicular compressive forces. The study of the central molecular zone is crucial to understanding the physical and temporal evolution of the central molecular zone and the central molecular zone is a common feature in galaxies. Our study examines the ultra-fast modifications in electrical and optical properties of metallic nickel induced by high-energy pulses, utilizing a multi-scale approach. 
We show that the redistribution of electrons significantly affects the non-linear absorption changes, even at high fluence levels where it cannot be ignored. 
We also investigate and find limitations of the standard approach based on the two-temperature model, particularly its failure to accurately model absorption variations. 
Through solving the resulting system of equations with finite differences, we obtain the modified reflectivity and transmittivity of the material. 
We also consider the impact of electron diffusion on modeling accuracy and find that it has a substantial influence on the absorbed energy and hence, a crucial factor that needs to be taken into account.

In the field of nanoelectronics, temperature is a critical factor. However, traditional temperature specifications are insufficient for nanoscale systems. In response to this, researchers have developed a novel temperature-sensing technique based on the fluctuation-dissipation theorem. By applying Arimoto's inequality and taking quantum effects into account, they determined the limit on accurate temperature measurement and found that it significantly differs from standard classical limits. Through simulation, they demonstrated the proposed method achieves high-resolution temperature measurement in the range of 10 mK and an accuracy within ±5%. By optimizing the voltage probe, they improved accuracy by up to 1000-fold, surpassing standard sensor specifications. This technique was applied to measure the temperature of a quantum dot and yielded a remarkable result of distinguishing a 1 mK change at 65 femto-Kelvin resolution, making it approximately four orders of magnitude below previously recorded values.

We use the quantum scissors technique to create complex entangled states of over 1000 multipartite polarized photon clusters, utilizing an efficiently detectable technique to count photons. This method leverages a highly entangled polarized photon pair source created via spontaneous parametric down-conversion and combines it with a tailored beam splitter to produce higher-order Fock states. We also developed a technique for improved efficiency using two down-converters and demonstrated its effectiveness in producing cluster states of up to 15 photons with a 13-photon probability of 2.1%. Although a direct application of quantum computing was not demonstrated, we inquired about the potential scalability of our method in generating large-scale quantum computing circuits.

For a parameter $\epsilon > 0$, we investigate the problem of determining online distance-preserving spanners with a specific structure. A distance-preserving spanner $H=(V\cup S, E)$ consists of a set of Steiner points $S$ and a weight function that ensures that the weight of the shortest path in $H$ between any two vertices $u,v \in V$ is within a $(1+\epsilon)$ factor of the distance between $u$ and $v$ in the original metric space. Within the algorithm's online framework, vertices $V$ are given incrementally, one at a time, and we aim to find the most efficient algorithm that uses the smallest possible number of Steiner points.

We make significant progress in understanding online distance-preserving spanners in one and higher dimensional settings. For one dimensional environments, we demonstrate that by incorporating Steiner points, the complex hierarchy of $(1+\epsilon)$-online spanners transforms into a more straightforward hierarchy where each level is proportional to $\epsilon^{-1}$. Conversely, in higher dimensional settings, we find that even with the inclusion of Steiner points, any $(1+\epsilon)$-online spanner exhibits exponential growth in its complexity, with a lower bound of $\epsilon^{-O(1/\epsilon)}$.

This study delves into the practical aspects of reducing costs associated with IoT device misclassification in coverage areas. We have developed a method to establish a threshold for the error tolerance level in order to minimize misclassification risks. We have also derived a formula that quantifies the risk of misclassifying devices and another formula that calculates the overall risk associated with coverage areas. Furthermore, a two-phase approach has been proposed to tackle the risk and cost-constrained problem of IoT device discovery. We have further examined a special case in which the risk is evenly spread across coverage areas and in which only the cost is a constraint. This study's findings are validated through theoretical proof and a comprehensive numerical analysis.

The original proof by D'Andrea and Hartonas of Godel algebra-duality is revised and adapted to an alternative formulation. This reformulated theorem establishes a dual relationship between finite Godel algebras and finite forests. A simplified, combinatorial demonstration of this result is presented.

Machine translation models require large amounts of parallel text data to function properly, and this requirement poses a significant challenge in many research fields.  Despite this challenge, new methods continue to emerge to tackle alignment problems in areas such as ancient texts, code, and non-aligned data, where finding parallel sentences is particularly difficult.  We investigate whether modern neural machine translation models can be adapted to process alignments between texts that don't come in matching pairs.  We propose a novel approach to training alignments without paired data and evaluate it against a traditional model on the task of translating Greek sentences.  The results indicate that our method is comparable to well-established tools, and further analysis reveals it to be slightly more accurate and efficient than its competitors.  We also demonstrate that a neural machine translation model trained on a small collection of Greek sentences can perform as well as one trained on a much larger corpus when paired with accurate parallel sentences.  We propose two strategies to maximize the effectiveness of machine translation models with limited training data.

The paper introduces an asynchronous block-iterative decomposition algorithm drawn from the relaxation theory of iterative methods. It uses the Chebyshev method as a guide and applies it to solve large linear systems efficiently. Testing with large scale models from a CFD simulation validates the method's performance benefits, particularly over the conventional iterative and conjugate gradient gradient methods.

We investigate the potential for detecting stellar-evolved PBMs in the Gaia database, specifically focusing on a region around 1.5 kiloparsecs from the center of the galaxy, various regions in the galaxy, and the galaxy itself, comparing the power of different detection methods. We find that the number of PBMs that can be found in an individual field of view is comparable to, or even exceeds, the number of stellar-evolved PBMs detected in an individual field of view, depending on the assumed mass distribution. Furthermore, the total number of PBMs that can be detected in the galaxy is estimated to be significantly higher than the total number of stellar-evolved PBMs that can be detected in the galaxy, with a range of $10^4$ to $10^5$ events. We find that the total predicted number of events is most sensitive to the assumed mass distribution, with a range of $10^3$ to $10^5$ events depending on the distribution, with a mean mass of $30 M_{\odot}$ leading to a total of $10^4$ events. We find that the total predicted number of events is generally higher than the total predicted number of events for stellar-evolved PBMs, with a factor ranging from $10$ to $10^2$.

By combining experimental data for hard dimer systems with numerical data for hyperfrustrated Ising models, a mapping has been established between the two systems, enabling the prediction of multiple phase transitions in a wide range of conditions. Specifically, a phase transition at 0.5 packing density results in structure formation, characterized by a periodic arrangement of polar crystalline patterns. At higher packing densities, two additional, frustrated crystalline phases emerge, exhibiting a polar and non-polar crystalline structure, respectively.

We have positive zonal functions $f$ on $\R^n$, and we have seen that under standard differentiation and integration operations, the positive definiteness of $f$ is preserved. Specifically, any standard integration of $f$ yields a function with positive definiteness, and the same holds for the result of applying any positive integer order differentiation to $f$. We have seen that these operations can be generalised to real numbers by breaking them down into a combination of integrations and differentiations, during which the positive definiteness of $f$ may not be preserved. We have shown a method of applying any real order operation, such as the fractional differentiation or integration, while preserving the positive definiteness of $f$. We have also found that the results of these operations can be expressed in terms of Gamma functions and hypergeometric functions.

A unique technique, quantum imaging, enables the interactive exploration of both sensitive and insensitve objects via a specialized form of interferometry. The proposed method, based on a simple and adaptable setup, facilitates interaction-free imaging without requiring complex experimental conditions. It leverages the principles of contextuality to produce clear pictures of objects that don't interact with the measurement process. Key features, including the difference in measurement contexts and non-termed observables, are demonstrated through specific examples. Contextuality-enhanced resolution significantly improves non-interaction imaging, and this improvement can be visually seen as a variation in the reconstructed image based on the degree of contextuality. Our results show that a 50% improvement in imaging resolution can be achieved through contextuality, and the technique even allows for a distinction between 'weak' and'strong' detection methods. Moreover, a novel approach to 'interactive free' imaging can be implemented by considering the partial transparency of the object, which can be fully interactively reconstructed through weighted integrals. The principle of contextuality underpins and improves non-interaction imaging process significantly.

To analyze the complex structure of foam, researchers employ a novel approach, describing the platform as the boundary between unconnected bubbles and identifying a Rugh factor that quantifies this platform's surface area. Through simulations of 2D and 3D deformable foam models, they demonstrate that this approach captures key characteristics of liquid foam, including its nearly plastic flow behavior, which causes the Rugh factor to plateau at an early stage of relaxation. Additionally, this method can discern distinct phases within various foam models, highlighting its versatility for studying materials with intricate internal structures.

This research presents an ensemble method based on convolutional neural networks, designed to improve accuracy and robustness for image classification tasks. By training multiple CNN models with different architectures and inputs, and aggregating their predictions through a voting mechanism, our proposed approach achieves superior performance and robustness compared to individual models. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method by achieving high accuracy for several benchmark datasets, including Fashion MNIST, EMNIST, and STMNIST.

Researchers employed ab-initio random phase approximation calculations to investigate the optical properties of monoclinic sodium. No significant structural or band structure modifications were detected when comparing results with experimentally validated metallic models. Notably, the "dipolar" electron-hole excitations exhibited a 10% mass enhancement, whereas the "monopole" hole excitations displayed a 4% enhancement in the $T$-matrix cross-sections. Additionally, a comparable 10% mass enhancement was found in the monopole hole excitations using a dipolar electron interaction. The researchers also validated that the "dipolar" excitations constitute the majority of electron-hole responses for wave vectors with a magnitude less than 0.5. Finally, the structural factor derived from the $T$-matrix was found to significantly differ from the standard approximation that neglects exchange and correlation effects.

We draw a clear line between dissipated work and the amount of internal work
done on a specific microstate, and we demonstrate that this concept of dissipated
work can be applied to both classical and quantum systems, even when varying
protocols or initial states are considered. Our approach clarifies and generalizes
previous theories of dissipated work and en熵, and we provide a new formula
for calculating the dissipated work in quantum systems that were initially in
mixed states.

Cotangent bundle cases in quantization often demonstrate a more intricate relationship with $Q$-deformation. Investigating the expression of curvature weights for cotangent bundle cases helps clarify how curvature contributes to Q-deformed expressions. This expression is also useful for putting Q-deformed expressions into a more manageable form. This expression is along the lines of the Birman-Kontsevich expression but with an additional factor related to a function that can be any smooth function on the underlying manifold, thus increasing its applicability. This new expression has potential to be extended to broader classes of manifolds.

In studies of Hertzian chains, two nonlinear frequencies emerge from exponentially small terms, each associated with a distinct Hertzian response, resulting in complex interactions. When connected by springs, these chains exhibit two distinct response patterns, leading to oscillating solitary waves that persist over extended periods. These peculiar patterns are driven by the product of two small factors and have been found to be in close agreement with theoretical models. The outcome of this research reveals an new approach to understanding complex interactions between small factors in the study of solitary waves, leading to new theories that were previously unexplored. Notably, this study also uncovers previously unknown oscillating solutions in near-homogeneous media.

A dynamic approach to non-Gaussian primordial fluctuations is developed and applied to multi-field inflation with sharp features in the potential. The method is based on a differential technique that linearizes the inflationary dynamics and identifies the nonlinear characteristics of the adiabatic mode. It is then used to analyze the signatures of sharp features in multi-field inflationary dynamics and their impact on observable signatures, particularly the distinctive signatures of features in angular correlations of primordial non-Gaussianities. The method effectively captures the signatures of features in the non-local contributions to adiabatic non-Gaussianities, which can be separated into distinct local and non-local components. The non-local contributions can be expressed in terms of two-point correlations of adiabatic features, enabling an efficient calculation through a parametric representation. The method is applied to a class of sharp features in potential-driven inflationary dynamics, which are driven by multi-field dynamics and can be characterized by their mass and amplitude. The results of the approximation are then compared to full results from in-situ simulations, which demonstrate its effectiveness in capturing the signatures of features in angular correlations and non-Gaussianities.

The accordion graph class $A[n,k]$ is an arrangement of $(k+2)$ quadrilaterals of increasing size, where $n$ represents the largest size and $k$ the number of internal quadrilaterals. It can be represented as $K_{2,2,...,2}$ with a partition of $2k+4$ vertices into two sets of sizes $n$ and $4+2k-2n$. We demonstrate that $2n-4 \le k$ results in a non-circulant accordion graph and provide a circulant representation for such graphs, discussing their uniqueness. Furthermore, we establish a one-to-one correspondence between a certain subfamily of accordion graphs and a larger class of topological graphs, where vertices are located on the outer boundary and all internal edges and quadrilateral faces lie within a unit disk.

In a two-dimensional non-circumferential quantum walk with a deterministic trajectory, we examine the spatial distribution of particle density as measured by the participation ratio, particularly in the case where the detrapping angle is closely approached, which typically results in localized walk behavior. We observe that, in the short term, the participation ratio increases exponentially with time up to a maximum value, which, as the detrapping angle is approached more closely, moves further out in the short term. Beyond a certain threshold, the participation ratio starts to decline. Our analysis also demonstrates that the participation ratio is influenced by the initial state vector, and we examine the participation ratio for a specific scenario where the trajectory becomes critically localized, finding that it exhibits a distinct pattern in its evolution.

Recent findings from self-supervised pretraining have surpassed supervised pretraining as a method for training Vision Transformers. In this preprint, we investigated how self-supervised methods utilize the structure of class information in the Clarity of Hierarchy (CoH) framework. Through class attention analysis, we found that self-supervised methods capture high-level class relationships but struggle with fine-grained relationships due to the absence of labels. To address this limitation, we developed supervision via Attention-guided Distillation (AD), a method that uses cluster centers as supervised signals for fine-grained attention. The AD technique enhances self-supervision by incorporating supervised information while preserving the cluster structure that self-supervision excels at capturing. In our best scenario, we found that AD successfully improves the Cluster Quality Score (CQS) of DINO by 10.6% and Day-Networks (DiNe) based on DINO by 13.3%, respectively.

A recent preprint introduced a viscous cosmological model that interprets the acceleration of the universe's expansion in relation to Finsler's fundamental model of a relativistic viscous fluid. By applying the Raychaudhuri equation, we have developed an analytical model for cosmological data and have verified its consistency with Hubble, Supernova, and Planck data. We have derived key universal parameters from a linear fit and further supported our model by comparing it with dark energy models using a description deficiency measure. Results show that our model performs similarly to some dark energy models in terms of its effectiveness. Model predictions indicate a transition from deceleration to acceleration, consistent with an early inflationary period and acceleration due to viscosity's time-dependent increase. This suggests an early influence of viscosity and a dominant effect due to increased model entropy in the later stages of cosmological evolution.

The Cauchy problem for incompressible Euler equations exhibits a phenomenon of non-smooth solution development, regardless of the initial condition, when considered in dimensions d≥3. This paper demonstrates that for any target level of non-smoothness, there exists a corresponding initial condition that will trigger it. As the degree of non-smoothness increases towards smooth solutions, the degree of non-smoothness in its corresponding initial condition will also increase in a corresponding manner. This was made possible through a combination of three key components: (a) an enhancement of the 2-bump function method to 3-bump function, (b) an application of a modified version of a technique by Koliha and Oh, and (b) a refined application of a bootstrap argument.

Artists play a crucial role in controlling the creative process. In line with this, we introduce Stable Artist, an approach that enhances user control over image creation, enabling users to establish their own artistic style and predetermined marking criteria. Able to function on the Stable Diffusion model, Stable Artist enables users to guide the image generation process with greater precision through artist-like techniques such as variational Markov Decision Processes and domain adaptation. Moreover, we refine the Artist's capabilities by introducing methods that address the challenges associated with artist-like approaches in the image creation process. Moreover, we refine the Artist's capabilities by developing self-correcting and ensemble methods that mitigate the limitations associated with artist-like approaches. Deep learning's appeal lies in its ability to outperform other methods on various tasks, but its uncertainty quantification methods are often unyielding, making them unsuitable for life-critical applications. A more rigorous probabilistic approach is required to tackle this uncertainty quantification challenge. We introduce a QLRP method that incorporates a prior and loss function into the training process to enable memory-efficient, simultaneous training and evaluation of predictive model uncertainty. Our results show that using the QLRP method with the ELBO and KL divergence provides the most accurate uncertainty estimates, as validated by multiple evaluation metrics and universal uncertainty calibration tests.

A new analysis of the $J/\psi$ decay into invisible particles provides an enhanced sensitivity to a specific nucleome-dark matter interaction within a simplified model. This study establishes tighter constraints on the cross-section between dark matter and nucleons, particularly for masses below the $J/\psi$ mass, accounting for the influence of non-resonant background through a divided sample analysis that enhances resolution. Consideration of the $\psi(2S)$ contributes to more precise limits. These findings are also relevant for detecting light dark matter, offering a complementary approach to existing searches by NA48, NA62, and NA62 for cross-section detection.

The objective of this study is to examine the movement and other characteristics of magnetic bright points (MBPs) in a solar observation, by analyzing the data provided by the Solar Dynamics Observatory's Helioseismic and Magnetic Imager instrument in the vicinity of a solar region (AR11429) that exhibited rapid development in the sunspot number. An advanced detection method based on the invariance of the optical flow field and the non-linear gradient is employed to identify and track the movement of magnetic bright points. The statistical analysis of their temporal movement and brightness changes indicates that all components of their movement and brightness follow a lognormal distribution pattern. Furthermore, these magnetic bright points exhibit an elliptical shape and display a diverse range of movement behaviors, with velocities ranging from 100 to 1000 meters per second. Their temporal brightness changes reveal that they follow a gamma distribution, with their mean brightness increasing over time.

The observation of dynamic processes is fundamental to our existence, yet existing vision challenges fail to effectively address this fundamental aspect, primarily because they rely on a singular, static camera and videos with redundant frames. These issues stem from unnecessary time and a lack of naturalistic lighting, which also makes them problematic. These problems are particularly pronounced in datasets that focus on a single subject, but the impact is even more significant when analyzing a larger group. These limitations have a direct correlation with limitations in the representation of human diversity. To overcome these constraints, we introduce a novel micro-movie-based framework for action recognition, which not only clarifies the fundamental role of dynamics in human visual perception but also enhances our understanding of racial representation. Our micro-movie-based approach achieves state-of-the-art results on three prominent action recognition benchmarks and offers a new, more natural representation of human actions, particularly rich in skin tone representation.

We've used the functional Schrödinger method to find a bound state solution for a Dirac monopole in a constant magnetic field. It was discovered that the Monopole-Harmonic field can restrict the monopole's natural wideation, effectively creating a bound state. Calculations of the monopole's mass and radius as functions of the B-field are presented. Additionally, it's been found that bound states of higher levels exist and their masses and radii also depend on the B-field. Their masses and radius are also investigated. It's been found that both monopoles and dyons exhibit similar behavior.

Deep learning based weather forecasting models have emerged as a leading approach, with several recent studies evaluating and comparing these methods. We undertake further evaluations of these models to address gaps identified in previous research, focusing on the impact of using a labeled dataset and normalizing the data, which are not universally applied in these studies. Our analysis indicates that both factors contribute significantly to accurate weather forecasting, with these considerations aiding in the standardization of model evaluation.

In a study of three-Higgs-doublet models, researchers investigate dark matter interactions via two interaction terms. The study reveals a significant relationship between the mass of the spin-0 particle that the dark matter interacts with and the CP violation in the dark matter interaction. Consequently, when CP is violated, the dark matter mass is confined within a narrower range. However, this limitation can be circumvented if the CP violation is minimal, thus allowing the dark matter mass to occupy a broader range. Furthermore, a broader dark matter mass range can be achieved by the dark matter interacting with multiple spin-0 particles.

A modified version of the PPT square conjecture, drawing from results of Schumacher and Verstraete, has led to significant advancements. The PPT pret transpose operation, defined for matrices with positive semi-definite conjugate pairs as elements, has been proven to constitute a well-defined nonlinear map across all matrix spaces with positive semi-definite conjugate pairs as elements. By leveraging the properties of the PPT pret transpose operation, which is idempotent and involution, we can derive an expression for the PPT square, which is defined as the PPT pret transpose of the matrix squared. The resulting formula for the PPT square, which is structurally analogous to the PPT singular value decomposition, provides a comprehensive and concise method for a full-scale PPT spectral decomposition. This novel approach has profound implications for understanding the mathematical theory of nonlinear transformations, as it facilitates a thorough analysis of the spectral properties of the PPT square, which is essential for a comprehensive understanding of its structure, applications, and relationships.

The efficient delivery of cargo to remote synapses in branched neurons relies on a carefully controlled system governed by the properties of motor proteins, the structure of microtubules and cellular organelles. Our study investigates the relationship between the mechanical structure of F-actin and microtubules and the transport efficiency of molecular cargo in a model system, utilizing a type of mismatched microtubules and fixed orientation and investigating how structural variations affect transport dynamics and efficiency. The results reveal that certain structural configurations of microtubules can enhance long-distance transport while others lead to a transition between different diffusion patterns, depending on the type of cargo. Our findings suggest that the mechanical structure of microtubules plays a crucial role in regulating intracellular transport processes.

In the realm of complex banking transactions, identifying fraudulent patterns is a challenging task. We introduce a novel approach called Fraudulent Graph Fraudulent Learning (FGFL), which utilizes Graph Convolutional Networks on artificially generated graphs to enhance fraud detection. To create realistic graphs in line with the constraints of banking transaction rules, we employ a innovative graph generation technique based on Euler paths. The efficacy of FGFL in accurately classifying novel and existing categories of fraudulent transactions has been confirmed through thorough evaluations. Moreover, FGFL exhibits a high degree of flexibility in terms of vertex and edge features, and can even accurately detect unknown types of fraudulent transactions.

Mass transfer from a donor star to a supermassive black hole via an accretion disc can cause galaxy mergers and star formation. This process is initiated by the star's mass shedding due to gravitational waves and magnetic braking. Donor stars can lose mass through multiple mechanisms, including tidal disruption, which significantly affects the final black hole mass. This paper explores the impact of a white dwarf star's mass loss on supermassive black hole mass growth. If the black hole's accretion rate exceeds a certain threshold, which varies based on a coefficient $\beta$ and the rate of mass shedding, most of the ejected material is incorporated into the accretion disc. This leads to the conclusion that the traditional model of donor star mass loss is inaccurate. This finding applies to various types of donor stars, including main sequence stars and giant stars, which can be verified through detailed calculations in this work.

The study of CP violations in interactions between leptons and other particles is a vital area of research. A promising, underexplored area within this study involves the decay of third-generation leptons into multiple particles. Research into the tau lepton's decay into three particles has the potential to yield information on fundamental parameters that other processes at current facilities would fail to reveal. We investigate tau decays into three neutrons and neutrinos, a rare process where we examine combinations of charge and CP symmetries, and energy distributions of observable particles. The analysis distinguishes between decays producing one or three neutrons from a B meson's decay. The latter, in particular, may be sensitive to certain parameters that other experiments would miss. The proposed analysis of these processes, utilizing data that current facilities like the Belle II, FCC-ee, and FCC-ee, could be able to collect, is expected to be able to measure parameters with high precision. This measurement is comparable to the most accurate measurements currently obtained by B meson decay experiments.

We identify the boundary of the convex set of all metrics defined by the symmetric Tversiny ratio models with real parameters $\alpha, \beta, \gamma, \delta$ nonnegative and sum to one. The points on this boundary are characterized by at least one parameter being zero, and we determine the structure of its topological closure, determining the extreme points of the set.

This paper presents a deconvolution network that utilizes a specialized refluent structure to separate a blurred image from its corresponding clear image. The network's REBlur module refines deconvolution operations by decomposing them into two distinct parts, which enhances its accuracy and adaptability to diverse blur types. Through experimental evaluation on established datasets, our proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art methods in multiple aspects.

Previous studies have demonstrated that an increasingly complex set of bistable enzymes in a chemical reaction network (CRN) can be captured by a linear circuit that mimics a learning neuron's membrane potential and plasticity, mimicking Hebbian learning in the brain. The following research expands upon an earlier algorithm, now a circuit-level approach, to show that a potential-based CRN can be constructed to model various forms of autonomous learning, reminiscent of the brain's behavior. By applying the circuit construction to a spiking neuron's membrane potential, we also develop a novel CRN algorithm that generates spontaneous and autonomous learning and memory of its equilibrium, mimicking the brain's plasticity. The concept of open completeness is a logical expansion to Ramsey theory that is based on the L\'evy hierarchy. We will define open completeness and examine how it applies to models of set theory. We will also investigate the relationship between the properties of a model and open completeness in its ultrapower. Specifically, models with a high degree of density will have the open completeness property reflected in their ultrapowers, while adding forcing Axiom COM[ℓ]+ will cause the model's and its non-measurable ultrapower's properties to coincide. However, if a model V has a measurable cardinal κ, then there is a P_κ^℘-generic filter G, for which the G-model is not open-complete.

In the era of data-driven science, benchmarking is crucial for guiding scientific discovery. This paper presents a novel, efficient benchmarking framework, suitable for numerical benchmarks of data-intensive scientific workflows.
